units.la: PRæclara, & memorabilis est apud Ciceronem libro. 1. de Oratore sententia, vsus frequens omnium artiū præcepta superat: nam, ut alio loco idem Cicero testatur, nec medici, nec imperatores, nec oratores, quamuis artis præcepta perceperint, quicquā magna laude dignum sine vsu & exercitatione cōsequi possunt. Vndè diuinus Plato in Gorgia sub persona Poli, & Aristoteles philosophorū princeps τῆς ἐμπειρίας experientiæ & vsui, tanquā præstantissimo magistro omnium artium & doctrinarum inventione & per-sectionem tribuere non dubitarunt. Quapropter toto coelo errant, & contra tentetiam[?] summorum philosophorum agunt, qui omne suum tempus, omnem operam & laborem in artium theorematis & praeceptis addiscendis ponunt: usum vero, qui praecipuus artium & doctrinarum finis constitui debet, vel omnino negligunt, vel obiter & frigide colunt. Nam illi perinde facete videntur, ac si agricola aliquis omne tempus & operam in agris colendis, arboribus ferendis, vitibus putandis consumeret: de fructibus vero colligendis, decerpendis, & recondendis vel nihil vel parum sollicitus esset. Tales itaque studijs suis male consulere, littus arare, imo oleum & operam perdere, nemo, opinor, sanæ mentis inficiabitur. Vt autem vsus in reliquis artibus & disci-plinis utilis & necessarius est: sic in logica plurimum utilitatis habet, & potissimum requiritur. Cum enim illa sit ὄργανον[?] ὀργάνων χεὶρ τῆς φιλοσοφίας artifex, magistra & dux reliquarum doctri-narum, narum,quis est,qui non intelligat ejus praecepta non solum cognoscenda & tenenda esse,sed etiam usu exercitatio-neque exploranda, ponderanda, & confirmanda. Visus vero ille non solum consistit in scholasticis de praeceptis cōtentionibus: sed etiam in intelligendis, resolvendis, ponderandis, explicandis & imitandis philosophis, poetis, oratoribus, historicis amplissimè versatur, atque tam late patet, ut Plato verissimè testatur, quàm ζῷον λόγον[?] sive vis rationis humanae. Neq; vero hoc quisquam mirari debet: etenim ut nō Gra-maticum aut oratorem eū definimus qui magna contentione de praeceptionibus Grammaticēs & Rhetorices disputare didicit: sed eum, qui istarum artium usum in bonis authoribus retexendis, cognoscendis & imitandis comprobat. Eodem modo logicum existimare debemus eum, qui artis usum lō-gè praestantissimum in omnibus hominibus bene differentibus explicandis, eorumque virtutibus exprimendis commonstrat. Ad talem tamque necessarium usum cum alij diligentes doctiq; viri dialecticam revocare laborarunt: tum vero Petrus Ramus indefatigabili studio, & admirabili industria contedit. Nam in totius vitæ cursu, qui ei certe laboriosissimus fuit, nihil tam spectavit, quam ut ex Aristotelicis & Socraticis principijs ejusmodi dialecticam deduceret, quæ non solum syllogismū conficere doceret, & modum in utràq; partem disputandi monstraret: sed etiā quæ usum suum per omnes philosophos, poëtas, oratores, historicos extenderet, & amplissimè demonstraret. Quid autem effecerit, & quàm operam bonis literis præstiterit, non est meum dicere: siquidem hoc ejus præclarissima ingenii monumenta aperte testantur, & doctissimi viri in Germania, Anglia, Gallia, Polonia testantur. Ejusmodi dialecticam cum te quoque, nobilissime Magne, expetere, ad eamque animum applicare non ignorem: imò te jam in ea nec parum, nec infeliciter processisse exploratum habeam, me non absre facturum esse visum est, si hanc meam lucubrationem logicam in tuo nomine apparere curarem: exiguam illam quidem, sed tamen amoris mei, qui in te est, & grati animi testimonium. Neque vero aliter animum inducere potuum, quam tibi hoc levidense munusculum gratum acceptumque futurum esse: idque ut faciam multis rebus adducor. Nam me non fugit te incredibili quadam bonarum literarum cupiditate ardere, easque, dum apud me fuisti, ita avide arripuisse, tanquam sitim diuturnam explere cupienti. Equidem ut tibi animi mei sensum aperiam, quoties de te, quoties de Petro Drechsleber-gio, Georgio Spiegelio, & Laurentio Muleno, quos familiariter novi, quoties de vestri similibus, de quibus audio, cogito: toties Daniae, regno nostra aetate florentissimo, non possum non gratulari, & bene ominari. Non solum enim illa Respub. beata censeri debet, in qua reges & principes viri sapiunt: sed etiam ea in qua nobilitate praestantes, qui seminariam, flos & columen regnorum sunt, florentem suam aetatem non in voluptatibus corporis, sed in studiis linguarum, & bonarum artium collocât & consumunt. Exiis siquidem tanquam ex abundantissimo fonte ratio rem recte prudenterque administrandi, tutandi, & conseruandi hauritur, & comparatur. Quæ cùm ita sint, nō posse dubitare quin hanc meam analysin logicam tuo nomini consecratam serena fronte sis accepturus, & etiam cōtra obtrectatorū morlus[?] defensurus. Idque eo magis quod nō nescius es me in eo potissimum elaborasse[?] ut artificium perpetua inuentionis dispositionisque serie continuatum docerem. Quod si quibusdam minus assecutus esse visus fuero, ij, si modò æqui rerum iudices & æstimatores esse voluerint, non mihi, non quam amplector[?], dialecticæ quaque sola tanquam instrumento usus sum: sed rei, circa quæ versatur noster labor, tribuent. Nā in hoc dialogo ordo interdum conturbatior, repetitiones crebriores, digressiones ad rem minus aptiores esse videntur: Id quod aperte & libere mecum fatetur testa-
units.tr: Cicero, in the first book of De Oratore, has a famous and memorable saying: frequent practice surpasses all the precepts of the arts. For, as the same Cicero testifies elsewhere, neither physicians, nor generals, nor orators, however well they have grasped the precepts of their art, can achieve anything worthy of great praise without practice and exercise. Hence the divine Plato, in the Gorgias, speaking through the character of Polus, and Aristotle, the prince of philosophers, did not hesitate to ascribe the invention and perfection of all arts and sciences to experience and practice, as to the most excellent teacher of all. Therefore they are utterly mistaken, and act contrary to the judgment of the greatest philosophers, who spend all their time, all their effort and labour, on learning the theorems and precepts of the arts, but either neglect practice altogether, which ought to be set up as the chief aim of the arts and sciences, or cultivate it in passing and coldly. For such people seem just as foolish as a farmer who spent all his time and effort on tilling his fields, planting trees and pruning vines, but cared little or not at all about gathering, picking and storing the fruit. No sane person, I think, would deny that such men do their studies no good: they are ploughing the shore, or rather wasting their oil and their labour. Just as practice is useful and necessary in the other arts and disciplines, so logic has very great usefulness and is especially required. For since logic is the instrument of instruments, the hand of philosophy, the skilled craftsman, the teacher and guide of the other sciences, who does not understand that its precepts must not only be known and held in memory, but also tested, weighed and confirmed by practice and exercise? This practice, moreover, does not consist only in the scholastic disputes about the precepts; it is also widely engaged in understanding, resolving, weighing, explaining and imitating philosophers, poets, orators and historians, and it extends as far as, as Plato rightly testifies, the reach of human reason itself. Nor should anyone be surprised at this. For just as we do not call a man a grammarian or an orator who has learned to dispute with great effort about the precepts of grammar and rhetoric, but rather the one who demonstrates the use of those arts in unfolding, understanding and imitating good authors, so we ought to regard as a logician the one who shows the most excellent use of the art in explaining all people who reason well, and in expressing their virtues. Other diligent and learned men have laboured to recall dialectic to this so necessary use, but Petrus Ramus strove for it with tireless zeal and admirable industry. For in the whole course of his life, which was certainly most laborious for him, he aimed at nothing so much as to derive from Aristotelian and Socratic principles such a dialectic as would not only teach how to construct a syllogism and show the method of disputing on either side, but would also extend its use through all philosophers, poets, orators and historians, and demonstrate it most fully. What he accomplished, and how much service he rendered to good letters, it is not for me to say; his most brilliant monuments of genius clearly bear witness to this, and the most learned men in Germany, England, France and Poland bear witness to it. Since I know that you too, most noble Magnus, seek this kind of dialectic and apply your mind to it, and indeed I have it as established that you have already made no small and not unsuccessful progress in it, I thought it not inappropriate to take care that this little logical work of mine should appear under your name: small indeed, but still a testimony of my love for you and of my grateful heart. Nor could I bring myself to think otherwise than that this slight little gift would be welcome and acceptable to you; and I am led to do this for many reasons. For I am not unaware that you burn with an incredible desire for good letters, and that while you were with me you seized them so eagerly, as one wishing to quench a long-standing thirst. Indeed, to open to you the feeling of my mind: as often as I think of you, of Peter Drechsleberg, George Spiegel and Laurence Mulenus, whom I know intimately, and as often as I think of men like you, of whom I hear, I cannot help rejoicing for Denmark, a kingdom flourishing in our age, and auguring well for it. For that commonwealth ought to be counted blessed not only in which kings and princes are wise, but also in which the outstanding men of the nobility, who are the seedbed, flower and pillar of kingdoms, spend and devote their flourishing age not to bodily pleasures but to the study of languages and the good arts. For from these men, as from a most abundant spring, the reason for managing, protecting and preserving affairs rightly and prudently is drawn and acquired. Since these things are so, I cannot doubt that you will receive this logical analysis of mine, consecrated to your name, with a serene brow, and will even defend it against the attacks of detractors. And this all the more because you are not unaware that I have laboured especially to teach the art as continuous through an unbroken sequence of invention and arrangement. If I should seem to have achieved less in some respects, those who are willing to be fair judges and evaluators of things will attribute this not to me, nor to the dialectic which I embrace and have used as my sole instrument, but to the subject with which our labour is concerned. For in this dialogue the order is at times more disturbed, the repetitions more frequent, and the digressions less fitting to the matter, as the author himself openly and freely confesses to me.

units.la: PRAEFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: testatur, & conquiritur clarissimus vir Hieronymus Wolfius, quem, ut par est, honoris causa nomino. Verba ejus hæc sunt: Si mihi, quod sentio dicere liceat: quædam ἀταξία & πολυλογία [?] in hoc dialogo esse videtur: inde fortassis orta, sive negotiis, sive valetudine, sive itinere aliquo impeditus, ex intervallis ad scribendum rediit. Hæc ille. Sed redeo ad te nobilissime Magne, tibique hanc meam qualemcunque lucubra-tionem dedico & inscribo: primò quia me non latet te hoc genere studiorum plurimum delectari: deinde ut sit perpetuum nostræ amicitiæ, quàm virtus, id est, idem bonarum literarum studiū contraxit, symbolum, & testimonium. Maximam verò spem habeo te, pro tua humanitate, amore, & meritis in me, hoc, μικρόν τι φίλον τι δῶρον [?] in bonā partem accepturum esse: quæ spes si me non fefellerit, maximum me ex hoc labore & vigiliis fructu accepisse arbitrabor. His igitur paucis, nobilissime Magne valebis me tui studiosissimum amabis in studiorum cursu, ut cœpisti, strenuè.
units.tr: So testifies and laments the most distinguished man Hieronymus Wolfius, whom I name out of due respect. His words are these: "If I may say what I think, there seems to be a certain disorder [ἀταξία] and wordiness [πολυλογία] in this dialogue. Perhaps it arose from this: he was hindered, either by business, or by ill health, or by some journey, and returned to writing at intervals." So he. But I return to you, most noble Magnus, and dedicate and inscribe to you this my little work, such as it is. I do so first because I am not unaware that you take great delight in this kind of study; and second, so that it may remain a lasting symbol and testimony of our friendship, which virtue, that is, the common pursuit of good letters, has united. Indeed I have the greatest hope that you, in your kindness, affection and goodwill toward me, will accept this, a little gift [μικρόν τι φίλον τι δῶρον], in good part. If that hope does not deceive me, I shall think I have gained the greatest fruit from this labour and these night-watches. And so, with these few words, most noble Magnus, farewell; love me, who am most devoted to you, and in the course of your studies, as you have begun, press on vigorously.

units.la: Tusimul & logicas omnes cotemseris artes, Nil quibus utilius maximus orbis habet; Sublato usu, contemnis scripta Platonis Spernus Aristotelis, qd monumeta docet. Scripsit Aristoteles, potius rationis ut usum, Monstraret, logices qua documenta tibi. His spretis pereunt, ta pulcre funditus artes Pressaq; sub pedibus, comoda multa jacet. Ergo nihil cures Momi studiosa juventus Scommata, nec dulci mista venena favo. Vix hominum quisqua ta fausto sidere natus Culparet quem non invida turba, fuit. Expediat tibi qd, reliqui diversa sequentes Quam quid vituperet, sit tibi cura prior. Atq; magis recta ductus ratione, & amore, Iudicio hoc totum conveniente legas.
units.tr: And if at the same time you have scorned all the logical arts, which the greatest world has nothing more useful than, and with its practice removed you despise the writings of Plato and scorn Aristotle, whom the monuments teach: Aristotle wrote so that he might show the use of reason, the lessons of logic by which you might be taught. Once these are spurned, the arts perish utterly and lie trampled underfoot, with many advantages lost. Therefore, studious youth, care for nothing of Momus' sneers, nor for poisons mixed with sweet honey. Scarcely any man was born under so fortunate a star that the envious crowd did not find fault with him. Let it be your first concern what profits you, not what others, pursuing different things, may find to blame. And being led more by right reason and by love, read this whole work with a judgment that agrees with it.

units.tr: If perhaps you scorn this study, reader, because of others' labours, I ask you to consider the good of it.

units.tr: When you see great volumes being written everywhere, read these few pages too, on the books of the ancients.

Atq; etiam post hac Latia Graiaq; Camœnæ, Quas habeant, per te fac retegantur opes. Ringetur reliqui, qd tū? tibi fortibus ausis. Nil obstet ceptum quin gradiaris iter. Nec invidos timeas morsus: meliora tenetur. Sit ua quis lacerat, jure docere tuis.
units.tr: Will the eager spirit of your students, dear to you, receive these verses with open brow and approve them? Go on, then, with this work for the study of schools, and fill them with the blessings they desire. And henceforth, let the Latin and Greek Muses reveal, through you, the riches they hold. Let the rest be disturbed by whatever it may be; by your brave daring, let nothing hinder you from pressing on along the road you have begun. Do not fear envious bites: better things are held in store. Let whoever tears you apart do so by right, and teach by your own.

Territa desidia ne in sœuam trasevat iram. Munere nō privet, quod dedit illa, cave. Nāq; et cura sagax, hæres et in artib. ardor. Arte quod occlusum est, id reserare valet. Tristia contemnens operi quæ tædia subsunt. Et simul aspersus munere, diva, tuo.
units.tr: Our life, as it grows, reproaches soft leisure, and the Muse cannot look upon it with a kindly light. When skilful Minerva has once chanced to see you at your studies and blessed you with a mind willing to work, do not let idleness, struck with fear, turn into savage anger, and do not, I warn you, deprive yourself of the gift she has given. For there is also a keen care, and in the arts an ardour that is heir to them. What has been shut up by art, art can unlock. Scorning the gloomy tedium that lies beneath the work, and sprinkled at the same time with your gift, goddess.

units.la: VINTVS Mutius Augur, Scævola multa narrare de C. Lelio socero suo memoriter, & jucundè solebat, nec dubitare illum in omni sermone appellare sapientem. Ego autem à patre ita erâ deductus ad Scævolam sumpta virili toga, ut quoad possem, & liceret à senis latere nunquam discederem. Itaque multa ab eo prudenter disputata, multa etiam breviter & commodè dicta memoriæ mandabam, fierique studebam eius prudentia doctior. Quo mortuo me ad pontificem Scævolâ contuli, quem unum nostræ civitatis & ingenio & industria
units.tr: Quintus Mucius the augur, Scaevola, used to tell many stories about his father-in-law Gaius Laelius, from memory and with pleasure, and he did not hesitate to call him wise in every conversation. As for me, I was taken by my father to Scaevola once I had assumed the toga of manhood, and as long as I could, and was allowed, I never left the old man's side. Thus I committed to memory the many things he discussed wisely, and the many things he said briefly and aptly, and I strove to become more learned through his prudence. When he died, I turned to the chief priest Scaevola, whom alone I dare to call the most outstanding of our state in both talent and diligence.

units.la: B præstantissimum audeo dicere. Sed de hoc alias, nunc redeo ad Augurem. Quum sæpe multa narraret, tu memi-ni domi in hemicyclo sedentem (ut solebat) quum & ego essem una & pauci admodum familiares, in eum sermo-nem incidere, qui tum fere multis erat in ore. Meministi enim profecto (ut o-pinor) Attice, & eo magis, quod P. Sul-pitio utebare, multum, quum is tribu-nus Pleb. capitali odio à Q. Pompeio, qui tum erat cosul, dissideret, qui cum conjunctissime & amantissime vixerat, quanta hominum esset vel admiratio, vel querela. Itaque tu Scævola, quum in eam ipsam mentionem incidisset, exposuit nobis sermonem Laelii de a-micitia habitum ab illo secum, & cum altero genero C. Fannio, Marci filio, paucis diebus post mortem Africani. Cuius disputationis sententias memoriæ mandavi, quas in hoc libro exposui meo arbitratu. Quasi enim ipsos in-troduxi loquentes ne inquam, & inquit sæpius interponeretur. Atq; ideo feci, ut tanquam, à præsentibus coram ha-beri beri sermo videretur. Cum enim me-cum sæpe ageres Attice, ut de amicitia scriberem aliquid, digna mihi res tum omnium cognitione, tum familiarita-te nostra visa est: itaque feci non invitus, ut prodessem multis rogatu tuo. Sed ut in Catone maiore feci(,qui est scriptus ad te de senectute,) Catonem induxi senem disputantem, cui nulla videbatur aptior persona, quæ de illa ætate loqueretur, quam ejus, qui & diutissimè senex fuisset, & in ipsa senectute præ cæ-teris floruisset: sic cum accepissemus à patribus maximè memorabilem, Lælij persona visa est idonea fuisse, quæ de amicitia ea ipsa dissereret, quæ disputata ab eo meminisset magister meus Scæ-vola. Genus autem hoc sermonū po-situm in hominum veterum authori-tate, & eorum illustrium, plus (nescio quo pacto) videtur habere gravitatis. Itaque ipse mea legens sic afficior interdum, ut Catonem, non me, loqui existimen. Sed ut tum ad senem senex de senectute, sic in hoc libro ad amicum amicissimus de amicitia scripsi. Tum est Cato loquutus, quo erat nemo fere senior seporibus illis, nemo prudentior nunc Lælius & sapiens (sic enim est habitus.) & amicitiæ gloria excellens, de amicitia loquitur. Tu velim à me animum paulum parumper avertas, Lælium loqui ipsum putes. C. Fannius & Q. Mutius ad socerum veniunt post mortem Africani, ab his sermo oritur: responder Lælius, cuius tota disputatio est de amicitia: quâ legens tu ipse cognosces.
units.tr: But of this another time; now I return to the augur. Since he often told many stories, you remember, Atticus, that at home, sitting in the semicircle (as he usually did), while I was there with a few very close friends, the conversation turned to that topic which was then on almost everyone's lips. For you certainly remember (I think), Atticus, and all the more because you were close to Publius Sulpicius, how great was the admiration or the complaint of men, when he, as tribune of the plebs, fell into deadly hatred with Quintus Pompeius, who was then consul, and with whom he had lived most intimately and affectionately. So when Scaevola had come to that very mention, he set out for us the discussion about friendship that Laelius had held with him and with his other son-in-law Gaius Fannius, son of Marcus, a few days after the death of Africanus. I committed to memory the opinions of that discussion, and I have set them out in this book in my own manner. For I have introduced them as if they were speaking themselves, so that I need not say "I say" and "he says" too often; and I did this so that the conversation would seem to be held in the presence of those taking part. For when you often urged me, Atticus, to write something about friendship, the subject seemed to me worthy of everyone's knowledge and of our friendship; so I did it not unwillingly, to be of service to many at your request. But just as I did in the Cato Maior, which is written to you on old age, where I introduced Cato, an old man, discussing, since no person seemed more fitting to speak about that age than one who had been an old man for the longest time and had flourished above others in old age itself; so, since we had received from our fathers that Laelius was most memorable, his character seemed fitting to discuss friendship itself, the very things that my teacher Scaevola remembered had been discussed by him. Moreover, this kind of conversation, based on the authority of men of old and of illustrious men, somehow seems to carry more weight. Thus, when I read my own work, I am sometimes so moved that I think Cato is speaking, not me. But just as then an old man wrote to an old man about old age, so in this book a most loving friend has written to a friend about friendship. Then Cato spoke, who was almost the oldest of those days, nobody more prudent; now Laelius, wise (for so he was regarded), and excelling in the glory of friendship, speaks about friendship. I would wish you to turn your mind a little away from me for a while, and to think that Laelius himself is speaking. Gaius Fannius and Quintus Mucius come to their father-in-law after the death of Africanus; the conversation arises from them; Laelius replies, and his whole discussion is about friendship; you yourself will learn this by reading.

units.la: Disputatio de amicitia duas habet partes: Exordium & de amicitia dialogum. In exordio de causis scriptionis huius, & forma sive decoro dialogi disputat.
units.tr: The discussion on friendship has two parts: a preface and the dialogue on friendship. In the preface it treats of the causes of this writing and of the form or fitness of the dialogue.

units.la: Quintus Mutius. Prima scriptionis causa fuit magister Ciceronis, Q. M. Augur Scævola: qui suis prudentibus sermonibus Ciceroni occasionem præbuit aliquid de amicitia scribendi. Describit autem illum hoc loco ab effectis ad hunc locum apprimè pertinentibus: nam is multa narrat de C. Lælio socero suo, quem Cicero hoc libro loquentem facit, ejus sapientiam in omni sermone celebrare solebat. Ego autem. Exponit causam causam praceptoris, tepus ,finem & effecta: quae omnia diligenter notanda sunt: Causa fuit pater Ciceronis: tempus exprimitur metonymia adjuncti: sumpta virili toga, i. cum è pueris excessisset Cicero: Finis est, perpetua cōversatio, assiduus comitatus: Effecta sunt, multa prudenter disputata, multa breviter & commode dicta memoriae mandare, & doctior fieri. Latere. i. corpore: synechdoche membri. Disputata, i. arte & ratione explicata: metaphora a fronditoribus, qui, dum arborum supervacuas frondes resecant, disputare dicuntur. Quo mortuo. Per digressionem incidit in mentionem alterius praeceptoris, Scævola pontificis: quem commendat ab adjuncto ingenio, & industria, per comparationem minorum. Sed de hoc. Redit ad priorem praeceptorem, ejusq; cum de aliis rebus, tum de amicitia sermones exponit: ubi haec notantur. 1. circumstantia loci, in quo Scævola sermones habebat. 2. auditores. 3. causa sermonis de amicitia. 4. Adjunctum temporis. 5. forma dialogi. Locus duplex, communis, domus Scævola, proprius, hemicyclus, sive sella dimidio circulo similis: in quo sedebat vel propter senectutem, vel propter consulentes de jure. Domus ∗. ejus cuncta Italiæ tanquam oraculum patebat. ⌣Auditores fuerunt Cicero & pauci familiares. Causa fuit capitale odium Sulpitij & Pompeij, hominumq; propter id admiratio & querela. Tempus exprimitur his verbis, post mortem. ⌣Africani. Forma explicatur inductione loquentium personarum, Lælij, Scævolæ, Fanny: ejusq; causa additur à fine: ut odiosa repetitio verborum, inquam & inquit, vitaretur: atq; ut oratio tanquam à præsentibus haberi videretur. Quum enim sæpè.
units.tr: Quintus Mucius. The first cause of the writing was Cicero's teacher, Quintus Mucius the augur Scaevola, who, by his prudent conversations, gave Cicero the occasion to write something about friendship. He describes him here from his effects, which bear closely on this point: for he used to tell many stories about Gaius Laelius, his father-in-law, whom Cicero makes the speaker in this book, and he used to praise his wisdom in every conversation. But I. The teacher's cause, time, end and effects are set out, all of which must be carefully noted: the cause was Cicero's father; the time is expressed by metonymy of the adjunct: "having assumed the toga of manhood", that is, when Cicero had left boyhood; the end is continuous association and constant attendance; the effects are: having many things wisely discussed, committing to memory many things briefly and aptly said, and becoming more learned. "Latere", that is, from the body: synecdoche of the part. "Disputata", that is, explained by art and reason: a metaphor from pruners, who are said to "prune" (disputare) while they cut away the superfluous leaves of trees. "Quo mortuo" (when he died). By digression he comes to mention another teacher, the chief priest Scaevola, whom he commends from the adjuncts of talent and diligence, by comparison of lesser things. "But of this". He returns to the earlier teacher, and sets out his conversations both about other matters and about friendship; where these points are noted: 1. the circumstance of place, where Scaevola held his discussions; 2. the hearers; 3. the cause of the discussion about friendship; 4. the adjunct of time; 5. the form of the dialogue. The place is twofold: general, the house of Scaevola; particular, the semicircle, or seat similar to a half-circle, in which he sat either because of his age or because of those consulting him about law. His house was open to all Italy like an oracle. The hearers were Cicero and a few intimate friends. The cause was the deadly hatred of Sulpicius and Pompeius, and the admiration and complaint of men on account of it. The time is expressed by these words, "after the death of Africanus". The form is explained by the introduction of the speaking persons, Laelius, Scaevola, Fannius; and the reason for it is added from the end: so that the tedious repetition of the words "I say" and "he says" might be avoided, and so that the speech might seem to be held as if by those present. "Quum enim sæpe" (for when often).

units.la: ⌣Altera scriptionis causa fuit rogatus Attici: cui, Cicero, ut pareret, duobus argumentis adductus fuit. 1. est adiunctum rei: quod amplificatur distributione subiecti per comparationem minorum: de amicitia scribere dignares est, cum omnium cognitione, tum vero amicitiæ Lælij & Scipionis. ⌣Alterum est finis. Cicero ideo Attico more gessit: ut ejus rogatu prodesset multis. Sed ut in Catone. ⌣Alter præfatio-nis locus de decoro dialogi: in quo primo disputat de persona cujus hic præcipuæ partes sunt. argumentatur autem à coniugatis per copa-rationem parium. Ut antea Cato senex de senectute disservit: sic nunc Lælius amicitia gloria insignis de amicitia disserit. Genus autem. Commendatio decori à subjectis adjunctis, & effectis, Subjecta sunt homines veteres & illustres: adjuncta sunt gravitas, & authoritas: effecta sunt: ita afficere Ciceronem, ut sua legens non se, sed Lælium loquì putet. Sed ut tum. Ad decorum etiam pertinet nuncupatio: nuncupatur autem T. P. Attico: ratio additur à conjugatis per comparationem parium: ut in Catone maiore senex scripsit ad senem de senectute: sic in hoc libro amicus scribit ad amicum de amicitia. Argumenti antecedens ornatur adjunctis, senectute & prudentia: quæ amplificantur comparatione parium per negationem impa-ris. Consequens ornatur adjunctus Lalij, sapientia, & amicitiæ gloria: quæ confirmatur testimonio communi omnium hominum.
units.tr: The second cause of the writing was the request of Atticus, to which Cicero was brought to comply by two arguments. 1. There is the adjunct of the matter: which is amplified by the division of the subject, by comparison of lesser things: it is worth writing about friendship, both for the knowledge of all men and especially for the friendship of Laelius and Scipio. The second is the end: Cicero therefore complied with Atticus's wish so that he might be of service to many at his request. "But just as in the Cato". The second place of the preface concerns the fitness of the dialogue: in which he first discusses the person whose principal part this is; and he argues from conjugates, by comparison of equals: just as Cato the old man previously discoursed about old age, so now Laelius, distinguished by the glory of friendship, discourses about friendship. "Genus autem". The commendation of fitness comes from the subjects, adjuncts and effects. The subjects are men of old and illustrious; the adjuncts are gravity and authority; the effects are that the reading of his own work so moves Cicero that he thinks Laelius, not himself, is speaking. "Sed ut tum". The dedication also belongs to the fitness: it is dedicated to T. P. Atticus; a reason is added from conjugates, by comparison of equals: as in the Cato Maior an old man wrote to an old man about old age, so in this book a friend writes to a friend about friendship. The preceding argument is adorned with adjuncts, old age and prudence, which are amplified by comparison of equals through the negation of the unequal. The following is adorned by the adjuncts of Laelius: wisdom and the glory of friendship, which is confirmed by the common testimony of all men.

units.la: FANNIUS. Sunt ista vera Læli, nec enim melior vir fuit Africano quisquam nec clarior: sed existimare debes, omnium oculos in te esse conjectos, unū te sapientem appellant & existimant. Tribuebatur hoc modò M Catoni: scimus L. Acilium apud patres nostros appellatum esse sapientem: sed uterq; alio quodam modo: Acilius, quia prudens esse in iure civili putabatur. Cato, quia multarum rerum usum haberet, multaq; ejus & in senatu, & in foro, vel provisa prudenter, vel acta constanter, vel acutè responsa ferebantur: propterea quasi cognomen jam habebat in senectute sapientis. Te autem alio quodam modo dicunt, non solùm,natura & moribus, verùm etiam studio & doctrina esse sapientem: nec sicut vulgus, sed ut eruditi sapientem appellare solent, qualem in reliqua Græcia neminem. Nam qui septem appellantur, eos qui illa subtilius quæsierunt, in numero sapientum non habent. Athenis unum accepimus, & cum quidem etiam Apollinis oraculo sapientissimum judicatum: Hanc esse in te sapientiam existimant, ut omnia tua in te posita esse ducas, humanosque casus virtute inferiores esse putes. Itaque ex me quaeruntcredo & ex hoc idè Scævola, quonam pacto mortem Africani feras, coque magis, quòd is proximis nonis, cū in hortos Decii Bruti Auguris commentādi causa, (ut assolet) venissemus, tu non affuisti: qui diligentissimè semper illum diem, & illud munus solitus esse obire. S C AE V O L A. Quaeruntquidem, C. Laeli multi, ut est à Fannio dictum: sed ego id respondeo, quod animadverti te dolorem, quem acceperis cum summi viri, tum amantissimi morte, ferrè moderatè, nec potuisse non commoveri, nec fuisse id humanitatis tuæ. Quod autem his Nonis in nostro collegio non affuisses, valetudinem respondeo causam, non mœstitiam fuisse. L AE L. Rectè tu quidem, Scæ-vola, & verè. Nec enim ab isto officio, quod semper usurpavi cum valerem, deduci incomodo meo debui: nec ullo casu arbitror hoc constanti homini posse contingere, ut ulla intermissio fiat officij. Tu autem, Fanni, qui mihi tantum tribui dicis, quantum ego nec agnosco, nec postulo, facis amice: sed, (ut mihi videris) nō rectè judicas de Catonè: aut enim nemo, quod quidem magis credo,) aut si quisquam est, ille sapiens fuit. Quomodo enim (ut alia omittam.) mortem filij tulit? Memineram Paulum, videram Cajum: sed hinc comparentur Catoni maximo, & spectato viro. Quamobrem cave, Catoni anteponas ne istum quidé ipsū, quē Appollo, (utait), sapientissimum judicavit. Hujus enim facta, illius dicta laudantur. De me autem (ut jam cum utroq; loquar,) sic habetote. Ego si Scipionis desiderio me moveri negem, quàm id rectè faciam viderint sapien-tes: sed certè mentior, moveor enim tali amico orbatus, qualis (ut arbitror) nemo unquam erit: & ut confirmare possum, nemo certè fuit. Sed non egeo medicina, me ipse consolor, & maximè illo solatio, quòd eo errore careo, quo amicorum discessu pleriq; angi solent. Nihil enim mali accidisse Scipioni puto: mihi accidit, si qd accidit. Suis autè incommodis graviter angi, non amicum, sed se ipsum amantis est. Cum illo verò, quis neget actum esse praecla-re. Nisi re?Nisi enim(,quod ille minime puta-bat,) immortalitatem optare vellet, quid non est adeptus,quod homini fas esset optare? Qui summam spem civi-um,quam de eo jam puero habuerant, continuo adolescens incredibili virtu-te superavit:qui consulatum petiit nū-quam,factus & consul hic,primum an-te tempus, iterum sibi suo tempore, Reip.pene fero: qui duabus urbibus e-versis inimicissimis huic imperio non modo praesentia, verum etiam futura bella delevit. Quid dicam de morib.fa-cilimis?De pietate in matrem?liberali-tate in fororles? bonitate in suos? iusti-tia in omnes?Haec nota sut vobis. Quā autem civitati carus fuerit, moerore funeris indicatum est. Quid igitur huc paucorum annorum accessio juvare potuisset? Senectus enim quamvis nō sit gravis (,ut memini Catonem uno anno ante, quam mortuus est, mecum & cum Scipione disserere,) tamen au-fert eam viriditatem,in qua etiam nunc erat Scipio.Quamob.vita quidem talis fuit,vel fortuna,vel gloria,ut nihil posset accedere: Moriendi autē senium ce-leritas abstulit: quo de genere mortis difficile dictu est, qd homines suspicen-tur, videtis. Hoc tamē vere licet dicere, P. Scipioni ex multis diebus, quos in vita celeberrimos, laetissimosque viderit illum diem clarissimum fuisse, cum se-natu dimisso domum reductus ad vesperam a patribus conscriptis, a populo Rom. sociis & Latinis, pridie quam ex-cessit e vita: ut ex tam alto dignitatis gradu ad superos videatur potius, quā ad inferos pervenisse. Neque enim assentior iis, qui haec nuper dissere coeperunt, cum corporibus simul animas interire, atq; omnia morte deleri. Plus apud me antiquorum authoritas valet, vel nostrorum maiorum, qui mortuis tam religiosa iura tribuerunt, quod non fecissent profecto, si nihil ad eos pertinere arbitrarentur: vel eorum qui in hac terra fuerunt, magnamq; Graeciam, (quae nunc quidem deleta est, tum florebat,) institutis & preceptis suis erudierunt: vel ejus, qui Apollinis oraculo sapientissimus est judicatus: qui non tum hoc, tum illud, ut in plerisq; ,sed idem dicebat semper, animos homi-num esse divinos, iisque, cum e cor-pore excessissent reditum ad cœ-lum patere, optimoque & justissimo, cuique expeditissimum: quod idem Scipioni videbatur. Qui idem quasi præsagiret, paucis ante morte diebus, cum & Philus & Manilius adessent, & alii plures, tuq; etiam Scævola me con-venisses, disservit triduum de Repub. cujus disputationis fuit extrema fere de immortalitate animorum: quæ se inquietè pervisum ex Africano audis-se dicebat. Id si ita est, ut optimi cujus-que animus in morte facillime evolet, tanquam e custodia vinclisque corpo-ris,cui censemus cursum ad Deos faci-liorem fuisse, quam Scipioni? Quocir-ca mœrere hoc ejus eventu vereor, ne invidi magis, quā amici fit. Sin autem illa vereor, ut idem interius animo-rum & corporum, nec ullus sensus mane-at: ut nihil boni est in morte, si certe ni-hil est mali. Sensu enim amisso fit idem quasi natus non esset omnino. Quem tamen esse natum & nos gaudemus, & hæc civitas dum erit, lætabitur.
units.tr: FANNIUS. That is true, Laelius, for no man was better than Africanus, nor more famous. But you should consider that all eyes are turned upon you; they call you alone wise and think so. This was said of Marcus Cato in former times. We know that Lucius Acilius was called wise among our forefathers, but each in a different way. Acilius was thought prudent in civil law. Cato had great experience of many things, and many of his prudent foresights, constant actions, and sharp replies, both in the senate and in the forum, were reported; so that already in old age he had, as it were, the surname of "the wise." But they say that you are wise in another way: not only by nature and character, but also by study and learning. And they call you wise not as the common people do, but as the learned are wont to call a man wise, a title nobody else in the rest of Greece has. For those called the Seven, who sought these things more subtly, are not counted among the wise. We have heard of one man at Athens, and he was judged the wisest even by the oracle of Apollo. They think you have this wisdom: that you count all your affairs as placed in your own power, and think human accidents inferior to virtue. Therefore Scaevola too, and I myself, ask you how you bear the death of Africanus, all the more because you were not present on the last Nones, when we had come, as usual, to the gardens of Decius Brutus the augur for the purpose of study; you, who had always most diligently been accustomed to observe that day and that duty. SCAEVOLA. Many ask this, Gaius Laelius, as Fannius has said. But I answer this: I saw that you bore the grief which you had received at the death of a man both great and most dear with moderation, and that you could not but be moved; nor was this unbecoming to your humanity. As for your not being present at our college on these Nones, I answer that ill health was the cause, not sadness. LAELIUS. You are right, Scaevola, and truly so. For I ought not to have been drawn away by my infirmity from that duty which I always performed while I was well; nor do I think that any accident can happen to a steadfast man so that his duty is ever interrupted. But you, Fannius, who say that so much is attributed to me, as I neither recognize nor claim, act like a friend; but, as it seems to me, you do not judge rightly of Cato. For either no one (which I rather believe) or, if anyone, he was wise. For how did he bear the death of his son? (To omit other things.) I remember Paulus, I saw Gaius; but let them be compared with Cato the Elder, a man of tested worth. Therefore take care not to place before Cato even that man whom Apollo, as it is said, judged the wisest. For Cato's deeds, and that man's sayings, are praised. As for me (to speak now with both of them) you should know this. If I should deny that I am moved by desire for Scipio, let the wise see how rightly I do it; but I would certainly be lying, for I am moved, bereaved of such a friend as (I think) no one will ever be, and as I can assert, certainly there never was one. But I do not need medicine; I console myself, and most of all with this comfort, that I am free of that error by which many are commonly distressed at the departure of friends. For I think no evil has befallen Scipio; it has befallen me, if anything has befallen. But to be grievously distressed over one's own misfortunes is the mark of a man who loves himself, not his friend. As for him, who would deny that his life was brilliantly completed? Unless (as he, least of all, thought) he should wish to desire immortality, what has he not attained that it would be right for a man to desire? He surpassed, by incredible virtue, the great hope of his fellow citizens which they had already conceived of him as a boy; he sought the consulship never, yet, made consul here, first before the proper time, and afterwards in his proper time, he almost bore the state; he destroyed, with the two most hostile cities overturned, not only the present wars against this empire but also the future ones. What shall I say of his most gentle manners? Of his piety towards his mother, his generosity to his sisters, his goodness to his own, his justice towards all? These things are known to you. How dear he was to the state was shown by the grief at his funeral. What, then, could the addition of a few more years have helped? For old age, though it is not heavy (as I remember Cato, a year before he died, arguing with me and with Scipio), nevertheless takes away that vigour in which Scipio was even now. So his life was such, both in fortune and in glory, that nothing more could be added; and speed took away the decline of dying. As to what kind of death this was, which men suspect, it is difficult to say; you see. Yet this may truly be said: of the many days of his life which were most celebrated and most joyful, that day was the most glorious for Publius Scipio, when, having laid down the senate, he was escorted home in the evening by the conscript fathers, by the Roman people, by the allies and the Latins, the day before he departed from life; so that from such a high step of dignity he seems to have gone rather to the gods above than to the dead below. For I do not assent to those who have lately begun to argue that souls perish together with bodies, and that everything is destroyed by death. The authority of the ancients weighs more with me, either of our forefathers, who attributed such sacred rights to the dead, which they surely would not have done if they thought nothing pertained to them; or of those who lived in this land and, by their institutions and precepts, trained great Greece (which now indeed is destroyed, but then flourished); or of him who was judged wisest by the oracle of Apollo, who did not say now this and now that, as in most cases, but always said the same: that the souls of men are divine, and that for those who have departed from the body a way back to heaven lies open, and most easily open for the best and most just. This same thing seemed right to Scipio. He too, as if he had a presentiment, a few days before his death, when Philus and Manilius were present, and many others, and you too, Scaevola, had come to me, discoursed for three days on the Republic; the last part of that discussion was almost about the immortality of souls, which he said he had restlessly seen in a vision of Africanus, as you heard. If it is so, that the soul of each best man flies most easily out at death, as if from a prison and the bonds of the body, what do we think his course to the gods was made easier than Scipio's? Therefore I fear that to grieve over this event of his is more the mark of an envious man than of a friend. But if, on the other hand, I should fear that the soul and body perish together, and that no sensation remains, then there is no good in death, if certainly there is no evil. For with sensation lost, it is as if he had not been born at all. Yet we rejoice that he was born, and this state will rejoice as long as it endures.

units.la: Quamobrem cum illo quidem(,ut supra dixi,)actum optime est,mecum autem iucondius: quem fuit æquius, ut prius introieram in vitam,sic prius exire de vita. Sed tamē recordatione nostræ amicitiæ sic fruor, ut beatè vixisse videar,quia cū Scipione vixerim, quo cum mihi coniunctō cura de Rep.& de privata fuit:quo cum domus fuit, & militia communis:& id in quo est omnis vis amicitiæ voluntatum, studiorū, sententiarum summa consensio. Itaq; non tam ista me sapientiæ(,quam modo Fannius commemoravit,)fama delectat, falsa præsertim, quàm quod amicitiæ nostræ memoriam spero sempiternam fore:idque mihi eo magis est cordi,quod ex omnibus sæculis vix tria,aut quatuor nominantur paria amicorum : quo in genere sperare videor Scipionis amicitiam, & Lælij notam posteritati fore.
units.tr: Therefore, as I said above, it has gone very well for him, but for me it has gone more pleasantly; for it was more just that, as I had entered life earlier, so I should leave it earlier. But nevertheless I enjoy the remembrance of our friendship so much that I seem to have lived a happy life, because I lived with Scipio, with whom I had shared both public and private concerns, with whom I had a common home and military service; and that in which lies the whole force of friendship: the highest agreement of wills, pursuits, and opinions. And so it is not so much that reputation for wisdom which Fannius lately mentioned (especially false) that delights me, as that I hope the memory of our friendship will be everlasting; and this is all the dearer to me because out of all the ages scarcely three or four pairs of friends are named; and in this class I seem to hope that the friendship of Scipio and the name of Laelius will be known to posterity.

units.la: Fannius. Exordio subjicitur dialogus: cu-ius dua[?] ius duæ sunt partes, exordium, & ipsa de a-mitia disputatio. In exordio via sternitur ad disputationem, dum multa dicuntur de sapientia Lalij, & morte Scipionis. Sunt ista vera. Fannius orditur dialogum ex abrupto: intelligendum igitur est Lælium antea de Scipione locutum esse, ejusq; morte deplorasse, utpote ex qua Respub. magnum detrimentum acceperit. Fannius igitur per concessionem sumit occasionem sapientiam Lalij extollendi ut sit sensus. Concedo tibi, Lali, optimum & præstantissimum virum fuisse Scipionem: sed tamen hoc te ignorare nolim, omnes in te tanquam virum sapien-tissimum respicere. Tribuebatur hoc.
units.tr: Fannius. The dialogue is introduced by a preface, which has two parts: the introduction and the discussion of friendship itself. In the introduction the ground is laid for the discussion, since much is said about Laelius's wisdom and the death of Scipio. These things are true. Fannius begins the dialogue abruptly, so it must be understood that Laelius had spoken earlier about Scipio and lamented his death, since the commonwealth had suffered a great loss through it. Fannius therefore, by way of concession, takes the opportunity to praise the wisdom of Laelius, so that the sense is this: "I grant you, Laelius, that Scipio was an excellent and outstanding man; yet I would not have you ignore that everyone looks to you as the most wise man." This was attributed to him.

units.la: Amplificat sapientiam Lalij comparatione dissimili: ipsum enim dissimiliter cum aliis, quibus hoc nomen tribuebatur, comparat, & omnibus anteponit. In propositione adducit duo exempla sapientum virorum, quorum tamen neutri tribuebatur eo modo sapientia, quo Lalio. L. Acilius sapiens dicebatur propter adiunctam prudentiam iuris civilis: Cato propter sua facta: quæ amplificantur distributione subiecti: senatus & fori: atq; adjunctis: facta ejus fuerunt constan-tia tia provisa prudentia, responsa acuta. Te autem alio. Antapodosis, qua Lælius Ascilio, Catoni, & septem Græcia sapientibus præfertur. Vbi primo causæ perfectæ sapientiæ explicantur, per comparationem minorum quæ sunt natura, mores, doctrina, studium. Deinde Lælij sapientia amplificatur exemplo Socratis: & qualis fuerit declaratur, scilicet despicientia rerum humanarum, animi magnitudo, & constantia. Itaq; ex me quæruntur. Altera pars orationis Fannii, in qua Lælio ansam præbet de Scipione, atq; adeo de amicitia differendi. Propositio est, homines ex me quærunt, & ex hoc Scævola, quomodo morte Africani feras. Hujus rei duas causas affert: prima sumitur ab adjuncto i. sapientia Lælij, quam antea mirifice laudavit: altera a factis: quod nuper in disputatione non adfuit, quod munus antea diligenter obire solitus fuit. Scævola. Confirmat orationis Fannii posteriorem partem, & exponit quid ipse quærentibus de Lælio respondeat: videlicet quod moderate ferat mortem Scipionis: idq; amplificat adjunctu Scipionis per comparationem minorum propositis cujus nota est superlativus gradus.
units.tr: The author amplifies Laelius's wisdom by an unlike comparison: he compares him differently with others to whom this name was given, and places him above them all. In the proposition he adduces two examples of wise men, neither of whom was called wise in the way Laelius was. Lucius Acilius was called wise because of his added knowledge of civil law; Cato because of his deeds. These are amplified by the distribution of the subject (the Senate and the forum) and by the circumstances: his deeds were marked by constancy, foresight in counsel, and sharp replies. But you, on the other hand... [The antapodosis, in which Laelius is preferred to Acilius, Cato and the seven wise men of Greece.] First, the causes of perfect wisdom are explained, by comparing the lesser qualities, which are nature, character, learning and study. Then Laelius's wisdom is amplified by the example of Socrates, and what sort of man he was is declared, namely contempt for human affairs, greatness of spirit, and constancy. Thus questions are put to me. [The second part of Fannius's speech, in which he gives Laelius an occasion to speak about Scipio and so about friendship. The proposition is: men ask me, and Scaevola here, how you bear the death of Africanus.] He gives two reasons for this: the first is taken from an attendant circumstance, namely Laelius's wisdom, which he praised a little earlier; the second from his deeds: that he was not present at the recent debate, though he was accustomed to discharge that office diligently before. Scaevola. He confirms the latter part of Fannius's speech, and sets out what he himself answers to those who ask about Laelius, namely that he bears the death of Scipio with moderation; and he amplifies this by the circumstance of Scipio, through a comparison of lesser things, whose mark is the superlative degree.

units.la: Deinde ipsum nonnihil commoveri morte Scipionis concedit: ejusque rei causam confert in humanitatem Lælÿ. Tertio argumento diuersorum causam, cur nuper in disputatione non adfuit, exponit: causa fuit non mæstitia, sed valetudo. Lælius. Oratio Lælÿ habet duas partes: in priore respondet generis suis, in posteriori de morte Scipionis agit. Recte tu quidem. Approbat responsum Scævolæ, removendo omnes causas, quibus homo ab officio abduci possit. Tu autem Fanni. Respondet orationis Fannÿ parti priori: ac laudem sapientiæ sibi à Fannio tributam non recipit: ne tamen ipsum offendat, causam ejus confert in amore Fannÿ. Sed ut mihi videris. Respondet etiam de Catone, & eum contra sententiam Fannÿ omnibus sapientibus anteponit: idque primò confirmat facto Catonis: quia mortem filÿ mode stissimè tulit: deinde comparatione minorū, cuius nota est negatio paris: Paulus, Cajus, Plato in pari sapientia cum Catone non possunt comparari. De me autem. Altera pars orationis, in qua disputat de morte Catonis. Ac primò quidem fatetur se moveri desiderio Scipionis: ejusque rationem red
units.tr: Then he concedes that he himself was somewhat moved by the death of Scipio, and he attributes the cause of this to Laelius's humanity. Thirdly, by a third argument, he sets out the reason why he was not present at the recent debate: the cause was not sadness but ill health. Laelius. Laelius's speech has two parts: in the first he answers Scaevola's remarks, in the second he deals with the death of Scipio. "Quite right, you indeed." He approves Scaevola's answer, removing all the causes by which a man might be drawn away from his duty. "But you, Fannius..." He responds to the first part of Fannius's speech, and does not accept the praise of wisdom which Fannius has ascribed to him; yet, so as not to offend him, he attributes the cause of this to Fannius's affection. "But, as it seems to me..." He also responds about Cato, and against Fannius's opinion he places him above all the wise men; and this he first confirms by a deed of Cato's, because he bore the death of his son most moderately; then by a comparison of lesser things, whose mark is the negation of equality: Paulus, Gaius and Plato cannot be compared with Cato in equal wisdom. "But as for me..." The second part of the speech, in which he discusses the death of Cato. And first he admits that he is moved by longing for Scipio, and he gives the reason for it from a circumstance of Scipio: because he was his best friend.

units.la: C dit ab adjuncto Scipionis: quia fuit optimus amicus: id vero rursus amplificatur dissimi-li: quo Scipio omnibus, qui fuerunt, sunt, & erunt, anteponitur. Deinde vero se dolori mederi, & moderari posse docet, quia sciat nihil mali Scipioni accidisse: id quod probat a persona Scipionis, & mortis genere. In persona Scipionis considerantur facta & adjuncta. Factum primum est: quod civium spe quam de puero habebant superavit: atq; hoc rursus amplificatur adjunctis subjecti, & causa. Subiectum est spes, quae hic summa dicitur, causa qua spem superavit, est virtus, quam incredibilem nominat. Alterum factum est: quod bis consulatum adeptus est: hoc augetur primo remotione causa: quae est petitio: nunquam petiit consulatum: deinde adjuncto temporis, quod exponitur comparatione dissimili: primo factus consul ante tempus: iterum suo tempore, sed Reipub. penè fero. Tertium est eversio Carthaginis & Numantiae: quae amplificatur adjuncto subjecti & effectu. Subjectum sunt urbes duae, quae inimicissimae dicuntur Imperio Romano. Effectum amplificatur argumento minorum, non solum praesentia bella, sed futura etiam sustulit. sustulit. Quid dicam. Hactenus facta: sequuntur adjuncta: quorum alia insunt in subjecto, atq; rursus amplificantur subjecto in quo occupantur: ea sunt pietas erga matrē liberalitas in sorores, bonitas in suos, justitia in omnes. Alia adsunt subjecto, ut funus honorificum, moeror civium, comitatus patrum conscriptorum, sociorum, Latinorum: quod postremum rursus amplificatur adjuncto temporis, & comparatione pariūm. Alia denique occupantur in subjecto, ut mors tempestiva.
units.tr: This in turn is amplified by an unlike comparison: Scipio is placed above all who have been, are, and will be. Then he teaches that he can heal and moderate his grief, because he knows that no harm has befallen Scipio; and he proves this from Scipio's person and the manner of his death. In Scipio's person facts and circumstances are considered. The first fact: that he surpassed the hope which the citizens had of him as a boy; and this in turn is amplified by the circumstances of the subject and the cause. The subject is the hope, which here is called high; the cause by which he surpassed the hope is virtue, which he calls incredible. The second fact: that he obtained the consulship twice. This is enhanced first by removing the cause, which is candidature: he never sought the consulship; then by the circumstance of time, which is set out by an unlike comparison: first he was made consul before the time, and a second time at his proper time, but almost to the ruin of the commonwealth. The third is the overthrow of Carthage and Numantia; this is amplified by the circumstance of the subject and the effect. The subjects are two cities, which are said to be most hostile to the Roman empire. The effect is amplified by an argument from lesser things: he removed not only the wars then present but also those to come. What shall I say? So far the deeds; there follow the circumstances, some of which inhere in the subject and are again amplified by the subject in which they are found: these are his piety towards his mother, his generosity towards his sisters, his kindness towards his own, his justice towards all. Others attend the subject, such as his honourable funeral, the grief of the citizens, the escort of the senators, of the allies and of the Latins; and this last is again amplified by the circumstance of time and by comparison with equals. Still others are found in the subject, such as an untimely death.

units.la: Neq; assentior.
units.tr: Nor do I agree.

units.la: Alterum argumentum, quibus probat Scipioni nihil mali ex morte accidisse, probat proprio animae adjuncto, quod est immortalitas. Eam autem confirmat primò factis Romanorum, eorumque fine: Romani mortuis religiosissima iura tribuerunt: ut mortuorum animabus viventibus prodesset. Deinde idem probat testimonio Pythagoreorum, Platonis, Scipionis. Atq; horum testimonium rursus amplificatur suis argumentis.
units.tr: The second argument, by which he proves that no harm came to Scipio from his death, proves it from a circumstance peculiar to the soul, which is immortality. He confirms this first by the customs of the Romans and their purpose: the Romans bestowed the most solemn rights upon the dead, so that these might benefit the souls of the living. Then he proves the same from the testimony of the Pythagoreans, of Plato, and of Scipio. And their testimony is again amplified by its own arguments.

units.la: Pythagoreos commendat: 1. à subjecto loco, in quo fuerunt, Italia videlicet: unde Italici philosophi nominati. 2. à factis: nam Graeciam magnam institutis praeceptisq; erudierunt. Socratem comendat.1.testimonio Apollinis. cujus oraculo sapientissimus est judicatus L.à constantia eius & immota de animi immortalitate, sententia qua amplificatur dissimili. Scipionis testimonium commendat ab adjuncto temporis: Scipio paucis diebus ante mortem de immortalitate animorum disservit.2.Ab auditoribus, Lælio, Philo, Manitio, Scævola, & aliis pluribus. Hanc disputationem vide apud Cic:in somnio Scipionis. Id si ita est. Concludit hunc locum egregia similitudine, & argumento parium: unde colligit Scipionus morte non mærendum esse. Sin autem. Idem colligit e contrariis.& Scipioni ex morte nihil male accidisse probat argumento parium. Si idem interitus est animi & corporis,& nullus sensus manet: ut nihil boni est in morte, sic certe nihil mali est. Quem.
units.tr: He commends the Pythagoreans: (1) from the place in which they were, namely Italy, whence they were called Italian philosophers; (2) from their deeds, for they educated Magna Graecia with their institutions and precepts. He commends Socrates: (1) by the testimony of Apollo, by whose oracle he was judged the wisest; (2) by his constancy and unshaken judgement concerning the immortality of the soul, which is amplified by an unlike comparison. He commends the testimony of Scipio by the circumstance of time: Scipio discoursed on the immortality of souls a few days before his death; (2) by his hearers: Laelius, Philus, Manilius, Scaevola and many others. See this discussion in Cicero's Somnium Scipionis. "If this is so..." He concludes this passage with an excellent simile and an argument from equals, from which he gathers that Scipio is not to be mourned for his death. "But if..." He draws the same conclusion from contraries, and proves by an argument from equals that no harm came to Scipio from his death. If the death of soul and body is the same, and no sensation remains, then as there is no good in death, so certainly there is no evil in it. Whom...

units.la: Per epanorthosin concludit disputationem de Scipione, amicitiam cum eo commendas, describens, & omnibus rebus anteponens.
units.tr: By epanorthosis he concludes the discussion about Scipio, commending friendship with him, describing it, and placing it above all things.

units.la: FANNIVS. Istud quidem, Læli, ita necesse est, sed quoniam amicitiæ metio-nem fecisti, & sumus[?] otiosi, pergratum mihi feceris, spero item Scævolæ, si quæ admodum solet de cæteris rebus, cum ex te quæruntur, si de amicitia disputaris, quid sentias, qualem existimes, quæ præcepta des. SCAEVOLA. Mihi vero crit gratum, atque id ipsum cùm tecum agere conarer, Fannius averterit. Quamobrem utriq; nostrum gratū admodum feceris. LAELIVS. Ego vero non gravarer, si mihi ipse considerem. Nam & præclara vita res est, & sumus(. ut dixit Fannius,) otiosi. Sed quis ego sum?aut[?] quæ in me est facultas? doctorum est ista consuetudo, eaq; Græcorū, ut ijs proponatur, de qua disputent, quam vis, subitò. Magnum opus est, egetq; exercitatione non parva. Quamobrē quæ disputari de amicitia possunt, ab ijs, censeo, petatis, qui ista profitentur. Ego vos hortari tantum possum, ut amicitiam omnibus rebus hu-manis anteponatis. Nil est enim tam natura aptum, tã coveniens ad res vel secundas, vel adversas. Sed hoc primū sentio, nisi in bonis amicitiam esse non posse. Neq; id ad vivum reseco, ut illi, qui hæc subtilius differunt, fortasse verè, sed ad communem utilitatem parū. Negant enim quenquam virum bonū esse, nisi sapientem. Sit ita sane:sed eam sapientiam interpretantur, quam adhuc mortalis nemo est consecutus. Nos autem ea quæ sunt in usu vitaq; communi, non ea quæ finguntur aut optantur, sperare debemus. Nunquam ego dicam C. Fabritium, M. Curium, T. Coruncanum, quos sapientes nostri maiores judicabant, ad istorum normam fuisse sapientes. Quare sibi habeant sapientiæ nomen & invidiosum, & obscurum, concedantq; ut hi boni viri fuerint. Neq; idquidem facient, negabunt id nisi sapienti posse concedi. Agamus igitur pingui Minerva, ut ajūt. Qui ita se gerunt, ita vivunt, ut eorum probetur fides, integritas, æqualitas, liberalitas: nec fit in eis ulla cupiditas, vel libido, vel audacia, sintq; magna constantia, ut hi fuerunt, quos modo nominavi: hos viros bonos, ut habiti sūt, sic etiam appellandos esse putemus, qui assequuntur, quantum homines possunt, naturam optimam recte vivendi ducem. Sic enim perspicere mihi videor, ita natos esse nos, ut inter omnes esset societas quædam: majorautem, ut quisq; proximè accederet. Itaq; cives potiores sunt, quam peregrini: & propinqui, quam alieni, cum his enim a-micitiam natura ipsa peperit, sed ea nō satis habet firmitatis. Namq; hoc præstat amicitia propinquitati, quòd ex propinquitate benevolentia tolli potest, ex amicitia autem non potest. Sublata enim benevolentia, amicitiæ nomen tollitur, propinquitatis manet.
units.tr: FANNIUS. That indeed must be so, Laelius; but since you have made mention of friendship, and we are at leisure, you will do me a most pleasing favour, and I hope Scaevola too, if you would discuss friendship: what you think of it, what sort you judge it to be, and what precepts you lay down, as you are usually asked about other matters. SCAEVOLA. To me it will indeed be welcome, and the very thing which I was trying to bring about with you when Fannius turned you aside. Therefore you will do us both a very great favour. LAELIUS. I for my part would not be reluctant, if I considered myself equal to it. For it is a fine thing, and we are (as Fannius said) at leisure. But who am I? Or what ability is in me? That kind of thing is a custom of the learned, and especially of the Greeks: that a subject should be proposed to them on which they may dispute, however suddenly. It is a great undertaking, and needs no small practice. Therefore, I think, you should ask those things which can be discussed about friendship from those who profess such matters. I can only urge you to place friendship above all human things. For nothing is so naturally fitted, so suited to both prosperous and adverse circumstances. But this I hold first of all: that friendship cannot exist except among good men. Nor do I cut this too finely, as those do who discuss these matters more subtly, perhaps truly, but with little use for common life. For they say that no one is a good man except the wise man. So be it: but they interpret that wisdom which no mortal has yet attained. We, however, ought to hope for those things which are in use and in common life, not those which are imagined or wished for. I shall never say that Gaius Fabricius, Marcus Curius and Tiberius Coruncanius, whom our ancestors judged to be wise, were wise by the standard of those men. Let them therefore keep the name of wisdom, which is both invidious and obscure, and let them concede that these were good men. Nor indeed will they do this; they will deny that this can be granted to any but the wise man. Let us therefore proceed with plain Minerva, as they say. Those who so conduct themselves, so live, that their faithfulness, integrity, evenness of temper and generosity are approved, and in whom there is no desire, lust or rashness, and who are of great constancy, as those were whom I have just named: let us think these men are to be called good men, as they are reckoned, who attain, so far as men can, nature, the best guide to right living. For thus I seem to perceive that we were born so that there should be a certain fellowship among all; but a greater one, the nearer each man is to another. Therefore fellow citizens are preferred to foreigners, and kinsmen to strangers; for with these nature herself has made friendship, but she does not provide enough firmness in it. For friendship has this advantage over kinship: that goodwill can be removed from kinship, but not from friendship. For when goodwill is taken away, the name of friendship is abolished, but the name of kinship remains.

units.la: Quanta autem vis amicitiæ sit, ex hoc intelligi maximè potest, quod ex infinita societate generis humani, quam conciliavit ipsa natura, ita contracta res est, & adducta in angustum, ut omnis charitas aut inter duos, aut inter paucos jungeretur.Est autem amicitia nihil aliud, nisi omnium divinarum, humanarumq; rerum cum benevolentia & charitate summa consensio. Qua quidem haud scio an excepta [?]sapientia, quicquam melius homini sit [?] à Diis immortalibus datum. Divitias alii præponunt,bonam alii valetudinem, alii potentiam,alii honores: multi etiam voluptates. Beluarum hoc quidem extremum est:illa autem superiora sunt caduca&incerta,posita non tam in nostris consiliis, quam in fortunæ temeritate.Qui autem in virtute summum bonum ponunt, præclarè illi quidem, sed hæc ipsa virtus amicitiam gignit, & continet: nec sine virtute amicitia ullo pacto potest.Iam virtutem ex consuetudine,vitæ sermonisq; nostri inter pretemur:nec metiamur eam(.ut quidam indocti.) verborum magnificentia, virosq; bonos eos, qui habentur, numeremus, Paulos, Catones, Cajos, Scipiones, Philos: his communis vita contenta est. Eos autem omittamus, q; omninò nusquam reperiuntur. Tales igitur inter viros amicitia tantas opportunitates habet, quantas vix queo dicere.Principio,cui potest esse vita vitalis(.ait Ennius.)qui non in amici mutua benevolentia conquiescat? Quid dulcius,quam habere quo cum omnia audeas sic loqui,ut tecum? Quis esset tantus fructus in prosperis rebus, nisi haberes qui illis æque ac tu ipse gauderet? Adversas vero res ferre difficile esset sine eo, qui illas gravius etiam quam tu ferret. Deniq; cæteræ res, quæ expe-tuntur opportunæ sunt singulæ rebus fere singulis, divitiæ ut utare, opes ut colare, honores ut laudere, voluptates ut gaudeas, valetudo ut dolore careas, & munera- bus fungare corporis: Ami-citia plurimas res continet, quoquo te verteris præsto est: nullo loco excludi-tur, nunquam intempestiva, nūquám molesta est. Itaq; non aqua non igni, nō aëre (ut aiunt.) pluribus locis utimur, quàm amicitia. Neq; ego nunc de vul-gari, aut de mediocri (quæ tamen ipsa delectat & prodest.) sed de vera & per-secta loquor, qualis eorum, qui pauci nominantur, fuit. Nam & secundas res splendidiores facit amicitia, & adver-sas partiens, communicansq; leviores. Cumq; plurimas & maximas commo-ditates amicitia contineat, tum illa ni-mirum præstat omnibus, quòd bona ipse prælucet in posterum: nec debilitari animos,aut cadere patitur: verum etiam jam amicum qui intuetur, tanquā exemplar aliquod intuetur sui. Quocirca & absentes adsunt, & egentes abundant, & imbecilles valent, & quod difficilius dictu, mortui vivunt: tantus eos honor, memoria, desiderium prosequitur amicorum. Ex quo illorum beata mors, videtur, horum vita laudabilis. Quod si exemplis ex natura rerum benevolentiæ conjunctionem, nec domus ulla, nec urbs stare poterit, nec agri quidem cultus permanebit. Id si minus intelligitur, quanta vis amicitiæ concordiæq; sit[?], ex dissentionibus, atq; ex discordiis percipi potest. Quæ enim domus tam stabilis, quæ tam firma civitas est, quæ non odijs, atq; dissidiis funditus possit everti? Ex quo quantum boni sit in amicitia judicari potest.
units.tr: Now the force of friendship can be understood above all from this: the whole infinite fellowship of the human race, which nature herself has established, has been so narrowed and drawn into a small compass that all affection is joined either between two people or among a few. Friendship is nothing other than complete agreement on all divine and human matters, joined with goodwill and love. I do not know whether anything better than this has been given to man by the immortal gods, except wisdom. Some prefer riches, others good health, others power, others honours; many also prefer pleasures. The last of these is surely a beast's good; the others are above it, but they are perishable and uncertain, resting not so much on our own counsels as on the recklessness of fortune. Those who place the highest good in virtue do so admirably, but this very virtue begets and sustains friendship, and without virtue friendship can in no way exist. Let us now judge virtue by the custom and practice of our own life and speech, and let us not measure it, as some unlearned people do, by the grandeur of words, and count as good men those who are so called: Paulus, Cato, Gaius, Scipio, Philus. Common life is content with these. But let us pass over those who are nowhere to be found at all. Friendship between such men therefore has such great advantages that I can scarcely tell them. In the first place, whose life could be lively (as Ennius says) if it did not rest upon the mutual goodwill of a friend? What is sweeter than to have someone with whom you may speak as freely as with yourself? What great fruit would there be in prosperity unless you had someone who rejoiced in your good fortune as much as you did yourself? To bear adversity would be hard indeed without someone who bears it even more heavily than you do. Finally, the other things that are sought are each suited to almost one purpose each: riches to be used, power to be respected, honours to be praised, pleasures to be enjoyed, health to be free from pain and to perform the duties of the body. Friendship embraces very many things; wherever you turn, it is at hand. It is shut out of no place, it is never untimely, never troublesome. Therefore we use friendship in more places than we use water, fire, or air (as they say). And I am speaking now not of the common or mediocre kind of friendship (which nonetheless delights and benefits), but of the true and perfect kind, such as belonged to those few who are named. For friendship makes prosperity more splendid, and by dividing and sharing adversity makes it lighter. And although friendship contains very many and very great advantages, this above all others is surely its excellence: it sheds the light of goodness on the future, and does not allow minds to be weakened or to fall. Moreover, whoever looks upon a friend looks, as it were, upon a kind of image of himself. Thus absent friends are present, the needy abound, the weak are strong, and, what is harder to say, the dead live: so great is the honour, memory, and longing with which friends follow them. From this, the death of the former seems blessed, and the life of the latter praiseworthy. But if by examples from the nature of things the union of goodwill were taken away, neither house nor city could stand, nor would even the cultivation of the fields endure. If this is understood less clearly, how great the power of friendship and concord is can be perceived from dissensions and discords. For what house is so stable, what state so firm, that it could not be utterly overthrown by hatreds and dissensions? From this it can be judged how much good there is in friendship.

units.la: Agrigentinum doctum quendam virum carminibus Græcis vaticenatum ferūt, quæ in rerum natura, totoq; mundo constarent, quæq; moverētur, ea cōtrahere amicitiam, dissipare discordiā. Atq; hoc quidem omnes mortales intelligunt, & reprobant. Itaq; si quando aliquod officium extitit amici in periculis aut adeundis, aut communicandis, quis est, qui id non maximis efferat laudibus? Qui clamores tota cavea nuper in hospitiis & amici mei M. Pacuvii fuerunt in nova fabula, cum ignorante rege uter eorum esset Orestes, Pylades Orestem se esse diceret, ut pro illo necaretur: Orestes autem, ita ut erat, Orestem se esse perseveraret? Stantes autem plaudebant in re ficta. Quid arbitramur in vera fuisse facturos? Facile judicabat ipsa natura vim suam, cum homines, quod facere ipsi non possset, id recte fieri in altero judicarent.
units.tr: They report that a certain learned man of Agrigentum, a prophet in Greek verses, taught that the things which stand in the nature of things and in the whole world, and which are moved, are held together by friendship and scattered by discord. And indeed all mortals understand this and approve it. Therefore, if on any occasion a friend's service has appeared in facing or sharing dangers, who is there who does not extol it with the greatest praises? What applause there was throughout the whole theatre recently at the inns of my friend Marcus Pacuvius, in a new play, when, while the king did not know which of them was Orestes, Pylades said that he was Orestes, so that he might be put to death in his place, and Orestes, as he was, persisted in saying that he was Orestes! And the audience stood and applauded in a fictional matter. What do we suppose they would have done in a real one? Nature herself easily judged her own power, when men judged in another person to be right what they themselves could not do.

units.la: Istud quidem. Hactenus proœmium, sequitur ipsa de amicitia disputatio: cuius propositio hoc loco ponitur a Fannio: Lælius disputabit de amicitia. Confirmatur autem quatuor argumentis. 1 sumitur a facto Lælij: quia amicitia mentionem fecit. 2 ab adiuncto otio: sumus otiosi. 3 a fine: facies nobis gratum: qui rursus amplificatur distributione subiectiper comparationem parium: ut mihi,sic etiam Scævola facies gratum. 4. à comparatione parium: ut de aliis rebus, quæ ad disputandum proponuntur, disputare consuevit Lælius: sic quoq; de amicitia disputabit. In hoc vero postremo argumento latet distributio dialogi trimembris: Lælius enim de amicitia dicet, quid sentiat, qualem existimet, & præcepta dabit. Mihi vero erit Scævola confirmat orationem. Fannÿ: eiusq; argumentum à fine petitum per comparationem parium & distributionem subiecti repetit. Ego vero non gravarer. Lælius modestè tergiversatur, & certis de causis disputationem de amicitia se subterfugere simulat: hocq; modo concludit.
units.tr: Thus far the proem; there follows the discussion of friendship itself. Its proposition is laid down at this point by Fannius: Laelius will discourse on friendship. It is confirmed by four arguments. (1) It is taken from the deed of Laelius, because he made mention of friendship. (2) From the attendant circumstance of leisure: we are at leisure. (3) From the end: you will make us grateful; which is again amplified by a subsequent distribution through comparison of equals: as you will make me grateful, so you will make Scaevola grateful too. (4) From the comparison of equals: as Laelius is accustomed to discourse on other matters proposed for debate, so he will also discourse on friendship. Indeed, in this last argument lies the threefold division of the dialogue: for Laelius will say on friendship what he thinks, what sort of thing he judges it to be, and will give precepts. Yes, indeed, it will be [a pleasure]. Scaevola confirms the speech of Fannius, and repeats his argument, taken from the end, through comparison of equals and distribution of the subject. I would not be reluctant. Laelius modestly evades, and feigning that for certain reasons he avoids the discussion of friendship, concludes in this way:

units.la: Si mihi considerem non gravarer de amicitia disputare:
units.tr: If I considered that I should not be reluctant to discourse on friendship:

units.la: At mihi non confido:
units.tr: But I do not trust myself:

units.la: Igitur disputare de amicitia gravor.
units.tr: Therefore I am reluctant to discourse on friendship.

units.la: Ego vero non. Propositionis sententia: cujus consequens probatur adjuncto disputationis hujus, & causa adjuvante. quia disputare de amicitia est res præclara: & otium suppetit. Sed quis ego. Assumptio: quæ seipsum extenuat remotione causarum, facultatis nimirum & doctrinæ: quæ ad dispu-tandas tandas[?] res necessaria sunt. Deinde suo exemplo opponit exempla doctorum, eorumq; Graecorum: qui de omnibus rebus ex tempore differere consueverunt. Tandem subiectum .i. rem ipsam amplificat suo adiuncto, & causa: disputatio de amicitia est magnum opus, & magnam requirit exercitationem. Quamobrem. Complexio syllogismi. Ego vos hortari. Concludit orationem suam Lælius cohortando generos ut amicitiā omnibus rebus anteponant: idq; confirmat comparatione minorum: quia nulla res tantas commoditates continet, quot amicitia. Rationis consequens exornatur distributione subiecti: amicitia est aptissima natura, & convenientissima ad res, easq; velsecundas, vel adversas. Sed hoc primùm. Suscipit tandem disputandi partes, ac primo omniū de subiecto, in quo amicitia versatur, disputat: quod sunt boni viri: nam inter malos nō amicitia, sed factio quaedam & coniuratio est: ut præclarè sentit Sallustius. Neque id ad vivum. Explicat suam de bonis viris sententiam: idq; facit contentione definitionis Stoicorum, & vulgi. Propositio igitur exponitur dissimili: non exactè & morosè boni viri nomè excutio:ut Stoici, quibus subtilius & exactius disputant. Huius antapodosin probat. 1. argumento diversorum: qui illi verè differunt, sed communi utilitati parum serviunt. 2. descriptioni boni viri, què Stoici fingunt: Nam illi contendunt neminem esse bonum virum, nisi sapientem: eam verò sapientiam interpretantur, quæ in hominem cadere non potest. Hanc igitur refutat Cicero argumento diversorum: Non ea quæ finguntur aut optantur, sed ea quæ sunt in vita communi, speranda sunt: quod argumentum rursus amplificatur inductione exemplorum per contradictionem. C. Fabricius, M. Curius, Titus Coruncanus maioribus nostris fuerunt sapientes. Stoicis verò non sunt sapientes. Stoici, ut author est Plutarchus in commentario περὶ εὐδαιμίας [?] sapientem non solum φρονίμον[?] δίκαιον[?] ἀνδρεῖον[?] ἀλλὰ ῥήτορα[?] στρατηγὸν[?] ποιητὴν[?] πλούσιον[?] βασιλέα[?] id est, prudentem, iustum, fortem, sed etiam oratorem, imperatorem, poëtam, divitem, & regem definiunt. Ad vivum. i. presius agere, subtilius & scrupulosius inquirere, indagare, & excutere: methaphora à tondetibus oves avidius, q decebat.
