Agamus igitur Subtilipotius, quàm utili Stoicorum definitioni opponit vulgarem & simplicem sapientis descriptionem, quam illustrat ex oppositis: Sapiens igitur est, qui ita se gerit, & ita vivit, ut eius probetur fides, integritas, æquitas, liberalitas, id est, qui studet virtuti: & in quo nulla est cupiditas. i. avaritia, vel libido, id est, amor impudicus, vel audacia: quia est magna constantia: qui assequitur, quantum homo potest, naturam optimam rectè vivendi ducem. Pingui Minerva. i. simplicius, nō exactè, & exquisitè. Vide Erasmū in chil. adag. 37. Sic. n. mihi perspicere. His verbis formam amicitiæ, qua à propinquitate distinguitur exponit: eam verò amplificat dissimili: in propositione amicitiæ naturalis. i. propinquitatis causas exponit: quarum prior desumitur à fine hominis, qui hominis causa creatus est: altera ab efficienti, quæ est ipsa natura, qua omnes homines cognatione quadam inter se continentur: tertia à materia, quæ sunt cives, peregrini, propinqui, alieni, De gradibus propinquitatis, qui plura requirit, videat Ciceronem. 1 offic. In antapodosi exponit propria utriusq; adjuncta, quibus à se invicem differre intelliguntur: ex propinquitate tolli potest benevolentia citra ejus perniciem & interitum:ex amicitia ve-rò non potest tolli, nisi illa nomen suum amit-tat, & per consequens extinguatur. Quan-ta autem. Probat amicitia formam esse benevolentiam, eamq; amplificat à raro & angusto subiecto:nam amicitia aut inter duos,aut inter paucos jungitur. Est autem amicitia. Definitio amicitia genere suo & forma constans: Genus,est summa consensio: juxta illud Salustij,idem velle,& idem nolle,ea demum firma amicitia est. Forma exprimitur propriis adjunctis, & distributione subiecti:propria adjuncta sunt benevolentia & charitas:subiectum sunt, res divina & humana. Qua quidem haud scio.
units.tr: Indeed I am not. The sense of the proposition, whose consequent is proved by the attendant circumstance of this discussion, with the cause assisting: because to discourse on friendship is a noble thing, and leisure is available. But who am I? The assumption, which diminishes himself by removing the causes, namely of ability and learning, which are necessary for debating matters. Then, by his own example, he sets against it the examples of learned men, and of the Greeks, who were accustomed to discourse on all matters extempore. Finally, he amplifies the subject, that is the matter itself, by its attendant circumstance and cause: discourse on friendship is a great work and requires great practice. Wherefore: the conclusion of the syllogism. I [would] exhort you. Laelius concludes his speech by exhorting the sons-in-law to set friendship above all other things, and confirms this by comparison of lesser things: because no thing contains so many advantages as friendship. The consequence of the reasoning is adorned by a distribution of the subject: friendship is by nature most fitting and most suited to affairs, whether prosperous or adverse. But this first. At last he takes up the parts of the discussion, and first of all discourses on the subject in which friendship is found: that it is among good men; for among the wicked there is no friendship but a kind of faction and conspiracy, as Sallust rightly observes. And not in the strict sense. He explains his own opinion about good men, and does so by contrasting the definition of the Stoics with the common one. The proposition is therefore set out in a dissimilar way: I do not examine the name of good man exactly and sullenly, as the Stoics do, with whom they dispute more subtly and exactly. He proves the counterpart of this by one argument drawn from differing persons: those who truly differ from the Stoics, yet serve the common good little. By a description of the good man, which the Stoics invent: for they contend that no one is a good man except the wise man, and they interpret that wisdom as something which cannot fall to man. Cicero therefore refutes this by an argument drawn from differing persons: not those things which are imagined or wished for, but those things which exist in common life, are to be hoped for; and this argument is again amplified by an induction of examples through contrast: Gaius Fabricius, Marcus Curius, Titus Coruncanius were wise among our ancestors; but they are not wise by the Stoics' reckoning. The Stoics, as Plutarch is the authority in his commentary On Happiness, define the wise man not only as prudent, just, and brave [phronimos, dikaios, andreios], but also as orator, general, poet, rich man, and king [rhētor, stratēgos, poiētēs, plousios, basileus]; that is, prudent, just, brave, and also orator, commander, poet, rich, and king. To the life: that is, to act more precisely, to inquire and search out more subtly and scrupulously, a metaphor from shearers of sheep more eagerly than was fitting. Let us therefore proceed. More subtly than with the useful definition of the Stoics, he opposes the common and simple description of the wise man, which he illustrates by contraries: the wise man, then, is one who so conducts himself and so lives that his faith, integrity, fairness, and liberality are approved, that is, one who strives after virtue, and in whom there is no craving, that is, avarice or lust, that is, shameless love, or rashness, because there is great constancy; who attains, as far as a man can, the best nature as guide to right living. With a fat Minerva: that is, more simply, not exactly and exquisitely. See Erasmus in the Chiliades of Adages, 37. Thus, for I seem to see it clearly. By these words he sets forth the form of friendship, by which it is distinguished from kinship, and he amplifies this by dissimilar means: in the proposition of natural friendship, that is, he sets out the causes of kinship, of which the first is taken from the end of man, who was created for the sake of man; the second from the efficient cause, which is nature herself, by which all men are bound to one another by a certain kinship; the third from matter, which are citizens, foreigners, kinsmen, strangers. On the degrees of kinship, which requires more, let him see Cicero, On Duties, book 1. In the counterpart he sets out the proper attendant circumstances of each, by which they are understood to differ from one another: goodwill can be taken away from kinship without its ruin and destruction; but from friendship it cannot be taken away unless friendship loses its name, and consequently is extinguished. But great. He proves that the form of friendship is goodwill, and amplifies it from a rare and narrow subject: for friendship is joined either between two or among a few. And friendship is. The definition of friendship, constant in its genus and form. The genus is the highest agreement, according to that saying of Sallust: to wish the same and to refuse the same, that alone is firm friendship. The form is expressed by its proper attendant circumstances and by distribution of the subject: its proper attendant circumstances are goodwill and love; the subject is divine and human matters. Which indeed I do not know.

units.la: Definitionem illustrat argumento comparatorum:amicitiam enim dissimiliter cū alijs rebus,qua vulgò appetuntur,comparat ysq;[?] anteponit.In propositione recenset ea qua à vulgò magni estimantur, & amicitia praeferūtur'ut sunt divitiae, bona valetudo, potentia, honores, voluptates: qua omnia suis argumentis extenuantur. Voluptatem igitur primò elevat argumento adversorum:
units.tr: He illustrates the definition with an argument from comparisons: he compares friendship with other things that are commonly sought, and places it above them, in a way unlike the others. In the proposition he lists those things that are commonly held in high esteem and set before friendship: riches, good health, power, honours, pleasures. All of these are weakened by his arguments. First he disposes of pleasure by an argument from its opponents:

units.la: Voluptas belluarum est, igitur non hominis: reliqua vero partim suis adjunctis, partim causa efficienti procreante & conservante per adversa: Sunt enim caduca & incerta, posita non in nostris consiliis, sed in fortunæ temeritate. Qui autem Antapodo-sis, qua amicitia omnibus rebus humanis anteponitur: utpote quæ in virtute posita sit: nam eam hoc loco amicitiæ causam procreantem & conservantem constituit. Iam virtutem. Relabitur ad popularem & communem, quam suprapofuit, virtutis & boni viri descriptionem: virtus siquidem & bonus vir relativa sunt, & se mutuo constituunt. Tales igitur inter. Commendatio amicitiæ ab effectis, cujus propositio generalis est: Sine amicitia vita vitalis esse non potest: prima ejus ratio sumitur a testimonio Ennij Poetæ: altera a distributione vitæ humanæ e subjectis: quæ consistit vel in consiliis & sermonibus communicandis, vel in rebus ipsis administrandis: quæ rursus distribuuntur ex adjuncto in secundas & adversas: illas autem amicitia splendidiores facit, has vero faciliores. Deniq; cæteræ res.
units.tr: Pleasure belongs to beasts, therefore not to man; the rest depend partly on their accompaniments, partly on the efficient cause that produces and preserves them amid adversity. For they are fleeting and uncertain, placed not in our own counsels but in the caprice of fortune. He sets up an antapodosis, in which friendship is placed above all human things, since it rests on virtue; for in this passage he makes virtue the efficient cause that produces and preserves friendship. Now as to virtue: he slides back to the popular and common description of virtue and the good man, which he set before, since virtue and the good man are relative terms and constitute each other. Such people, then, among themselves. A recommendation of friendship from its effects, whose general proposition is: without friendship life cannot be truly alive. Its first reason is drawn from the testimony of the poet Ennius; the second from a division of human life by its subjects, which consists either in communicating counsels and conversation or in managing affairs themselves; these in turn are divided by their accompaniments into prosperous and adverse, and friendship makes the former more splendid and the latter easier to bear. Finally, the other things.

units.la: Exaggerat amicitiæ effecta comparatione dissimili: cuius sensus est: Caterae res omnes, quae expetuntur, singulae aptae & accommodatae sunt singulis rebus: amicitia vero omnibus rebus praesto & necessaria est. Protasin amplificat inductione specierum, opum, honorum, voluptatum: valetudinis: quae singulae ad singulas res accommodantur. In reddi-tione praedictarum specierum fines omnes amicitiae tribuuntur: idq; per distributionem subiecti, temporis, locorum: nam amicitia omnium rerum est tam secundarum quam adversarum, omnium locorum, omnium temporum. Itaq; non aqua. Amplificatio antapodoseos a comparatione parium per negationem imparis: amicitiae enim fines varios & multiplices exaggerat comparatione trium rerum, quibus vita humana carere non potest: ut sunt aqua, ignis, aër. Neque ego nunc. Per prolepsin amicitiam triplicem constituit: ut videlicet declaret, cui tot tantasque utilitates tribuat. Prima igitur est vulgaris: cuius finis est voluptas: subiectum adolescentes, mulierculae, & viri effeminati. Altera est mediocris, cuius finis est utilitas, vitaeque necessitas: subiectum est vulgus & vita communis, in qua versatur & cen& conspicitur. Tertia est vera & perfecta: cuius causa procreans & conservans, est virtus: subiectum boni viri cui soli competunt iam modo commemorata bona. Nam & secundas. Redit ad effecta amicitiae perfectae, eaq; rursus amplificat distributione subiecti: nam amicitia versatur circa res praesentes aut futuras: praesentes vel sunt secundae: quas amicitia splendidiores facit, vel adversae: quas leviores reddit. Res futuras amplificat primo comparatione minorum, cuius nota est cum, tum. Amicitia cum plurimas utilitates, tum vero illam continet, quod praelucet bona spe in posterum, nec debilitari aut desperare animos sinit. Verum enim amicum.
units.tr: He magnifies the effects of friendship by a dissimilar comparison, the sense of which is: all the other things that are sought, taken singly, are suited and adapted to single things; friendship, however, is present and necessary for all things. He amplifies the protasis by enumerating the kinds: wealth, honours, pleasures, health, each of which is adapted to a particular matter. In rendering these kinds, all the ends of friendship are assigned to it, and this by a division of its subject, time and places: for friendship is of all things, both prosperous and adverse, of all places, of all times. Therefore not as water. He amplifies the antapodosis by comparison with things alike, through the negation of the unlike: for he magnifies the varied and manifold ends of friendship by comparing three things without which human life cannot exist, such as water, fire and air. Nor do I now. By prolepsis he sets up a threefold friendship, so as to make clear to which kind he assigns so many and such great advantages. The first, then, is the common kind, whose end is pleasure, and whose subjects are young men, weak women and effeminate men. The second is the middling kind, whose end is utility and the necessity of life; its subject is the crowd and ordinary life, in which one lives and is seen. The third is true and perfect, whose producing and preserving cause is virtue, and whose subject is the good man, to whom alone the goods just mentioned belong. For both the prosperous... He returns to the effects of perfect friendship and amplifies them again by a division of the subject: for friendship concerns present or future things; present things are either prosperous, which friendship makes more splendid, or adverse, which it makes lighter. He amplifies future things first by comparison with lesser things, whose mark is "not only... but also." Friendship not only contains very many advantages, but also this, that it shines a good hope upon the future and does not allow spirits to be weakened or despair. Truly a friend.

units.la: Probat consequens superioris argumenti a testimonio Pythagorae, cuius quidem nomen reticetur, sententia tamen exprimitur: Φιλία inquit, ἴσο̃ς τὴν ψυχὴ ἀλλ᾽ ὁ φίλ ἕτερος αὐτός id est, amicitia aequalitas, una anima, & amicus alter ipse. Unde intelligitur illa, quae sequuntur, contraria, privantia, quod scilicet absentes adsint, egentes abundent, imbecilles valeant, mortui vivant, nō pugnare, neq; hyperbolice dicta esse. Nam dum amicus unus adest, abundat, valet, vi-vit, necesseest ut exemplar ipsius, amicus scilicet quoq; abundet, adsit, valeat, vivat. Alij hunc locum sic interpretantur: absentes adsunt: quia amici absentium non minus meminerunt quam præsentium: egentes abundant: quia amicorum omnia cōmunia: imbecilles valent: quia quæ ipsi per se non possunt per amicos exequuntur: mortui viuunt: qa à superstitibus amicis honorantur & desiderantur. Quod si excmeris. Amicitiæ effecta amplificat à contrario: quia sine amicitia vita humana consistere non potest.
units.tr: He proves the consequence of the previous argument by the testimony of Pythagoras, whose name is indeed left unmentioned, though the saying is expressed: "Friendship," he says, "is equality, one soul, and a friend is another self" [Φιλία ἰσότης, τὴν ψυχὴ ἀλλ' ὁ φίλος ἕτερος αὐτός]; that is, friendship is equality, one soul, and a friend another self. Hence it is understood that those things which follow, contrary and privative, namely that the absent are present, the needy abound, the weak are strong, the dead live, do not conflict with this nor are said hyperbolically. For while one friend is present, he abounds, is strong, lives; it is necessary that his counterpart, that is, his friend too, abound, be present, be strong, live. Others interpret this passage thus: the absent are present, because friends remember absent friends no less than present ones; the needy abound, because all things are common among friends; the weak are strong, because what they cannot do by themselves they accomplish through friends; the dead live, because they are honoured and missed by surviving friends. But if you should object... He amplifies the effects of friendship from the contrary: because human life cannot subsist without friendship.

units.la: Notandum autem vitam humanam è subiecto tripliciter considerari: aut enim versatur in domo, aut in urbe, aut in agris. Illa itaq; tria sine amicitia stare non posse rursus probat à contrariorum effectis: nam domus urbes, & agri discordiis, dissensionibus & odiis labefactantur, & evertuntur. Deinde idem probat testimonio Empedoclis Pythagoræi: cuius carmina à Lacertio referuntur:
units.tr: It must be noted that human life is considered threefold with respect to its subject: for it is conducted either in the household, or in the city, or in the fields. He proves again, from the effects of contraries, that these three cannot stand without friendship: for households, cities and fields are shaken and overthrown by discords, dissensions and hatreds. Then he proves the same by the testimony of Empedocles the Pythagorean, whose verses are related by Laertius:

units.la: Ἄλλοτε μὲν φιλότητι συνερχόμενα εἰς ἓν ἅπαντα τα, Ἄλλοτε δ' αὖ δίχα ἕκαστα φορεύμενα νείκεος ἔχθει.
units.tr: Ἄλλοτε μὲν φιλότητι συνερχόμενα εἰς ἓν ἅπαντα τα, Ἄλλοτε δ' αὖ δίχα ἕκαστα φορεύμενα νείκεος ἔχθει. [Sometimes all things come together into one through love; at other times again each is carried apart by the hatred of strife.]

units.la: Nonnunquam connectit amor simul omnia, rursus.
units.tr: Sometimes love binds all things together, and again,

units.la: Nonnunquam seiuncta iubet contentio ferri.
units.tr: Sometimes strife bids them be borne apart and separated.

units.la: Vt vero testimonium maiorem authoritate habeat, eius authorem commendat ab adiuncta patria & sapientia. Atq; hoc quidem. Concludit primam dialogi partem reprehendendo hominum perversitate, qui laudant eos, qui fideles erga amicos sunt, ipsi vero tales imitari nolunt: id quod declarat fabuloso Pyladis & Orestis exemplo.
units.tr: So that the testimony may carry greater authority, he commends its author from his native land and wisdom. And this indeed. He concludes the first part of the dialogue by rebuking the perversity of men, who praise those who are faithful towards friends, yet are unwilling themselves to imitate such men; this he declares by the fabled example of Pylades and Orestes.

units.la: Hactenus mihi videor de amicitia cp [?] sentire potissimè dixisse: si qua praeterea sunt (credo autem esse multa) ab iis, si videbitur, qui ista disputant, quaeritote.
units.tr: Thus far it seems to me that I have spoken most of what I think about friendship; if there are any other things besides (I believe there are many), ask them, if it seems good, of those who discuss these matters.

units.la: FANNIUS. Nos autem a te potius quamquam, etiam ab istis, saepe quaesivi, & audivi non invitus, equidem, sed aliud quoddam expetimus filum orationis tuae.
units.tr: FANNIUS. But we have often asked you, rather than those others, and I have heard you not unwillingly, indeed; but we desire a certain other thread of your discourse.

units.la: SCAEUOLA. Tu magis id diceres, Fanni, si nuper in hortis Scipionis, cum est de Rep. disputatum, assuefes, qualis tum patronus iustitiae fuit contra accuratam orationem Philii. Fannivs. facile id quidem fuit, iustiti-am iustissimo viro defendere. Scaevola. Quid amicitiam? nonne facile ei erit, qui obeam summa fide, constantia, iuftitiaq; seruatam, maximam ceperit gloriam? Laelivs. vim hoc quidem eftafferre[?]. Quid enim refert qua me ratione cogatis? Cogitis certè: studiis enim generorum, præsertim in re bona, cum difficile est, tum ne æquû quidem obsistere. Sæpissime igitur mihi de amicitia cogitanti, maxime illud considerandum videri solet, num propter imbecillitatem, atq; inopiam desideranda fit amicitia: ut in dandis, recipiendisq; meritis, quod quifq; minus per fe posset, id acciperet ab alio viciffimq; redderet: an effet hoc quidem proprium amicitiæ, sed antiquior, & pulchrior, & magis à natura ipsa profecta alia causa effet. Amor enim (ex quo amicitia est nominata) princeps est ad benevolentiam coniungendam. Nam utilitates quidem etiam ab iis percipientur sæpe, qui simulatione amicitiæ coluntur, & obseruantur causa temporis. ris. In amicitia autem nihil fictum, nil simulatum, & quicquid in ea est, idem verum & voluntarium est. Quapropter a natura mihi videtur potius, quâ ab imbecillitate orta amicitia, & applicatione magis animi cum quodam sui amandi, quàm cogitatione, quantum illa res utilitatis effet habitura. Quod quidem quale sit, etiam in bestiis quibusdam animadverti potest, quæ ex se natos ita amant, ad quoddam tempus, & ab iis ita amantur, ut facile earum appareat sensus. Quod in homine multo est euidentius. Primum ex ea charitate quæ est inter natos & parentes quæ dirimi (nisi detestabili scelere) nō potest. Deinde cum similis sensus extitit amoris, si aliquem nacti sumus, cuius cum moribus & natura congruamus, quod in eo quasi lumen aliquod probitatis & virtutis perspicere videamur. Nihil est enim amabilius virtute, nihil ꝑ[?] magis alliciat homines ad diligendum: quippe cum propter virtutem & probitate eos etiam, quos nunquam vidimus, quodam modo diligamus; Quis est, qui C. Fabritii,M.Curii cum charitate aliqua, & benevolentia memoriam non usurper,quos nunquam viderit? Quis aute est,qui Tarquinium Superbu, qui S P. Callium, S P. Melium nō oderit? Cū duobus ducibus de imperio in Italia de certatum est, Pyrrho,& Annibale: ab altero propter probitatem eius nominis,non alienos animos habemus: Alterum propter crudelitatem eius semper haec civitas oderit.Quod si tanta vis probitatis est, ut eam vel in eis, quos nunquam vidimus,vel quod maiuseft in hoste etiam diligamus:quid mirum est,si animi hominum moveantur,cū eorum,quibus cum usu coniuncti esse possint,virtutem,& bonitatem perspicere videantur?Quanquam confirmatur amor,& beneficio accepto, & studio perspecto,& consuetudine adiuncta,quibus reb.ad illum primum motum animi,& amoris adhibitis, admirabilis quaedam exardescit benevolentiae magnitudo:quam si qui putant ab imbecillitate proficisci,ut fit per quam quisque assequatur quod desideret, humihumilem lanè relinquunt, & minimè generosum[?](ut ita dicam)ortum amicitiæ,quam ex inopia,atq; indigentia nasci volunt.Quod si ita esset,ut quisq; valetudinis minimum in se esse arbitaretur,ita ad amicitiam esset aptissimus: quod longe secus est. Vt enim quisq; sibi plurimum confidit, & ut quisq; maxime virtute & sapientia sic munitus est,ut nullo egeat,fuaq;omnia in ipso posita iudicet,ita in amicitiis expetendis[?],colendisq; maxime excellit. Quid enim erat Affricanus indigens mei?Minimè hercle.At ne ego quidem illius; sed ego admiratione quadam virtutis eius,ille vicissim opinione fortassis nonnulla,quam de meis moribus habebat, me dilexit: auxit benevolentiam consuetudo.Sed quanquam utilitates multæ & magnæ consequutæ sunt, nō sunt tamen ab earum spe causæ diligendi profectæ. Vt enim benefici, liberalesq; sumus,non ut exigamus gratiam( neq; enim beneficium fœneramur, sed natura propensi ad liberalitatem sumus) sic amicitiam non spe mercedis adducti, sed quod omnis eius fructus in ipso amore est, expetendam putamus. Ab iis qui pecudum ritu ad voluptatem omnia referunt, longe dissentimus. Nec mirum: nihil enim altum, nil magnificum, ac divinum suspicere possunt, qui suas omnes cogitationes abiecerunt in rem tam humilem, tamque contemptam. Quamobrem hos quidem ab hoc sermone removeamus: ipsi autem intelligamus a natura signi sensum diligendi: & benevolentiæ charitatem facta significatione probitatis: quam qui appetiverunt, applicant sese, & propius admovent, ut & usu eius, quem diligere coeperunt, fruantur, & moribus, sintque pares in amore, & æquales, propensioresque; ad bene merendum, quam ad reposcendum. Atque hæc inter eos sit honesta certatio.
units.tr: SCAEVOLA. You would say so more, Fannius, if you remembered how, not long ago in the gardens of Scipio, when the Republic was discussed, what a champion of justice he was against the careful speech of Philus. FANNIUS. That indeed was easy: to defend justice before the most just of men. SCAEVOLA. And what of friendship? Will it not be easy for one who has kept it with the greatest loyalty, constancy and justice, and has won the greatest glory? LAELIUS. This, indeed, is a matter for force to bring out. For what does it matter by what reasoning you compel me? You do compel me, certainly: for to the wishes of kinsmen, especially in a good cause, it is both difficult and not even right to resist. Therefore, when I think about friendship, it is usually most of all this that seems worth considering: whether friendship is to be desired on account of weakness and want, so that in giving and receiving services each person may receive from another what he could not do by himself and in turn repay it; or whether this would indeed be a property of friendship, but another cause, older, more beautiful, and proceeding more from nature itself, were the true one. For love (from which friendship has its name) is the first thing that joins goodwill. For advantages are often gained even from those who are courted and observed under the pretence of friendship, for the sake of the moment. In true friendship, however, nothing is feigned or counterfeit, and whatever is in it is both true and voluntary. Wherefore friendship seems to me to arise from nature rather than from weakness, and from a kind of inclination of the mind towards loving itself, rather than from calculating how much advantage that thing would bring. How this is so can be noticed even in certain beasts, which love their offspring and are loved by them for a certain time, so that the feeling is plainly evident. In man it is far more evident: first from that affection which exists between children and parents, which cannot be dissolved (except by a detestable crime). Then, when a similar feeling of love arises, if we have found someone whose character and nature agree with ours, in whom we seem to perceive a kind of light of probity and virtue. For nothing is more lovable than virtue, nothing attracts men more to love; since by virtue and probity we in a way love even those whom we have never seen. Who is there who does not recall Gaius Fabricius and Manius Curius with some affection and goodwill, though he has never seen them? And who is there who does not hate Tarquin the Proud, or Spurius Cassius, or Spurius Maelius? When two generals contended in Italy for supremacy, Pyrrhus and Hannibal: towards the one, on account of the probity of his name, we do not have unfriendly feelings; the other, on account of his cruelty, this city will always hate. But if there is such a power of probity that we love it even in those whom we have never seen, or, what is greater, even in an enemy, what wonder is it if men's minds are stirred when they seem to perceive virtue and goodness in those with whom they can be joined by intercourse? Although love is strengthened both by a benefit received, and by observed zeal, and by added familiarity; and when these things are applied to that first movement of mind and love, a wonderful greatness of goodwill flares up. Those who think that this proceeds from weakness, as happens when someone seeks through another what he desires, leave the origin of friendship very humble indeed, and by no means noble (so to speak), wanting it to be born from want and need. But if it were so, that each person would be most fit for friendship in proportion as he judged himself to have the least need of it; and it is far otherwise. For in seeking and cultivating friendships, the more each person trusts in himself, and the more he is fortified by virtue and wisdom so as to need nothing and to judge all his concerns to lie in himself, the more he excels. For what did Africanus need from me? Certainly nothing, by Hercules. Nor indeed did I need anything from him; but I loved him from a certain admiration of his virtue, and he in turn loved me, perhaps somewhat from the opinion he had of my character; familiarity increased the goodwill. But although many and great advantages have followed, yet the reasons for loving did not proceed from the hope of these. For just as we are generous and liberal, not so that we may demand gratitude (for we do not lend out a benefit at interest, but we are naturally inclined to liberality), so we think friendship worth seeking, not because we are drawn by hope of reward, but because all its fruit lies in love itself. We strongly dissent from those who refer everything to pleasure after the manner of cattle. Nor is this surprising: for those who have cast all their thoughts into a matter so humble and so despised can conceive nothing lofty, nothing magnificent or divine. Wherefore let us remove these from this discussion; but let us ourselves understand that the sense of loving comes from nature, and the affection of goodwill from the manifest sign of probity; those who desire these draw near and bring themselves closer, so that they may enjoy both the use of the one they have begun to love, and their manners, and may be equal and alike in love, and more inclined to do good than to demand back. And let this be the honourable rivalry between them.

units.la: Sic & utilitates ex amicitia maximæ capientur, & erit ejus ortus a natura, quâ ab imbecillitate, & gravior, & verior. Nam si utilitas amicitias conglutinaret, eadem commutata dissolveret. Sed quia natura mutari non potest, idcirco vere amicitiæ sempiternæ sunt.
units.tr: Thus the greatest advantages will also be gained from friendship, and its origin will be from nature, by which it is both weightier and truer than from weakness. For if utility bound friendships together, the same utility, once changed, would dissolve them. But since nature cannot be changed, therefore true friendships are everlasting.

units.la: Hactenus mihi, Conclusio prima partis, qua Lælius, quid de amicitia sentiret, expositi: cum appodioxi longioris disputationis, & cohortatione, utab aliis, qui ista disputant plura quærant. Nos autem àtc. Fannius respondet Lælio argumento minorum & dissimili: Quærimus cum ab aliis, tùm vero à te: neq; volumus ut tali, quali cæteri, orationis genere utaris. Filum. Genus, materiam, ornatum: metaphora à textoribus sumpta. Tu magis. Confirmatio orationis Fannij à facto Lalij: quod describitur à subjecto loco subjecta materia & adversario. Facile id. Confirmatio facti Lalij argumento coniugatorum; facile fuit iustissimo viro iustitiam defendere: atq; hoc modo Lælio non solum eloquentia, sed iustitia quoq; laus tribuitur. Quid amiciti-am Scævola arripit idem argumentum à coniugatis, & ad amicitiam transfert, videturq; argumetari à pari: Vt facile fuit iustissimo viro iustitiam defendere: sic facile erit amicitia gloria excellenti amicitiam defendere. Vbi exprimuntur tres amicitiæ causæ confervantes,fides,iustitia,cõstantia. Vim quidem. Assentitur tandem La-lius, & argumentatur à relatis: Non possum vestræ petitioni non satisfacere: quia gene-ri mei estis: id autem amplificat duplici co-paratione minori: cum difficile est tum iniquum, cum in aliis rebus, tum in re bona stu-dys generorum repugnare. Sæpissime igitur: Hoc loco explicat qualem amicitiam existimet, id est eius causas efficientes, & conservantes inquirit: quas in natura & virtute constituit: atque hoc modo concludit.
units.tr: Hitherto, my friend, the first conclusion of the part in which Laelius set out what he thought about friendship, with an appendix of a longer discussion and an exhortation, so that others who discuss these matters may seek more. But we now... Fannius answers Laelius with an argument from the lesser and the unlike: We ask this of others, and above all of you; nor do we want you to use the kind of style the others use. The thread. Genus, matter, ornament: a metaphor taken from weavers. You rather. Confirmation of Fannius's speech from the deed of Laelius, which is described from the subject place, the subject matter and the opponent. That was easy. Confirmation of the deed of Laelius by the argument from the married: it was easy for a most just man to defend justice; and in this way Laelius is praised not only for eloquence but for justice too. What of friendship. Scaevola seizes the same argument from the married and transfers it to friendship, and seems to argue from parity: as it was easy for a most just man to defend justice, so it will be easy for a man of outstanding glory to defend friendship. Here three causes of friendship that preserve it are expressed: faith, justice, constancy. Indeed the force. Laelius at last assents and argues from relatives: I cannot refuse your request, because you are my sons-in-law; this he amplifies by a double comparison from the lesser: it is both difficult and unjust to oppose sons-in-law, in other matters as well as in a good study. Most often therefore: Here he explains what kind of friendship he thinks it is, that is, he inquires into its efficient and preserving causes, which he places in nature and virtue; and in this way he concludes.

units.la: Aut ab utilitatis spe, aut à virtute oritur amicitia.
units.tr: Friendship arises either from the hope of advantage or from virtue.

units.la: Sed non oritur ab utilitatis spe.
units.tr: But it does not arise from the hope of advantage.

units.la: Igitur à virtute.
units.tr: Therefore it arises from virtue.

units.la: Num propter. Propositio: ita cuius consequente observanda notatio amicitiæ à causa: amicitia, ex amore, unde orta est, nominatur: unde colligit amicitiæ appetitum hominis naturalem esse. Nam utilitates. Assumptio: ab utilitatis spe non oritur amicitia: id quod confirmat argumento contrariorum: utilitates etiam percipiuntur ab iis, qui simulatione colunturin amicitia autem ni-
units.tr: Not on account of. Proposition: thus, in the consequent, the notation of friendship from its cause is to be observed: friendship is named from love (amor), from which it has arisen; from this he gathers that the human appetite for friendship is natural. For advantages. Assumption: friendship does not arise from the hope of advantage; this he confirms by the argument of contraries: advantages are also gained by those who are cultivated in friendship by pretence; but in friendship nothing

units.la: hilfictum, nihil falsum, sed omnia vera & voluntaria. Quapropter. Complexio expositia argumento maiorum bimembri: a natura potius quam imbecillitate: & applicatione potius cum quodam sensu amandi, quam cogitatione quantum illa res utilitatis sit habitura, orta videtur amicitia.
units.tr: is feigned, nothing false, but all things are true and voluntary. Wherefore. An expository complex, by the argument from the greater, in two parts: friendship seems to arise from nature rather than from weakness, and from an application accompanied by a certain feeling of love rather than from the thought of how much advantage the thing will bring.

units.la: Quod quidem quale. Illustrat complexionem comparatione minorum: quod si bestiae suos foetus non ipse natura diligunt, sed impulsu naturae: quanto magis idem in homine fieri debet. Hac de re si plura scire laboras, lege commentarium Plutarchi de amore prolis. Nihil est enim. Comparationis apodosin probat adiunctis & effectis virtutis: quae proponuntur argumento pari, hoc modo: Si quid est amabile, amabilis est virtus, si quid allicit ad diligendum allicit virtus. Et hoc rursus probat signis i.e. effectis: Virtus efficit ut etiam ignotos diligamus: id quod probat contrariis exemplis, C. Fabricii, M. Curii, Tarquinii, Sp. Cassii, Sp. Melii, Pyrrhi & Hannibalis: nam illos propter virtutem omnes diligunt, hos vero propter improbitatem omnes oderunt. Quod si tanta. Concludit virtutis effecta ex superioribus exemplis per comparationem minorum: Si virtutis tanta vis est, ut eam non solum in ignoto sed etiam in hoste diligamus: quanto magis in iis cum quibus vivimus, quosq; non vivimus, eam diligemus. Quanquam.
units.tr: Which indeed how. He illustrates the complex by a comparison from the lesser: if beasts do not love their offspring by nature itself but by a natural impulse, how much more ought the same to happen in man. If you labour to know more about this matter, read Plutarch's treatise on love of offspring. For there is nothing. He proves the apodosis of the comparison by the adjuncts and effects of virtue, which are set forth by a parallel argument in this way: if anything is lovable, virtue is lovable; if anything attracts us to love, virtue attracts us. And he proves this again by signs, that is, by effects: virtue makes us love even those we do not know; this he proves by contrary examples: Gaius Fabricius, Marcus Curius, Tarquin, Spurius Cassius, Spurius Maelius, Pyrrhus and Hannibal; for all love the former on account of their virtue, but all hate the latter on account of their wickedness. But if so great. He concludes the effects of virtue from the preceding examples by a comparison from the lesser: if virtue has such power that we love it not only in a stranger but even in an enemy, how much more shall we love it in those with whom we live, and those with whom we do not live. Although.

units.la: Per concessionem attingit causas conservantes amicitiam, quae sunt beneficii acceptum, studium perspectum, & consuetudo adiuncta. Non tamen esse primos, amicitiae motum probat argumento contrariorum quia hoc modo amicitiae ortus humilis & abiectus, minime vero generosus relinquetur.
units.tr: By concession he touches on the causes that preserve friendship, which are the received benefit, the perceived zeal, and the attached habit. He proves, however, that these are not the first movers of friendship by the argument of contraries, since in this way the origin of friendship would be low and abject, and by no means noble.

units.la: Quod si ita effer[?]. Spem utilitatis non esse causam amicitiae procreantem probat ta li syllogismo connexo:
units.tr: But if it is so... He proves by the following connected syllogism that the hope of advantage is not the cause that begets friendship:

units.la: Quod si amicitia ab imbecillitate & spe utilitatis proficisceretur, ut quisq; minimum in se esse arbitraretur, ita ad amicitiam esset aptissimus:
units.tr: But if friendship proceeded from weakness and the hope of advantage, so that each man thought himself least in himself, he would be most fit for friendship in that measure:

units.la: At consequens falsum est:
units.tr: But the consequent is false:

units.la: Falsum igitur antecedens.
units.tr: Therefore the antecedent is false.

units.la: Quod si. Propositio: cuius consequens augetur comparatione parium. Quod longe secus. Assumptionis sententia confirmata a contrario per comparationem parium. Vt quisq; sibi plurimum confidit, & om-nia sua nia sua in se posita esse ducit, nullo[?] eget: ita in amicitiis expetendus, & colendis excellit.
units.tr: But if... Proposition: the consequent of which is amplified by a comparison of equals. Far otherwise. The sense of the assumption is confirmed from the contrary by a comparison of equals: as each man trusts himself most and considers all his goods to be placed in himself, and needs nothing, so he excels in being sought after and cultivated in friendships.

units.la: Quid enim. Alia assumptionis proba-tio ab exemplo Scipionis & Lalii: quorum amicitiæ causa falsa, utilitatis nimirum spes primo removetur: deinde causæ procreantes quæ fuerunt admiratio virtutis, opinio de moribus, & conservans, quæ fuit consuetu-do, exponuntur. Sed quanquam Prole-psis, quæ argumento diversorum respondet obiectioni: quamq; magnæ utilitates ex nostra amicitia ceperimus, non tamen illæ causæ fuerunt amicitiæ idq; illustrat comparatione similium, cuius sensus est. Ut liberalitatis causa non est exactio gratiæ, aut fœnus beneficii sed ipsa natura sic amicitiæ causa nō est utilitatis spes, sed amor à natura insitus, quod rursus amplificat à repugnanti sententia eorum, qui omnia ad voluptatem pecudum ritu referunt. Quamobrem. Complexio syllogismi: in qua tres gradus amicitiæ exponuntur, è quibus prima & principalis amicitiæ causa cognoscitur: primus gradus est significatio probitatis, à qua gignitur sensus amandi: alter est appetitio eius probitatis, ad eamq; propior applicatio: tertius gradus est bene promerendi studium. Nam ii [?] utilitas. Vtilitatem non conglutinare amicitias probat a contrario, tali syllogismo connexo concludit:
units.tr: For indeed. Another proof of the assumption from the example of Scipio and Laelius: the false cause of their friendship, namely the hope of advantage, is first removed; then the begetting causes, which were admiration of virtue and the opinion about manners, are set out, and the preserving cause, which was habit. But although a prolepsis, which answers an objection by the argument of those who differ, [is used], and although we have gained great advantages from our friendship, yet those were not the causes of friendship; and he illustrates this by a comparison of similars, whose sense is this: as the cause of generosity is not the exacting of gratitude nor the interest of a benefit, but generosity itself, so the cause of friendship is not the hope of advantage, but love implanted by nature; which again he amplifies from the opposing opinion of those who refer everything to pleasure after the manner of cattle. Wherefore. A complex of the syllogism, in which three degrees of friendship are set out, from which the first and principal cause of friendship is known: the first degree is the signification of goodness, from which the feeling of loving is begotten; the second is the desire for that goodness and a nearer application to it; the third degree is the zeal to deserve well. For those [...] advantage. He proves from the contrary that utility does not bind friendships together, and concludes by the following connected syllogism:

units.la: Si utilitas amicitiam conglutinaret, eadem commutata dissolveret: Sed consequens falsum: natura enim mutari non potest idcirco vera ami-citiae sempiternae sunt. Igitur & antecedens.
units.tr: If utility bound friendship together, the same utility, once changed, would dissolve it: but the consequent is false; for nature cannot be changed, therefore true friendships are everlasting. Therefore the antecedent too.

units.la: Ortum quidem amicitiae videtis, nisi quid adhuc forte vultis. SCAEVOLA. Tu vero perge Laelj, pro hoc enim qui minor est natu, meo iure respondeo, FANNIVS. Recte tu quidem, quamobrem audiamus. LAELIVS. Audite vero optimi viri ea, quae sæpissime inter me, & Scipionem de amicitia disserebantur, quanquam ille quidem nihil difficilius esse dicebat, quàm amicitiam usq; ad extremum vitae diem permanere. Nam vel ut non idem expediret utriq; incidere sæpe, vel ut de Re-pub. non idem sentiret. Mutari etiam mores hominum sæpè dicebat, aliàs adversis rebus, alias ætate ingravescen-te. Atq; earum rerum exemplum ex si-militudine capiebat incuntis ætatis, quod summi puerorum amores sæpe una cum prætexta, & toga deponeren-tur. Sin autem ad adolescentiam per-duxissent, dirimi tamen interdum contentione, vel uxoriæ conditionis vel commodi alicujus, quod idem adipis-ci uterq; non posset. Quod si qui longius in amicitia provecti essent, tamen sæpe labefactari, si in honoris contentionem incidissent. Pestem enim majorem nullam esse in amicitiis, quam in plerisq; pecuniæ cupiditatem, in optimis quibusq; honoris certamen, & gloriæ: ex quo inimicitias maximas sæpe inter amicissimos extitisse. Magna etiam dissidia, & plerunq; iusta nasci cum aliquid ab amicis, qd[?] rectum non esset, postularetur, ut aurlibidinis[?] ministri, aut adiutores essent ad iniuriam. Quod qui recusarent, quamuis honeste id facerent, ius tamen amicitiæ deserere arguerentur ab iis, quibus obsequi nollent: illos autem, qui quid vis ab amico auderent postulare, postulatio-ne ipsa profiteri omnia se amici causa esse facturos. Quorū querela inveterata non modo familiaritates extingui solere, sed etiam odia gigni maxima, atque sempiterna. Haec ita multa quasi fato impedere amicitiis, ut omnia subterfugere non modo sapientiæ, sed etiam felicitatis diceret sibi videri
units.tr: You see the origin of friendship, unless perhaps you wish something further. SCAEVOLA. Do you go on, Laelius; for in this matter I, who am the younger by birth, rightly answer on my own right. FANNIUS. Rightly indeed; let us therefore hear you. LAELIUS. Listen then, best of men, to what was most often debated between Scipio and me about friendship, although he used to say that nothing is more difficult than for friendship to last to the last day of life. For either it often happened that the same thing was not advantageous to both, or that he did not think the same about the commonwealth. He also often said that the characters of men change, sometimes through adverse circumstances, sometimes as age advances. And he took an example of these things from the likeness of boys who are entering on life: the greatest loves of boys were often laid aside together with the bordered robe and the toga. But if they had carried their friendship on into adolescence, still at times they were broken off by rivalry, either over a marriage or over some advantage which both could not obtain. And if others had advanced further in friendship, yet they were often shaken if they fell into a contest for office. For he said there is no greater pest in friendships than, in most men, the desire for money, and in the best men the contest for honour and glory; from which the greatest enmities have often arisen even between the closest friends. Great quarrels also, and generally just ones, arise when something not right is demanded of friends, as that they should be the servants or helpers of one's lust or of an injury. Those who refuse, even though they do so honourably, are charged with abandoning the right of friendship by those whom they refuse to obey; but those who dare to demand anything at all from a friend profess, by the very demand, that they will do everything for the sake of the friend. From the long-standing complaints of these, he said, not only do intimacies usually die out, but the greatest and everlasting hatreds are born. He said that these many things, as if by fate, hinder friendships, so that to escape them all seemed to him a mark not only of wisdom but of happiness.

units.la: Ortum quidem. Concludit disputa-tionem de causis efficientibus, & hortatu ge-nerorum progreditur ad explicationem cau-sarum, quibus amicitia extinguitur. Ponit igitur primo generalem propositionem, eam-q; confirmat testimonio Scipionis & amplificat argumento parium: nihil difficilius est ut Scipioni videbatur, quam amicitiam ad extremum vitæ diem permanere. Consequens probatur primo inductione trium causarum, quibus amicitia tollitur: 1.est non eadem utilitas: 2.diversa de Repub sententia: 3.mutatio morū: cuius duæ causæ adduntur, res scilicet adversa, & ætas ingravescens. Atq; earum. Altera probatio sumitur à distinctione ætatum duplici,in quibus sin-gulis gulis amicitia facile deponitur aut dirimi-tur. Prima aetas est pueritia: cuius amicitia dissolvendi nullas causas exponit: quia res per se nota est, ut nulla probatione indigeat. Altera est adolescentia: in qua amicitia dis-solvenda duae causae proponuntur, contētio vx-oria conditionis, & eiusdem commodi appe-titio. Tertia est constans sive virilis aetas: in qua amicitia interitus tres causae afferun-tur. Duae priores proponuntur comparatio-ne parium, ornantur metaphora, & ampli-ficantur distributione subiecti, & effectis: comparatio parium intelligitur ex negatio-ne imparis: metaphora continetur in voca-bulo pestis: subiectum sunt vulgus, in quo in-est prima causa, pecunia scilicet cupiditas. deinde boni viri, in quibus est altera, conte-tio bonorum: Effecta sunt inimicitia maxi-ma: quae amplificantur subiecto, quod sunt amicissimi. Tertia causa est postulatio iniqua & iniusta, eiusq; recusatio: quae suis argumen-tis amplificatur: primum petitur a proprio amicitia adiuncto: quod est summa studio-rum & voluntatum consensio: alterum ab adiuncto i. affectione & voluntate eorum, qui iniusta postulant: idq; rursus videtur augeri comparatione parium: quod enim petunt ab amicis, idem facturi erant pro ami-cis: tertium ab effectus per comparationem minorum. hinc namq; non solum amicitiae extinguuntur, sed etiam odia gignuntur maxima & sempiterna. Haec quasi. Concludit hunc locum exponens causam tot tantorum malorum, quae est fatum, id est, ine-vitabilis quaedam necessitas: deinde explicat causas quibus ista mala avertuntur per comparationem minorum: subterfugiuntur enim non solum sapientia, sed etiam felicitate.
units.tr: Ortum quidem. The author concludes the discussion of efficient causes and, with the exhortation of the great men, proceeds to explain the causes by which friendship is extinguished. He therefore first puts forward a general proposition and confirms it by the testimony of Scipio and amplifies it with the argument from equals: nothing, as it seemed to Scipio, is more difficult than for friendship to last until the last day of life. The consequence is proved first by the induction of three causes by which friendship is destroyed: (1) the interests are no longer the same; (2) the opinions about the commonwealth are different; (3) the characters change. To these two causes are added: adverse circumstances, and advancing age. And of these. The second proof is taken from a twofold distinction of ages, in each of which friendship is easily laid aside or dissolved. The first age is childhood: for it sets out no causes of dissolving friendship in that age, because the matter is known of itself and needs no proof. The second is adolescence: in which two causes of dissolving friendship are proposed, the victorious rivalry over a condition, and the pursuit of the same advantage. The third is the settled or manly age: in which three causes of the destruction of friendship are given. The first two are set out by the comparison of equals, adorned by a metaphor, and amplified by the distribution of the subject and the effects: the comparison of equals is understood from the denial of unequals; the metaphor is contained in the word "pest"; the subjects are the common people, in whom the first cause lies, namely the desire for money; then good men, in whom is the second, the rivalry of the good. The effects are the greatest enmities, which are amplified by the subject, since they are very close friends. The third cause is an unjust and unfair demand, and the refusal of it; this is amplified by its own arguments: first, it is sought from what is proper to friendship, namely the greatest agreement of pursuits and wills; second, from what is attached to it, that is, the disposition and will of those who make unjust demands; and this again seems to be increased by the comparison of equals: for what they ask of their friends, they would themselves have done for their friends; third, from the effects, through the comparison of lesser things. For from this not only are friendships extinguished, but the greatest and everlasting hatreds are also engendered. "These things as if..." He concludes this passage by setting out the cause of so many and such great evils, which is fate, that is, a certain unavoidable necessity; then he explains the causes by which these evils are averted, by the comparison of lesser things: for they are avoided not only by wisdom but also by happiness.

units.la: Quamobrem id primum videamus si placet, quatenus amor in amicitia progredi debeat. Num si Coriolanus habuit amicos, ferre contra patriam arma illi cum Coriobano debuere? Nam Becillinum amici regnum appetente, num S. P. Melium iuuare debuerunt? Tyberium quidem Gracchum Repub. vexantem a Q.Tuberone, aequalibus-q; amicis derelictū videbamus. At C. Blosius Cumanus hospes nostrae familiae, Scaevola, cum ad me, qui aderam cum Lenate, & Rutilio consulibus in consilio,de precatum venisset,hanc, ut sibi ignoscerem,causam afferebat, q; tanti Tyb. Grachum fecisset,ut quicquid ille vellet,sibi faciendum putaret: Tum ego,etiam nc,inquâ, si te in Capitolium faces ferre vellet? Nunquam, inquit,volujsset id quidem:sed si volusset,parvissem. Videtis quam nefaria vox & hercle ita fecit, vel plus etiam, quam dixit. Non enim paruit ille Tyberii Grachi temeritati,sed etiâ præsuit: nec se comitem illius furoris , sed ducem præbuit.Itaq; hac ametia quæstione nova præterritus in Asiam profugit,ad hostes se cotulit, pœnas reipub. graves,iustasq; persolvit. Nulla est igitur excusatio peccati, si amici causa peccaueris.Nam cùm conciliatrix amicitiæ virtutis opinio fuerit, difficile est amicitiā manere, si à virtute defeceris. Quòd si rectum statuerimus ut concedere amicis quicquid velint,vel impetrare ab amicis quicq; velimus, perfecta quidem sapientia sumus,si nihil habeat res vitii:sed loquimur de iis amicis, qui ante oculos sunt, quos [illegible, ~4 letters]demus,aut de quibus memoriâ accepi- mus,aut quos novit vita communis. Ex hoc numero nobis exempla sumê- da sunt,& eorum quidem maximè,qui ad sapientiam proximè accedunt. Vidi- mus Paulum AEmilium C. Lucinio familiarè fuisse (sic à patribus accepi- mus)bis unaconsules & collegas in cē- sura:tum etiam cum iis,& inter se coniu&tissimos fuisse M. Curium,& T.Co- runcanum memoriæ traditam est.Igi- tur ne suspicari quidem possumus quê- quam horum ab amico quippiam con- tendisse, quod contra fidem, contra iusiurandum,contra rempub.essct. Nam hæc quidem in talibus viris quid atti- net dicere? si contendissent,scio impe- traturos non fuisse,cum illi sanctissimi viri fuerint.AEque autem nefas sit ta- le aliquid & facere rogatum, & rogare. At verò Tyberium Gracchum: sequebantur C. Carbo, C. Cato,& minimè tunc quidem Caio fratri,nunc idem a- cerrimus inimicus.
units.tr: Let us therefore first see, if you please, how far love ought to go in friendship. If Coriolanus had friends, ought they to have borne arms against their country along with him? For when Becillinus aimed at kingship, ought his friends to have helped Spurius Maelius? We saw Tiberius Gracchus, while he was harassing the commonwealth, abandoned by Quintus Tubero and his friends of the same age. But Gaius Blossius of Cumae, a guest of our family, when he came to me, who was present with Scaevola in the council in the consulship of Lenas and Rutilius, to beg pardon, offered this reason for me to forgive him: that he had so esteemed Tiberius Gracchus that he thought he must do whatever he wished. Then I said: "Even if he wished you to carry torches to the Capitol?" "He would never have wished that," he said, "but if he had wished it, I would have obeyed." You see how wicked a saying this was; and indeed he did it, or even more than he said. For he did not merely yield to the recklessness of Tiberius Gracchus, but even led it; he was not his companion in that madness, but offered himself as its leader. And so, driven by this unprecedented frenzy of friendship, he fled into Asia, betook himself to the enemies, and paid the heavy and just penalties to the commonwealth. There is therefore no excuse for a sin if you have sinned for the sake of a friend. For since the opinion of virtue is the originator of friendship, it is difficult for friendship to remain if you have departed from virtue. But if we lay down as right that we should grant our friends whatever they wish, or obtain from our friends whatever we wish, we would indeed be possessors of perfect wisdom, if the matter had no fault. But we are speaking of those friends who are before our eyes, whom we have seen, or of whom we have received report from memory, or whom ordinary life knows. From this number our examples must be taken, and above all of those who come closest to wisdom. We have seen that Paulus Aemilius was intimate with Gaius Lucinius (so we have received from our fathers), twice consuls together and colleagues in the censorship; and it is recorded in memory that Marcus Curius and Tiberius Coruncanius were also most closely united with these and with each other. Therefore we cannot even suspect that any of these men asked anything of a friend that was against good faith, against an oath, or against the commonwealth. For what is the point of saying these things about such men? If they had asked, I know they would not have obtained it, since they were most upright men. And it is equally wrong both to do such a thing when asked and to ask it. But as for Tiberius Gracchus, Gaius Carbo and Gaius Cato followed him, and by no means then against his brother Gaius, who is now his most bitter enemy.

units.la: Quamobrem id primum. Causa po-strema strema dissoluendi amicitiam subÿcit num quæstionem quatenus amor in amicitia progredi debeat .i. quatenus amicis postulantibus aliquid parendum, & obsequendum sit.
units.tr: Therefore, first of all. The last cause of dissolving friendship subjoins the question how far love ought to go in friendship, that is, how far one must comply with and obey friends when they ask something.

units.la: Hanc igitur quæstionem illustrat tribus specialibus exemplis:1.est Coriolani, qui patria bellum intulit:2. est Becillimi:3. Spurÿ Melÿ:quorum uterq; regnum iniuste effectauit.
units.tr: This question he illustrates by three special examples: (1) that of Coriolanus, who made war on his country; (2) that of Becillinus; (3) that of Spurius Maelius; each of whom aimed at kingship unjustly.

units.la: Quæritur igitur si tres isti amicos habuissent, num illis opem & auxilium ferre debuissent. Tyberium.
units.tr: The question therefore is: if these three had been friends, ought they to have brought aid and help to them? Tiberius.

units.la: Antequam ad quæstionem respondeat, proponit duo exempla contraria, quibus probat hanc quæstionem maximè necessariam esse: quippe cū tale quid acciderit. Primum exemplum est Q. Tuberonis & reliquorum amicorum, qui T. Grachum Rempub. oppugnantem dereliquerūt.
units.tr: Before he answers the question, he sets out two contrary examples, by which he proves that this question is most necessary, since something of the kind has happened. The first example is that of Quintus Tubero and the rest of his friends, who abandoned Tiberius Gracchus while he was attacking the commonwealth.

units.la: Alterum est C. Blosÿ Cumani: cuius primo dictum, deinde factum explicatur. Dixit se tanti fecisse T. Grachum improbum ciuē ut in gratiam ipsius omnia sibi faciunda, putârit.
units.tr: The second is that of Gaius Blossius of Cumae: of whom first what he said is explained, then what he did. He said that he had so esteemed Tiberius Gracchus, an unscrupulous citizen, that for his sake he thought everything had to be done for him.

units.la: Factum ejus amplificatur argumento minorum bimembri: plùs fecit quàm dixit: non solum enim paruit temeritati Grachi, sed etiam prafuit, non comes illius, sed dux fuit.
units.tr: His deed is amplified by the argument from lesser things in two members: he did more than he said; for he not only yielded to Gracchus's recklessness, but even led it; he was not his companion, but his leader.

units.la: Hoc verò factum amplificatur denuò
units.tr: Hoc vero factum amplificatur denuo

units.la: à pœna, cuius tres gradus ponuntur: 1. in Asiam exulatum abyt[?]: 2. ad hostes se contulit: 3. pœnas Reipub: persolvit: quia seditionis supplicium luit. Nulla igitur. Hoc demum loco respondet ad quæstionem, amici scilicet causa nullo modo peccandum esse: idq; confirmat à causa efficiente procreante & conservante amicitiæ quæ est virtus. Sensus est: Cum virtus amicitiam conciliet & conser-vet,non potest illa manere si virtutem dese-rueris:[?] cessante enim causa cessat effectum. Quòd si rectum. Alterum argumentum sumitur à distinctione perfecti sapientis, & ejus, qui ad sapientiam pr[?]xime accedit: videtur, tali syllogismo connexo concludi:
units.tr: From the penalty, of which three degrees are set out: (1) he went into exile in Asia; (2) he betook himself to the enemies; (3) he paid the penalties to the commonwealth, because he suffered the punishment of sedition. Therefore there is no excuse. At this point at last he answers the question, namely that on no account must one sin for the sake of a friend; and he confirms this from the efficient cause which both produces and preserves friendship, which is virtue. The meaning is: since virtue both brings about and preserves friendship, friendship cannot remain if you have abandoned virtue; for when the cause ceases, the effect ceases too. But if we lay down as right. A second argument is taken from the distinction between the perfect wise man and one who comes closest to wisdom; it seems to be concluded by a connected syllogism:

units.la: Si omnia amicis quæ volunt, concedimus & contra ab ijs, quæ volumus, impetramus, perfecta sapientia sumus: Sed consequens non est.
units.tr: If we grant our friends everything they want, and conversely obtain from them what we want, we are of perfect wisdom. But this consequence does not hold.

units.la: Igitur nec antecedens esse potest.
units.tr: Igitur nec antecedens esse potest.

units.la: Quòd si rectum. Propositionis sententia in qua prius distinctionis membrum exponitur. Sed loquimur. Assumptio, in qua distinctionis posterius membrum explicatur, & homo minus perfecta sapientia varÿs adiunctis describitur: qui videli-cet est ante oculos, quem videmus, de quo memoria accepimus, quem novit communis vita. Per sapientiam hic intelligo omnes virtutes, quae in hominem cadere possunt: ut in hoc vocabulo sit synecdoche generis. Ex horum numero. Conclusio ornata contrariis exemplis: Cum non simus perfecta sapientia, nec vivamus cum perfectis hominibus, ÿ nobis imitandi sunt, qui quam proxime ad sapientiam accedunt, ÿ contra fugiendi, qui ab ea quam longissime recedunt. Prioris generis exempla quatuor proponuntur, P. Aemilÿ, C. Lucinÿ, M. Curÿ, T. Coruncanÿ: ubi notanda est descriptio rerum turpium: quae sunt contra fidem: contra jus-jurandum, contra Rempub. Posterioris modi exempla duo afferuntur, C. Carbonis & C. Catonis.
units.tr: But if we lay down as right. The sense of the proposition, in which the first member of the distinction is set out. But we are speaking. The assumption, in which the second member of the distinction is explained, and the man of less than perfect wisdom is described by various attributes: namely, the one who is before our eyes, whom we see, of whom we have received report from memory, whom ordinary life knows. By wisdom I here understand all the virtues that can fall to a human being, so that in this word there is a synecdoche of the genus. From this number. The conclusion, adorned with contrary examples: since we are not of perfect wisdom, nor do we live with perfect men, we must imitate those who come as near as possible to wisdom, and on the contrary shun those who recede from it as far as possible. Four examples of the former kind are set out: Publius Aemilius, Gaius Lucinius, Marcus Curius, Tiberius Coruncanius; where the description of shameful things is to be noted: they are against good faith, against an oath, against the commonwealth. Two examples of the latter kind are given: Gaius Carbo and Gaius Cato.

units.la: Haec igitur prima lex in amicitia sanciatur, ut neque rogemus res turpes, nec faciamus rogati. Turpis enim excusatio est, & minime accipienda, cum in caeteris peccatis, tum si quis contra Rempub. se amici causa fecisse fateatur. Etenim eo loco, Fanni & Scævola, locati sumus, ut nos longe prospicere debeat futuros casus reipub. Deflexit enim iam aliquantulum de spatio, curriculoq; consuetudo maiorum. Tyb. Grachus regnum occupare conatus est, ut rogavit is quidem paucos menses. Nūquid simile pop. Rom. audierat, aut viderat? Hunc etiam post mortem secuti amici, & propinqui. Quid in P. Scipionem Nasicam effecerint, sine lachrymis non queo dicere. Nam Carbonem quoq;, quę modo potuimus, propter recentem pœnam Tyb. Grachi fusti-nuimus. De C. Grachi autem tribunatu quid exspectem, non libet augurari. Serpit enim deinde res quæ proclivis ad perniciem cū semel cœpit, labitur. Videtis in tabella iam ante quanta sit facta labes, primo lege Gabinia, biennio autem post, Cassia. Videre iam videor populum Rom. à senatu disjunctū, multitudinisq; arbitrio maximas, res agi. Plures enim discent quemadmodum hæc fiant, quam quemadmodum his resistatur. Quorsum hæc? quia
units.tr: Let this therefore be the first law sanctioned in friendship: that we neither ask for dishonourable things, nor do them when asked. For an excuse is a shameful thing and must by no means be accepted, both in other sins and especially if anyone admits that he did something against the commonwealth for the sake of a friend. For we are placed, Fannius and Scaevola, in such a position that we ought to foresee far ahead the future dangers of the republic. For the custom of our ancestors has already somewhat departed from its course and its track. Tiberius Gracchus tried to seize royal power, and indeed he asked for it for a few months. Had the Roman people heard or seen anything similar? After his death his friends and relatives followed him too. What they did to Publius Scipio Nasica I cannot tell without tears. For we also endured Carbo, as best we could, because of the recent punishment of Tiberius Gracchus. But what I should expect from the tribunate of Gaius Gracchus I do not care to predict. For once a thing that tends toward ruin has begun, it slides; it gathers pace. You see how great a stain was already made on the tablet before, first by the Gabinian law, and two years later by the Cassian. I seem already to see the Roman people separated from the senate, and the most important matters being decided by the will of the crowd. For more will learn how these things are done than how they are resisted. Why these remarks? Because

units.la: sine sociis nemo quicquam tale cona-tur. Præcipiendum est igitur bonis ut si in ejusmodi amicitias ignari aliquo casu inciderint, ne existiment ita se al-ligatos, ut ab amicis in magna re aliqua in Rembub. peccantibus non discedet. Improbis autem pœna statuenda est: nec minor vero iis, qui alterû sequuti erunt, quam iis, qui ipsi fuerint duces impietatis. Quis clarior in Græcia The-mistocle? quis potentior? qui cùm imperator bello Persico servitute Græciâ liberasset, propterq; invidiam in exilium missus esset, ingratæ patriæ invidiam non tulit, quam ferre debuit. Fecit idem quod XX. annis ante apud nos fecerat Coriolanus. His adjutor contra patriam inventus est nemo: itaq; mortem sibi utercq; conscivit[?]. Quare talis improborum consensio non modo excusatione amicitiæ tegenda nō est, sed potius omni supplicio vindicanda est, ut ne quis concessum putet, amicū bellum patriæ inferentem sequi. Quo quidem, ut res cœpit ire, haud scio an aliquando futurum sit. Mihi autem nō
units.tr: no one undertakes anything of this kind without accomplices. Good men must therefore be taught that if, through ignorance and by some chance, they fall into such friendships, they should not think themselves so bound that they may not withdraw from friends who are offending against the commonwealth in some important matter. But a penalty must be set for the wicked; and it should be no lighter for those who followed the other than for those who were themselves the leaders of the impiety. Who was more famous in Greece than Themistocles? Who more powerful? He, when as commander in the Persian war he had freed Greece from slavery, and was then sent into exile on account of envy, did not bear the ill will of his ungrateful country as he ought to have borne it. He did the same thing that Coriolanus had done among us twenty years before. No one was found to help him against his country, and so both of them brought death upon themselves. Therefore such a consensus of the wicked must not only not be covered by the excuse of friendship, but must rather be punished with every penalty, so that no one may think it permitted to follow a friend who makes war on his country. Whether this will ever come to pass, given how things have begun to go, I do not know for certain. But for me

units.la: minori curæ est, qualis respub. post mortem meam futura sit, quam qualis hodie sit: Hæc igitur prima lex amicitiæ sanciatur, ut ab amicis honesta petamus amicorum causa honesta faciamus: neq; exspectemus quidem dum rogemur, sed studium semper adsit, cū-ctatio absit: consilium verum dare gaudeamus libere. Plurimum in amicitia amicorum bene suadetium valeat authoritas: eaq; adhibeatur ad monendū non modo aperte, sed etiam acriter, si res postulabit, & authoritati adhibitæ parcant.
units.tr: the concern for what the commonwealth will be after my death is no less than the concern for what it is today. Let this therefore be sanctioned as the first law of friendship: that from friends we seek honourable things, and for the sake of friends we do honourable things; and that we should not wait to be asked, but let zeal always be present and hesitation absent; let us gladly give true counsel with freedom. In friendship, the authority of those who give good advice should have the greatest weight; and let it be used for admonishing not only openly but also sharply, if the matter requires it, while sparing the authority that is applied.

units.la: Hæc igitur. Ex hactenus dictis sancit legem amicitiæ primam & præcipuam, ut videlicet, neq; rogemus res turpes, neq; faciamus rogati.
units.tr: Therefore, this. From what has been said so far he sanctions the first and chief law of friendship, namely that we neither ask for dishonourable things nor do them when asked.

units.la: Turpis enim. Ratio legis sancitæ ab adiuncto per comparationem minorum: quia cum in cæteris peccatis turpis est excusatio, minimeq; accipienda, tum vero in iis, quæ contra Rempub. commissa sunt.
units.tr: For an excuse. The reason for the law sanctioned is drawn from an adjunct by comparison from the lesser: since, while in other sins an excuse is shameful and not to be accepted, it is all the more so for those sins committed against the commonwealth.

units.la: Etenim. Digressio quædam, quæ de statu Reipub. misero, & in peiora mutato coqueritur.
units.tr: Indeed. A certain digression, which laments the wretched state of the commonwealth, changed for the worse.

units.la: Præcipiendum. Duo porif-mata mata legis lata: 1. est ut boni viri, si ignari casu aliquo in tales amicitias inciderint, ut ab amicis potius discedant, quàm se impie-tatis & iniustitiae ministros praebeant: 2. est, ut improbis poena statuatur, quae amplifica-tur distributione subiecti per comparationem parium: tam puniendi sunt, qui faciunt ro-gati res turpes, quàm qui rogant. Quis clarior. Duo legis corollaria duobus illu-strat exemplis Themistoclis & Coriolani: quorum uterq; cum patria bellum inferre vellet, ab amicis derelictus est: atq; ideo suae impietatis gravissimas & iustissimas poenas luit. Unde concludit Lælius argumento mi-norum, consensionem improborum non mo-do amicitiae praetextu palliandam non esse, sed omni supplicio afficiendam: quod rursus confirmat à fine, ut omnes intelligant nihil contra patriam, ut ante dixit, nihil contra fidem, iusiurandū, & aequitatem amici causa faciendum esse. Hęc igitur. Repetit primam amicitiae legem per contrarium: eamq; quibusdam circumstantiis plenius explicat: prima est, ut nostra sponte in bonis rebus gratificemur: id quod illustratur a contrario: studium adsit, cunctatio abest. Altera est, ut demus[?] consilium:quod describitur duobus ad-iunctis: quorum prius pertinet ad causam, alterum ad effectum. Gaudeamus consilium dare.i.simus promptiad consilia danda: demus autem consilia vera, & libera. Tertia est authoritas amicorum, qua in amicitia multum valere debet:in qua tria notantur: 1.finis,qui est admonitio,2.modus siue forma, qua explicatur argumento minorum: ea adhibenda non modo aperte, sed etiam acriter,si necesse fuerit:3.effecta:plurimum valere,eiq;parere debet.
units.tr: Let there be a warning. Two corollaries of the proposed law: 1. that good men, if through ignorance by some chance they fall into such friendships, should withdraw from their friends rather than make themselves ministers of impiety and injustice; 2. that a penalty be set for the wicked, which is increased by the distribution of the subject through comparison of equals: those who do dishonourable things when asked must be punished just as much as those who ask. Who was more famous. Lælius illustrates the two corollaries of the law with two examples, Themistocles and Coriolanus: when each of them wished to make war on his country, he was abandoned by his friends, and therefore paid the most serious and most just penalties for his impiety. From this Lælius concludes, by the argument from the lesser, that the consensus of the wicked is not to be covered by the pretext of friendship but must be visited with every punishment; which he again confirms from the end, so that everyone understands that nothing against the country, as he said before, nothing against faith, an oath, and fairness, is to be done for a friend's sake. Therefore this. He repeats the first law of friendship by the contrary, and explains it more fully through certain circumstances: the first is that we should of our own accord show favour in good matters; this is illustrated by the contrary: let zeal be present, hesitation absent. The second is that we should give counsel; this is described by two adjuncts, of which the first pertains to the cause and the second to the effect: let us rejoice to give counsel, that is, let us be ready for giving counsel; we should give true and free counsel. The third is the authority of friends, which ought to carry much weight in friendship; in which three things are noted: 1. the end, which is admonition; 2. the mode or form, which is explained by the argument from the lesser: it is to be applied not only openly but also sharply, if it is necessary; 3. the effects: it should carry great weight and be obeyed.

units.la: Nam quibusdam, quos audio sapientes fuisse habitos in Graecia, placuisse opinor mirabilia quaedam: sed nihil est,quod illi non persequantur suis argutiis: partim fugiendas esse nimias amicitias ne necesse sit unum solicitu esse pro pluribus: satis superq; esse sibi suarum cuiq; rerum curam, alienis nimis implicari molestum esse: commodissimum esse quam laxissimas habenas habere amicitiae,quas vel adducas cum velis,vel remittas.Caput n.est ad beate viuendum securitatem qua frui non possit animus, fi tanquam parturiat vnus pro pluribus. Alios autem dicere aiunt multo etiam inhumanius, quem locum breviter perstrinxi paulo ante, prasfidii, adiumentiq; causa non benevolentiae, neq; charitatis amicitias esse expetendas. Itaq; ut quisq; nimium firmitatis habeat, minimumq; virium, ita amicitias appetere maxime. Exeo fieri ut mulierculae magis amicitiarum prasfidia quaerant, quam viri, & inopes, quam opulenti: & calamitosi, qua ii, qui putantur beati. O praeclaram sapientiam. Solem enim e mundo tollere videntur, qui amicitiam e vita tollunt: qua a diis immortalibus nihil melius habemus, nihil iucundius. Quae est enim ista securitas? specie quidem blanda sed re ipsa multis locis repudianda est. Neq; enim est consentaneum ullam honestam rem, actione mue, ne solicitus sis, aut non suscipere, aut suceptam deponere. Quod si curam fugimus, virtus fugienda est, quae necesse est ut cum aliqua cura res sibi contrarias aspernetur, atq; oderit, ut bonitas malitiam,temperantiam libidinem,ig-naviam fortitudo.Itaq;videas rebus in-iustis iustos maximè dolere, imbecilli-bus fortes, flagitiosis modestos. Ergò hoc proprium est animi bene constitu-ti,&lætari bonis rebus,& dolere con-trariis. Quamobrem fi cadit in fapien-tem animi dolor,qui profecto cadit,ni-fi ex eius animo extirpatâ humanitate arbitremur,quæ causa est ut amicitiam funditus tollamus è vita,ne aliquas ꝓ[?]-pter eam suscipiamus molestias. Quid enim interest(motu animi sublato) nō dico inter pecudem & hominem,sed inter hominem, & saxum,aut truncū, aut quid vis generis eiusdē? Neq; enim sunt audiendi isti,qui virtutem duram & quasi terream esse volunt: quæ quidem est tum multis in rebus,tum in a-micitia tenera,atq; tractabilis,ut ex bo-nis amici quasi diffundatur,& incom-modis contrahatur. Quamobrem an-gor iste,qui pro amico læpe capiendus est,nō tantū valet,ut tollat è vita amici tiā,nō plus,q̈ ut virtutes,quia nōnullas curas, & molestias afferūt, repudietur.
units.tr: For some men, whom I hear were held to be wise in Greece, held, I think, certain strange opinions; yet there is nothing that they do not pursue with their subtleties: partly that too many friendships should be avoided, lest it be necessary for one man to be anxious on behalf of many; that each person's care for his own affairs is enough and more than enough, and that to be entangled too much in the affairs of others is burdensome; that it is most convenient to hold the reins of friendship as loose as possible, so that you may tighten them when you wish or let them go. For the chief thing for living happily is a security of which the mind cannot be deprived, if one man is, as it were, in labour for many. Others, they say, speak of something much more inhuman, a point I touched on briefly a little while ago: that friendships are to be sought for protection and help, not for goodwill or affection. And so the more firmness and the less strength a man has, the more he seeks friendships. From this it happens that little women seek the protection of friendships more than men, and the needy more than the wealthy, and the afflicted more than those who are thought to be happy. O splendid wisdom! For they seem to take the sun out of the world who take friendship out of life, which we have from the immortal gods as nothing better, nothing more pleasant. For what is this security? It is indeed attractive in appearance, but in fact it must be rejected in many respects. For it is not consistent that any honourable thing should be either undertaken or, once undertaken, abandoned, in order that you may not be anxious. If we flee from care, virtue must be fled, which necessarily despises and hates things contrary to it with some care, as goodness does wickedness, temperance lust, and courage cowardice. Thus you may see that the just grieve most at unjust things, the brave at weak things, the modest at disgraceful things. Therefore this is the mark of a well-ordered mind: to rejoice at good things and to grieve at their opposites. Wherefore, if grief falls into the wise man's mind, as surely it does, unless we think that humanity has been wholly rooted out of his mind, which is the reason why we should utterly remove friendship from life, so as not to take on any troubles on its account. For what difference is there (when the emotion of the mind is removed) not merely between a beast and a man, but between a man and a stone, or a stump, or whatever thing of that kind? For those people are not to be listened to who wish virtue to be hard and, as it were, earthen: which indeed in many matters, and in friendship especially, is tender and pliable, so that it is, as it were, poured out in the good fortunes of a friend and drawn together in his misfortunes. Therefore that anxiety which must often be felt on a friend's behalf is not so great as to remove friendship from life, nor so much as to make us reject the virtues because they bring some cares and troubles.

units.la: Nam quibusdam. Digressio in reprehensionem duarum sententiarum Epicureorum de amicitia.
