Prima est fugiendas esse multas amicitias: quae sententia primo confirmatur a fine: ne scilicet necesse sit unum pro pluribus sollicitum esse: 2. ab adjunctis satis superq;[?] est sibi suarum rerum cura: alienis implicari molestum est 3. illustratur allegorica metaphora. A simili ab equis desumpto: amplificatur a contraria securitate animi, quadum[?] pro multis sollicitus es, frui non potes. Altera sententia est Amicitiam non a natura sed spe lucri oriri & proficisci. Proponitur autem illa sententia primo a genere: egentissimus ad amicitiam est aptissimus: deinde explicatur per species oppositas mulierum & virorum, inopum & opulentorum, calamitosorum, & beatorum. O praeclaram. Accedit ad refutationem primae sententiae per ironicam exclamationem comparatione similium, & minorum explicatam. Quae enim. Primum argumentum sumitur a pari, & concluditur tali syllogismo connexo.
units.tr: For some. Digression on the refutation of two Epicurean sentences about friendship. The first is that many friendships are to be avoided. This opinion is first confirmed from the end: namely, so that it is not necessary to be anxious for many on account of one. 2. From the attendants: it is enough and more than enough to have care of one's own affairs; to be entangled in another's affairs is troublesome. 3. It is illustrated by an allegorical metaphor, taken from horses. It is amplified from the contrary security of mind: you cannot enjoy yourself if you are anxious for many. The other sentence is that friendship does not arise and proceed from nature but from hope of gain. That sentence is first put forward from the genus: the most needy person is the most apt for friendship. Then it is explained through the opposed species of women and men, of the poor and the wealthy, of the afflicted and the happy. O splendid! It goes on to the refutation of the first sentence by an ironic exclamation, explained by comparison of like things and lesser things. For what... The first argument is taken from equals and is concluded by a connected syllogism of this kind.

units.la: Si amicitiam propter curam fugimus virtus quoque erit fugienda: Sed consequens est falsum: Igitur etiam antecedens.
units.tr: If we flee friendship on account of care, virtue too will have to be fled. But the consequent is false. Therefore the antecedent too.

units.la: Neque enim est. Assumptio primo loco ponitur. Quod si curam. Propositio cuius consequens sive pradicatum probatur argumento effectorum: nam virtus cum aliqua cura res sibi contrarias aspernatur, atque odit: id quod illustrat inductione specierum contrariarum, bonitatis & malitiae, temperantiae & libidinis, ignaviae & fortitudinis, iustorum & iniustorum, imbecillium & fortium, flagitiosorum & modestorum.
units.tr: For it is not... The assumption is put first. But if care... The proposition, whose consequent or predicate is proved by the argument from effects: for virtue, together with some care, spurns and hates things contrary to itself. This it illustrates by induction of contrary species: of goodness and wickedness, of temperance and lust, of cowardice and courage, of the just and the unjust, of the weak and the strong, of the disgraceful and the modest.

units.la: Quamobrem. Complexio autem duplici reprehensione Stoicorum: primo quod omnem tollant animi motum, i.omnes affectus: quod refutat Lælius primo a differentia hominis & saxi sive trunci. Deinde quod virtutem duram & quasi ferream esse volunt, ut nullis rebus moveatur. Hanc sententiam refutat ab adjunctis contrariis per comparationem minorum. Virtus tenera atque tractabilis cum in aliis rebus, tum in amicitia: id quod rursus probat a contrariis effectis: ex bonis enim amici quasi diffunditur, id est, lætatur, & incommodis contrahitur, id est, tristatur. Cùm autem contrahat virtus amici-tiam (ut supra dixi) si qua significatio virtutis elucceat, ad quam se similis animus applicet, & adjungat: id cum contingit, amor ibi exoriatur necesse est. Quid enim tam absurdum, quam delectari multis inanibus rebus, ut honore, ut gloria, ut aedificio, ut vestitu, cultuque corporis, animo autem virtute praedito, eo, qui vel amare, vel (ut ita dicam) redamare possit, no admodum delectari? Nihil est enim remuneratio-ne benevolentiæ, nihil vicissitudine studiorum, officiorumque jucundius. Quod si etiam illud addimus, quod re-cte addi potest, nihil esse quod ad se re [?] ullam tam alliciat, & tam attrahat, quà ad amicitiam similitudo: concedatur profecto esse verum, ut bonos boni diligant, adsciscantque sibi quasi propinquitate conjunctos, atque natura. Ni-hil est enim appetentius similium sui, nihil rapacius, quam natura. Quamobrem hoc quidem Fanni, & Scævola constat (ut opinor) bonis inter bonos quasi necessariam benevolentiam esse, quæ est amicitiæ fons à natura consti-tutus. Sed eadē bonitas etiā ad multitu-dinē pertinet: non est enim inhumana virtus, neq; immunis, neq; supba, quæ etiā populos, universos tueri, eisq; optimè consulere soleat: quod non fa-ceret profecto, si à charitate vulgi abhorreret. Atq; atiā mihi quidem videntur, qui utilitatis causā amicitias fingunt, amabilissimum nodum amicitiæ tol-lere: non enim tam utilitas, parta per amicum quā amici amor ipse delectat.
units.tr: Wherefore. The passage contains a double refutation of the Stoics: first, because they remove every motion of the mind, that is, all the affections; this Laelius refutes first from the difference between a man and a stone or a log. Then, because they want virtue to be hard and as it were iron, so that it is moved by nothing. This opinion he refutes from the contrary attendants, by comparison of lesser things: virtue is tender and pliable, both in other things and in friendship. This he proves again from contrary effects: for from the good things of a friend it is as it were spread out, that is, it rejoices, and by his misfortunes it is drawn together, that is, it grieves. Since, however, virtue draws friendship together (as I said above), if any sign of virtue shines forth to which a like mind may apply and join itself, when this happens, love must necessarily arise there. For what is so absurd as to take delight in many empty things, such as honour, glory, a building, clothing, and care of the body, but not greatly to take delight in a mind endowed with virtue, one who can love, or (as I may say) love in return? For nothing is more delightful than the repayment of goodwill, nothing than the exchange of pursuits and kindnesses. And if we add that also, which can rightly be added, that nothing attracts and draws a person to itself so strongly as likeness does to friendship, let it be granted that it is truly so: that good people love good people and, as it were joined by kinship and by nature, take them to themselves. For nothing seeks its like more eagerly than nature does, nothing is more grasping. Therefore this, Fannius and Scaevola, is agreed (as I think) among good people: that goodwill, as it were necessary, is present, and this is the source of friendship, established by nature. But the same goodness also extends to the multitude: for virtue is not inhuman, nor selfish, nor proud, but is accustomed to protect even whole peoples and to provide for them most excellently; which it certainly would not do if it shrank from the affection of the common people. And indeed they seem to me to remove the most lovable bond of friendship, who invent friendships for the sake of usefulness: for it is not so much the usefulness obtained through a friend that delights, as the very love of a friend.

units.la: Tumq; illud fit, quod ab amico est profectum, iucundum, si cum amore, & studio est profectū. Tantumq; abest ut amicitiæ propter indigentiam colan-tur, ut ii, qui opibus, & copiis, maxime-q; virtute præditi (in qua plurimum est præsidii) minimè alterius indigent, liberalissimi fiunt, & beneficentissimi atq; haud scio, an ne opus sit quidem nihil unquam omnino amicis deesse. Ubi enim studia nostra viguissent[?], si unquā studio, unquam consilio, opera nostra nec domi, nec militiæ Scipio eguis-set? Non igitur utilitatem amicitiæ, sed utilitas amicitia consequuta est. Non ergo erunt homines divitiis affluentes audiendi, si quando de amicitia, quam nec usu, nec ratione habent cognitam, disputabunt. Nam quis est, (proch deum fidem atq; hominum) qui velit ut neq; diligat quenquam, nec ipse abullo diligatur, circumfluere omnibus copiis, atq; in omnium rerum abundantia vivere? Hæc enim est tyrannorum vita, nimirum in qua nulla fides, nulla charitas, nulla stabilis benevolentiæ potest esse fiducia: omnia sèper suspecta, atq; solicita sunt nullus locus est a-micitiæ. Quis enim aut eum diligat quē metuit, aut cū à quo putet metui? Coluntur tamen simulatione amicitiæ duntaxat ad tempus, quod si forte (ut fit plerunq;) ceciderint, tum intelligiturq; fuerint inopes amicorum. Quod Tarquinium dixisse ferunt tum cum esset exul, se intellexisse quos fidos, amicos habuisset, quosq; infidos, cum iam neutris gratia referre posset. Quāquam miror in illa superbia, & importunitate, si quenquam habere potuit,
units.tr: And then that which has come from a friend is pleasant, if it has come with love and zeal. And so far is it from being the case that friendships are cultivated on account of need, that those who are most endowed with resources and means, and above all with virtue (in which there is the greatest protection), are least in need of another, and become most generous and most beneficent; and I am not sure whether it is even necessary that nothing should ever be lacking to friends at all. For when would our zeal have flourished, if Scipio had ever lacked zeal, ever lacked counsel, ever lacked our labour, either at home or in war? Therefore it is not that the usefulness of friendship has followed; rather, usefulness has followed friendship. Therefore men abounding in riches should not be listened to if, on some occasion, they discourse about friendship, which they know neither by experience nor by reason. For who is there (good God, and good faith of men!) who would want to flow about with every resource, and live in an abundance of all things, and yet neither love anyone nor be loved by anyone? For this is the life of tyrants, truly in which there can be no trust, no charity, no firm confidence of goodwill: all things are always suspect and anxious, and there is no place for friendship. For who loves the one whom he fears, or believes that he himself is feared by the one with whom he lives? Yet they are courted, for the time being, merely by a pretence of friendship; but if perhaps (as usually happens) they fall, then they realise that they have been poor in friends. They say that Tarquin said, when he was an exile, that he then understood whom he had had as faithful friends and whom as faithless, when he could repay neither with favour. Although I wonder, in his pride and arrogance, whether he was able to have anyone at all.

units.la: Atq; ut huius(quê dixi)mores,veros amicos parare non potuere, sic multorum opes praepotentium excludunt amicitias fidelis. Non enim solum ipsa fortuna caeca est: sed eos etiam plerunque efficit caecos, quos complexa est: itaque illi efferuntur fastidio tere, & contumacia, neque quicquam insipiente fortunato intolerabilius fieri potest. Atq; hoc quidem videre licet, eos, qui antea commodis fuerunt moribus, imperio, potestate, prosperis rebus immutari, sperniq; ab iis veteres amicitias, & indulgere novis. Quid autem stultius, quàm ut plurimu copiis, facultatibus opibus possint, caetera parare, quae parantur, pecuniâ, equos, famulos, vestes, gloriam, vasa praeciosa: amicos non parare optimam, & pulcherrimam, vitae (ut ita dicâ) luppellectile? Etenim caete ra cū paratur cui paretur nesciunt, nec cuius causa laborēt. Ejus enim est istorū quicquid est, qui vincit eos viribus: amicitiarum sua cuiq; permanet stabilis & certa possessio: ut etiam si illa manent, quae sunt quasi fortunae dona, tamē vita inculta, & deserta ab amicis non possit esse iucunda. Sed haec hactenus.
units.tr: And just as his ways (as I said) could not obtain true friends, so the power of the mighty, of many, shuts out faithful friendships. For fortune is not only itself blind, but it also very often makes blind those whom it embraces; and so they are puffed up with disdain and obstinacy, and nothing can become more intolerable than a foolish, fortunate man. And indeed one can see this: that those who before were of agreeable character are changed by command, power, and prosperous circumstances, and that old friendships are spurned by them, and they indulge in new ones. And what is more foolish than that, while they can with their great wealth, resources and means acquire the other things that are acquired with money: horses, slaves, clothing, glory, precious vessels, yet do not acquire friends, the best and most beautiful furniture of life (as I may say)? For the other things, when they are acquired, the acquirers do not know for whom they acquire them, nor for whose sake they labour. For whatever those things are, they belong to the one who surpasses others in power; but the stable and certain possession of friendships remains to each person his own: so that even if those things remain which are, as it were, gifts of fortune, nevertheless a life that is uncultivated and deserted by friends cannot be pleasant. But so much for these matters.

units.la: Cum autem contrahat. Refutat hoc loco alteram sententiam, quod scilicet amicitia oriatur ab indigentia, non a virtute. Refutationis propositio est: cum virtus contrahat amicitiam, si qua significatio virtutis eluceat in aliquo, ad quam se similis animus applicet, & ibi amor oriatur necesse est. Quid enim. r. argumentum sumitur a minore. Hoc genus argumenti vulgo dicitur absurdum, sed revera est in eo comparatio minoris ad majus: & hoc modo resolvitur. Si delectatur homines multis inanibus rebus, quarum hic quinq[?] species recensentur, quanto magis delectabuntur animo virtute predito. Nihil est enim. Consequens probatur ab adjuncto per comparationem parium: quae intelligitur ex negatione imparis. Quod si etiam. Alterum argumentum sumitur ab effectis similitudinis, quae amplificantur comparatione minorum per negationem paris, & concluduntur tali syllogismo.
units.tr: Since, however, it contracts. Here he refutes the other sentence, namely that friendship arises from need, not from virtue. The proposition of the refutation is: since virtue draws friendship together, if some sign of virtue shines forth in someone, to which a like mind may apply itself, love must necessarily arise there. For what... The first argument is taken from the lesser. This kind of argument is commonly called absurd, but in truth it contains a comparison of the lesser to the greater: and it is resolved in this way. If people take delight in many empty things, of which five kinds are here enumerated, how much more will they take delight in a mind endowed with virtue. For nothing... The consequent is proved from the attendant by comparison of equals, which is understood from the negation of the unequal. But if also... A second argument is taken from the effects of likeness, which are amplified by comparison of lesser things through the negation of equals, and are concluded by a syllogism of this kind.

units.la: Si nihil tam allicit ad amicitia quam similitudo morum & studiorum. necesse est ut amicitia inter bonos sit naturalis.
units.tr: If nothing attracts to friendship so much as likeness of character and pursuits, it is necessary that friendship among good people be natural.

units.la: Sed antecedens verum est.
units.tr: But the antecedent is true.

units.la: Verum igitur consequens.
units.tr: Therefore the consequent is true.

units.la: Tam alliciat. propositio. Nihil enim. Assumptio ornata adiunctis similitudinis & naturæ per comparationem pariū. Quamobrem. Complexio. Sed eadem. Tacita epanorthosis complexionis, qua de subiecto bonitatis et virtutis disputat, videturque argumentari a minore: Virtus, bonitas, amicitia non solum ad paucos eosq; sapientes sed etiam ad multitudinem pertinent. Consequens probatur adiunctis virtutis & effectus. Adjuncta ex oppositis declarantur, quae sunt, inhumanitas, & superbia: effecta sunt universos populos tueri, & ijs bene consu-lere. Per virtutem autem intellige[?] homines virtute[?] praeditos ut sit metonymia adjuncti, qua adjunctum pro subiecto ponitur. Atque etiam. Tertium argumentum sumitur ab effecto, quod exornatur egregia metaphora a rebus corporeis. Sensus est. Qui amicitiae causam statuunt indigentiam, sua vissimum amicitiae nodum quo copulatur, pulatur dissoluunt. Hoc rursus probatur co-paratione, minorum per negationem paris. Non tam utilitas, quæ capitur ex amicis, quàm amor & studium, unde illa proficiscitur delectat. Est igitur hic comparatio causæ cum effecto: Causa effecto suo præstantior T.n:umq;. Quartum argumentum à contrario per comparationem minorum: Indigentia tam non est causa amicitiæ, ut potius y quæ omnia sua in se posita esse ducunt, & omnibus bonis circum-sluunt, sint ad amicitiam propensissimi & aptissimi. Non ergo erunt. Reprehensio opulentorum hominum, qui de amicitia sibi prorsus ignota disputare, & tanquam cæcus de coloribus pronunciare volunt: ubi ponuntur duæ causæ amicitiæ cognoscendi: usus & ratio: quæ certè duo ad omnes artes & doctrinas cognoscendas & iudicandas non solùm utiles, sed etiam necessaria sunt. Sed redeo ad reprehensionem, quæ primò amplificatur exclamatione, qua Deos obtestatur vera esse illa, quæ dicturus sit. Deinde confirmatur ab adjuncto omnium hominum: Nemo est qui malit in summa rerum abundantia vivere, & à nemine diligi: id quod rursus confirmatur adjuncto: quia hac est tyrannorum vita: qua hoc loco describitur ex oppositis: Tyrannorum vita est iniqua, nulla fides, nulla charitas, nulla stabilis benevolentia, fiducia esse potest: omnia semper suspecta, atq; sollicita sunt. Coluntur ta-men. Prolepsis qua declarat tacitam objectionem: objici poterat. At tyranni coluntur. Respondet Lælius explicando causas: coluntur non amore, sed simulatione amoris, quae pficiscitur vel metu, vel spe utilitatis. Unde amor ille firmus stabilisq; esse non potest, id quod probat testimonio & exemplo Tarquinij Superbi. Atq; ut hujus Tyrannis connumerat homines fortunatos, & insipientes: qui raro quoq; fideles amicos habet: cujus rei causam confert in fortunam per comparationem minorum. Fortuna non solum caeca est, sed eos etiam caecos reddit, quibus nimium favet, & indulget. Potest etiam argumentum esse a coniugatis, in quo disputatur a causa ad effectum. Vide Ramum in cap. de coniugatis. Caecitatis autem, cujus causa fortuna est, effecta explicantur, quae sunt fastidium, contumacia, superbia, & insolentia, quae amicitias veteres spernuntur, & repudiatur, nova vero expetuntur, & contrahuntur trahuntur. Quid autem stultius. Reprehendit homines amicitiae negligentes per comparationem minorum, hoc modo: Si in caeteris rebus comparandis multum operae & laboris ponunt homines, multò plus amicitiae tribuere debent. Antecedes ornatur enumeratione speciei, pecuniae, equorum, famulorum, vestium, vasorum. Consequens ornatur metaphora, id est, similitudine uno vocabulo suppellectilis comprehensa. Confirmatur autem comparatione dissimili: Caetera cui paretur incertum est: amicitia cui paretur certum est: Caetera sunt dubia & incerta: amicitia stabilis & certa.
units.tr: It would attract so strongly. (Proposition.) For nothing (is so attractive as likeness of character and of pursuits). (Assumption, embellished with the accompanying circumstances of likeness and nature, by comparison of equals.) Therefore: (the conclusion, a complexio). But the same (holds). (A tacit epanorthosis of the complexio, in which he disputes concerning the subject of goodness and virtue; and he seems to argue from the lesser: virtue, goodness and friendship pertain not only to a few, and those wise, but also to the multitude.) The consequent is proved from the accompaniments and effects of virtue. The accompaniments are declared from their opposites, which are inhumanity and pride; the effects are that they protect all peoples and provide well for them. By "virtue," however, understand men endowed with virtue, so that it is a metonymy of the accompaniment, in which the accompaniment is put for the subject. And indeed (a third argument is taken from the effect, which is adorned by an excellent metaphor drawn from bodily things). The sense is: those who make need the cause of friendship dissolve the most sacred knot by which it is joined. This again is proved by comparison, of the lesser by the denial of the equal: it is not so much the usefulness that is derived from friends that delights, as the love and zeal from which that usefulness proceeds. Here, then, there is a comparison of cause with effect: the cause is always more excellent than its effect. The fourth argument is from the contrary, by comparison of the lesser: need is not so much the cause of friendship that rather those who consider that all their goods are placed in themselves, and who overflow with all good things, are most inclined and most apt for friendship. Therefore they will not be... (The rebuke of wealthy men, who wish to dispute about friendship, which is utterly unknown to them, and to pronounce about it like a blind man about colours; here are set out two means of knowing friendship: experience and reason, which two are certainly not only useful but also necessary for knowing and judging all arts and disciplines.) But I return to the rebuke, which is first amplified by an exclamation, in which he calls the gods to witness that those things are true which he is about to say. Then it is confirmed from the accompaniment of all men: no one would prefer to live in the greatest abundance of things and be loved by no one; which is again confirmed by an accompaniment, because this is the life of tyrants, which here is described from its opposites: the life of tyrants is unjust; there is no faith, no charity, no stable goodwill; trust is impossible; all things are always suspect and anxious. Yet they are courted. (A prolepsis, which declares an objection tacitly raised: it could be objected, "But tyrants are courted.") Lælius answers by explaining the causes: they are courted not by love but by a pretence of love, which proceeds either from fear or from hope of advantage. Hence that love cannot be firm and stable, which he proves by the testimony and example of Tarquin the Proud. And, as he counts such tyrants among the fortunate and the foolish, who seldom also have faithful friends, he assigns the cause of this to fortune, by comparison of the lesser: fortune is not only blind but also makes blind those whom she favours and indulges too much. There may also be an argument from conjugates, in which one disputes from cause to effect; see Ramus in the chapter on conjugates. The effects of that blindness, of which fortune is the cause, are explained: they are disdain, obstinacy, pride and insolence, by which old friendships are scorned and rejected, and new ones are sought and drawn in. (Then what is more foolish?) He rebukes men who neglect friendship by comparison of the lesser, thus: if men take much trouble and labour in acquiring other things, they ought to give much more to friendship. The antecedent is embellished by an enumeration of kinds: money, horses, servants, clothes, vessels. The consequent is embellished by a metaphor, that is, by a likeness comprehended in one word, "furniture." It is confirmed, moreover, by a dissimilar comparison: it is uncertain for whom other things are acquired; it is certain for whom friendship is acquired. Other things are doubtful and uncertain; friendship is stable and certain.

units.la: Constituendi autem sunt, qui sint in amicitia fines, & quasi termini di-ligendi: de quibus tres video sententias fieri, quarum nullam probo. Vna, ut eodem modo erga amicos affecti si-mus, quo erga nosmetipsos. Alteram, ut nostra in amicos benevolentia illorum erga nos benevolentiae pariter, aequaliterq; respondeat. Tertiam, ut quā-ti quisq; seipsum facit, tanti fiat ab ami-cis. Harum trium sententiarum nulli prorsus assentior: nec enim illa prima vera est, ut quemadmodum in se quisq; sic in amicum sit animatus. Quàm multa enim,quæ nostra causa unquam faceremus, facimus causa amicorum? precari amicis ab indigno, supplicare, tum acerbius in aliquem invehi, inse-ctarique; vehementius,quæ in nostris rebus non saris[?] honestè, in amicorum fiunt honestissimè: Multæq; res sunt, in quibus de suis cōmodis viri boni multa detrahunt,detrahiq; patiuntur,ut iis amici potius,quam ipsi fruantur. Altera sententia est, quæ definit amicitiam paribus officiis,ac voluntatibus. Hoc quidem est nimis exiguè,& exiliter ad calculos vocare amicitiam,ut par sit ratio acceptorum,& datorum. Ditior mihi,& affluentior videtur esse vera amicitia, ne observare restrictè ne plus reddat,quam acceperit:Neq; enim verendū est,ne quid excidat, aut ne quid in terrâ defluat aut ne plus æquo quid in amicitia congeratur. Tertius verò ille finis determinatus[?], ut quanti quisque se ipsum faciat tanti fiat ab amicis. Sæpè in quibusdam aut animus abiectior est, aut spes amplificandae fortunae fractior: non est igitur amici talem esse in cum[?], qualis ille in se est: sed potius debet enití, & efficere, ut amici iacentem animū excitet inducatq; in spem, cogitationeq; meliorem.
units.tr: We must, however, determine what the limits of friendship are, and as it were the boundaries of love; concerning these I see three opinions put forward, none of which I approve. The first is that we should be disposed toward friends in the same way as toward ourselves. The second is that our goodwill toward friends should answer to their goodwill toward us equally and in like measure. The third is that each should be valued by his friends as highly as he values himself. I assent to none of these three opinions: for the first is not true, that each person should be minded toward a friend as he is toward himself. For how many things would we ever do for our own sake that we do for the sake of friends? To beg favours of an unworthy person, to entreat, to inveigh against someone more bitterly and to attack more vehemently, things which in our own affairs are not done quite honourably but in our friends' affairs are done most honourably. And there are many matters in which good men take much from their own advantages and allow themselves to be deprived, so that their friends may enjoy them rather than themselves. The second opinion is that which defines friendship by equal duties and wills. This is indeed too meagre and petty a way of calling friendship to account, so that the reckoning of receipts and payments is balanced. True friendship seems to me richer and more abundant: it does not strictly observe lest it return more than it has received; for one need not fear lest anything be lost, or lest anything run down onto the ground, or lest more than is fair be heaped up in friendship. And that third limit, as determined, is that each should be valued by his friends as highly as he values himself. Often in some people either the spirit is more abject, or the hope of enlarging their fortune is more broken; it is not right, therefore, that a friend should be such toward him as he is toward himself; rather he ought to strive and bring it about that his friend rouses his lowly spirit and leads him into better hope and thought.

units.la: Constituendi autem. sequitur tertia dialogi pars, qua praecepta dat Laelius, id est amicitiae fines constituit. Primo itaq; tres de iis sententiae refutantur, deinde veri fines constituuntur. Prima falsa sententia est, ut erga amicum eodem modo, quo erga nosmetipsos affecti simus. Altera ut par sit utriusq; benevolentiae remuneratio. Tertio, ut quanti quisq; seipsum facit, tanti fiat ab amico. Has refutat Cicero Nec enim. Refutatio primae causae ex argumento effectorum, quae amplificantur contrario fine & subiecto: amicorum causa multa facimus, quae nostri gratia non faceremus: deinde multa in amicorum rebus fiunt honeste quae in nostris non fiunt honeste: tertio multa saepe de nostris rebus detrahi patimur, ut fructus illorum ad amicos redeat. Altera. Refutatio alterius sententia ex adjunctis & effectis amicitia: Amicitia est dives & affluens, nec observat strictè ne plus reddat, quàm acceperit, neque veretur ne quid excidat, aut ne quid in terram defluat, aut ne plus æquo quid in amicitia congeratur. Tertius verò. Tertiam sententiam primò amplificat argumento minorum: dua priores sententia sunt mala, sed haec tertia omnium deterrima: id quod probat adjuncto & subjecto: in multis animus est abiectior, & spes amplificandi suas fortunas fractior. Unde colligit Lælius è contrario: non debere amicum alterum talem quoq; fieri, sed debere animum amici iacentem excitare, inducereq; inspem cogitationemq; meliorem.
units.tr: "Constituendi autem" (But the limits are to be determined). This begins the third part of the dialogue, in which Laelius gives precepts, that is, he determines the limits of friendship. First, therefore, three opinions about them are refuted; then the true limits are laid down. The first false opinion is that we should be disposed toward a friend in the same way as toward ourselves. The second, that the return of goodwill on each side should be equal. The third, that each should be valued by his friend as highly as he values himself. Cicero refutes these. "Nec enim" (For neither). The first opinion is refuted by an argument from effects, which are amplified by the contrary end and subject: for the sake of friends we do many things which we would not do for our own sake; then, in our friends' affairs many things are done honourably which in our own are not done honourably; third, we often allow many things to be taken from our own affairs, so that their fruit may return to our friends. "Altera" (The second). The refutation of the second opinion is drawn from the accompaniments and effects of friendship: friendship is rich and abundant, and does not strictly observe lest it return more than it has received, nor fear lest anything be lost, or lest anything run down onto the ground, or lest more than is fair be heaped up in friendship. "Tertius vero" (But the third). He first amplifies the third opinion by an argument from the lesser: the two former opinions are bad, but this third is the worst of all; this he proves by an accompaniment and a subject: in many people the spirit is more abject, and the hope of enlarging their fortunes more broken. Hence Laelius concludes from the contrary: a friend ought not to be made such also, but ought to rouse the lowly spirit of his friend and lead him into better hope and thought.

units.la: Alius igitur finis veræ amicitiæ constituendus est, si prius, quod maximè reprehedere Scipio solitus sit edixero. Negabat ullam vocem inimicicioré amicitiæ reperiri potuisse, quam eius qui dixisset ita amare oportere, ut aliquando esse osurus. Nec verò se adduci posse, ut hoc (quemadmodum putaretur) à Biate esse dictum crederet, qui sapisapiens habitus esset unus e septem: sed impuri cuiusdam, & ambitiosi, aut omnia ad suam potentiam revocantis, esse sententiam. Quo nam enim modo quisquam amicus esse poterit, cuius se putabit inimicum esse posse? Quin etiam necesse erit cupere & optare, ut quam saepissime peccet amicus, quo plures det sibi tanquam ansas ad repre-hendedum: rursum autem recte factis, commodisque amicorum necesse erit angi, dolere, invidere. Quare hoc quidem praeceptu cuiuscunq; est, ad tollen-dam amicitiam valet. Illud potius praeci-piendum fuit, ut eam diligentiam ad-hibeamus in amicitiis comparandis, ut ne quando amare inciperemus eum, quem aliquando odisse possemus. Quin etiam si minus felices in deligen-do fuissemus, ferendum id Scipio potius, quam inimicitiarum tempus co-gitandum putabat.
units.tr: Another, therefore, is the end of true friendship to be determined, if first I may state what Scipio was accustomed to rebuke most. He used to say that no saying more hostile to friendship could be found than that of the man who said that one ought to love in such a way as one day to be about to hate. Nor could he be brought to believe that this was said (as it was thought) by Bias, who was held wise and was one of the seven; but that it was the opinion of some impure and ambitious man, or of one who refers everything to his own power. For in what way could anyone be a friend whom he thinks he may one day be an enemy to? Indeed it will be necessary to desire and wish that a friend sin as often as possible, so that he may give more handles, as it were, for reproach; and conversely, it will be necessary to be vexed, to grieve and to envy when a friend does well and enjoys advantages. Therefore this precept, of whoever it is, serves to destroy friendship. Rather, the precept should have been that we apply such diligence in acquiring friendships that we never begin to love one whom we might one day hate. Indeed, Scipio thought that even if we had been less fortunate in choosing, it was better to bear that than to have to think of a time of enmity.

units.la: Alius igitur. Antequam veros amicitiæ fines constituat reprehedit ex sententia Scipionis dictū cuiusdam de amicitia & primo exponit & amplificat comparatione parium per negationem imparis: Nulla vox est capitalior quam cuius qui dixit, ita amare oportere, ut aliquando esset usurus. Deinde de causa. i. authore huius dicti disputat, idq; removet a Biante in impurum quendam, & ambitiosum, aut omnia ad suam potentiam revocantem. Tertio refutat: primo a contrario. Nemo poterit amicus esse, cuius se putabit inimicum esse posse: deinde ab effectis, quae amplificantur a contrario: Necesse hoc modo erit Cupere & optare, ut quam sapissime peccet amicus: contra vero recte factis commodisq; amicorum angi, dolere, invidere. Unde colligit hoc dictum valere ad tollendam amicitiam. Denique huic sententiae opponit contrarium praeceptum: scilicet in diligendis amicitiis eam adhibendam diligentiam ut nunquam amare incipiamus, quem ali-quando odisse possemus: idq; confirmat a minori: Quin etiam, inquit, si minus felices in diligendo fuerimus, id potius feremus, quam inimicitiarum tempus cogitemus.
units.tr: Another, then. Before defining the true limits of friendship, he criticises a saying about friendship, attributed to Scipio, by first setting it out and enlarging on it through a comparison of equals, by the denial of unequals: "There is no saying more dangerous than that of the man who said that one ought to love in such a way as one day to be hostile." Next he discusses the source, that is, the author of this saying, and removes it from Biantes to some impure and ambitious man, or one who refers everything to his own power. Third, he refutes it: first from the contrary: "No one can be a friend whom he thinks he may one day be an enemy to." Then from the effects, which are enlarged by the contrary: "In this way it will be necessary to wish and desire that a friend sins as often as possible; on the other hand, to be troubled, grieved and envious at a friend's good deeds and advantages." From this he concludes that this saying serves to abolish friendship. Finally he sets against this opinion the contrary precept: that in choosing friends one should take such care as never to begin to love someone whom one might one day hate. He confirms this from the lesser case: "Indeed," he says, "if we have been less fortunate in choosing, we will bear that rather than think about a time of enmity."

units.la: His igitur finibus utendum arbitror, ut cum emendati mores sint amicorum, tum fit inter eos omnium rerum, consiliorum, & voluntatum sine ulla exceptione communitas: ut etiam si qua fortuna acciderit, ut minus iuste amicorum voluntates, adjuvandæ sint, in quibus eorum aut de capite agatur, aut fama, declinandum est de via, modo ne summa æquatur turpitudo. Est n. quatenus amicitiæ dari veniam possit. Nec vero negligenda est fama. Nec mediocre telum ad res gerendas exis-timare oportet benevolentiam civium: quā blanditiis, & assentationibus colligere turpe est. Virtus, quam sequitur charitas, minimè repudianda est. Sed sæpè (redeo enim ad Scipionem, cujus omnis sermo erat de amicitia) quærebatur, quod in omnibus rebus essent diligentiores: ut capras, ut oves quot quisq; haberet, dicere posset amicos quot haberet, dicere non posset: & in illis quidem parandis curam adhibere, in amicis eligendis negligentes esse: nec habere quasi signa quædam, & notas, quibus eos, qui ad amicitiam idonei essent judicarent. Sunt igitur firmi & stabiles, & constantes, eligendi, cujus generis est magna penuria; & judicare difficile est sane, nisi expertum.Experiendum autem est in ipsa amicitia, ita præcurrit amicitia judicium, tollitq; experiendi potestatem. Est igitur prudentis sustinere ut curlum[?], sic impetum benevolentiæ: quo utamur quasi aquis tentatis, sic amicitiis, aliqua parte periclitatis moribus amicorum. Quidam sæpe in parva pecunia, perspiciuntur quam sint leves: quidam autem quos parva movere non potuit, cognoscuntur in magna. Si vero erunt aliqui reperti, qui pecuniam præferre amicitiæ sordidum[?] existimet: ubi eos inveniemus, qui honores, magistratus, imperia, potestates opes, amicitiæ non anteponant? ut cum ex altera parte proposita hæc sint, ex altera vis amicitiæ, nō multo illa malint? Imbecilla enim humana natura est ad contemnendam potentiam, quam etiam si neglecta amicitia cofequuti[?] sunt, excusatum iri se arbitrantur, quia non sine magna causa neglecta fit amicitia. Itaq; verç[?] amicitiæ difficilime reperi-untur unturin iis,qui in honoribus,req;pub-lica versantur. Vbi enim istum inveni-as,qui honorem amici suo anteponat? Quid?(hæc ut omittam quam graves) quam difficiles plerisq; videntur calamitatum societates?ad quas non est facile inventus,qui descendat. Quanquā Ennius rectè inquit,
units.tr: We ought, I think, to use these limits so that, when the morals of friends are improved, there arises between them a fellowship in all things, in counsels and wishes, without any exception. So that even if some chance should happen whereby the less just wishes of friends must be helped, in matters where their life or reputation is at stake, one must turn aside from the road, provided that the greatest baseness does not come to equal it. For there is a limit to how far indulgence can be granted to friendship. Nor indeed is reputation to be neglected. Nor should we think the goodwill of citizens a small weapon for carrying out affairs; it is shameful to gather it by flattery and fawning. Virtue, which charity follows, is by no means to be rejected. But often (for I return to Scipio, whose whole talk was of friendship) he complained that people were more careful in all matters: how many goats or sheep each man had, he could say; how many friends he had, he could not say; and that they took care in acquiring those, but were careless in choosing friends; nor did they have certain marks and signs by which they might judge those who were fit for friendship. Therefore those who are firm, stable and constant are to be chosen, and of this kind there is a great scarcity; and indeed it is hard to judge without experience. But experience must be gained within friendship itself, since friendship runs ahead of judgement and takes away the chance of testing. It is therefore the mark of a wise man to restrain the onset of goodwill just as one restrains a horse on the course; as we use waters that have been tested, so in friendships, we should first test the morals of friends in some part of the relationship. Some are often found out, in small sums of money, to be how light they are; while others, whom small things could not move, are known in great ones. But if there were found some who think it base to prefer money to friendship, where shall we find those who do not put honours, magistracies, commands, powers and wealth before friendship? Since these things are set on one side, and on the other the force of friendship, would they not much rather choose the former? For human nature is weak in despising power; and even if they have obtained these things by neglecting friendship, they think they will be excused, because the neglect of friendship did not happen without a great cause. And so true friendships are found most rarely among those who are engaged in offices and public life. For where will you find that man who puts a friend before his honour? What then (to pass over how grave these things are) of the fellowships in calamity, which seem to most people so difficult, and for which it is not easy to find anyone who will go down into them? Although Ennius rightly says:

units.la: Amicus certus in re incerta cernitur. tamen hæc duo levitatis,& infirmitatis plerosq; convincunt: aut si in bonis rebus amicos contemnunt, aut si in malis deserunt. Qui igitur utraq; in re gravem, constantem, stabilem se in amicitia præstiterit, hūc ex maxime raro hominum genere iudicare debemus, & pene divino. Firmamentum autem stabilitatis,constantiæq; est ejus, quam in amicitia quærimus fides. Nihil enim stabile est, quod infidum est. Simplicé præterea,& communem, & consentientem,& qui rebus iisdem moveatur, eiigi par est:quæ omnia pertinent ad fidelitatem. Neq; enim fidum potest esse multiplex ingeniū, & tortuosum, neq; vero qui non iisdem rebus movetur, & natura consentit, fidus aut stabilis esse potest. Addendum eodem est, ut nè criminibus aut inferendis delectetur amicus, aut credat oblatis : quæ omnia ad eam pertinent, quam jamdudum tractò, constantiam. Ita fit verum illud, qp[?] initio dixi, amicitiam nisi inter bonos esse non posse. Est enim boni viri (quæ[?] eundem licet sapientem dicere) hæc duo tenere in amicitia. Primum, ne quid fictum sit, nève simulatum, aperte enim vel odisse alium, magis ingenuū est quàm fronte occultare sententiam. Deinde, non solum ab aliquo oblatas criminationes, depellere sed ne ipsum quidem suspitiosum, semper aliquid existimantem ab amico esse violatum. Accedat huc suavitas quædam oportet sermonum, atqŭ morum, haud quaquā mediocre condimentū amicitiæ. Tri-stitia autem, & in omni re severitas absit. Habet illa quidem gravitatem, sed amicitia remissior esse debet, & liberi-or, & dulcior, & ad omnem co-mitatem, facilitatemq; proclivior.
units.tr: "A certain friend is seen in an uncertain matter." Yet these two things convict most people of levity and weakness: either they despise friends in good fortune, or they desert them in bad. Therefore the man who has shown himself serious, constant and stable in friendship in both circumstances, we ought to judge to be of a very rare kind of men, and almost divine. But the foundation of stability and constancy is that faith which we seek in friendship. For nothing is stable which is faithless. Moreover, one ought to choose a man who is simple, of the same mind, agreeing, and moved by the same things; all of which pertain to fidelity. For a manifold and crooked nature cannot be faithful, nor can one who is not moved by the same things and does not agree in nature be faithful or stable. It must be added to this that a friend should neither delight in bringing accusations, nor believe those brought to him; all of which pertain to that constancy which I have been treating. Thus that saying which I stated at the beginning is true: that friendship cannot exist except among good men. For it is the mark of a good man (who may also be called wise) to keep these two things in friendship. First, that there be nothing feigned or pretended; for it is more noble to openly hate another than to hide one's opinion behind a face. Second, not only to repel accusations brought by someone, but not even to be suspicious himself, always supposing that something has been violated by a friend. To this should be added a certain sweetness of speech and manners, no small seasoning of friendship. But sadness and severity in every matter should be absent. Such gravity indeed has its place, but friendship ought to be more relaxed, freer and sweeter, and more inclined to all courtesy and easiness.

units.la: His igitur finibus. Exponit verosa-micitia fines, quorum tres sunt: primus per-tinet ad constituendam amicitiam: alter ad conservandam: tertius ad dissolvendam. Hisce vero finibus maioris lucis gratia duo praemittit: primum est descriptio verae amicitia, a subiecto: in quo inest quod sunt emen-dati mores amicorum: a subiecto circa quod versatur: est enim communitas omnium consiliorum & voluntatum sine ulla exceptione.
units.tr: "His igitur finibus." He sets out the limits of true friendship, of which there are three: the first pertains to establishing friendship, the second to preserving it, the third to dissolving it. But before these limits, for the sake of greater clarity, he sets down two things: first, the description of true friendship from its subject, in which is contained that the morals of friends are improved; and from its subject-matter, with which it is concerned, which is the fellowship of all counsels and wishes without any exception.

units.la: Alterum est, quatenus amicis opes ferendae eorum voluntates juvandae sint. Ut scilicet, si quando acciderit, ut amicorum minus iustae voluntates juvandae sint, in rebus difficilibus, ubi de capite & fama eorum agitur, de via declinemus: sed hac cautione ne turpitudo sequatur ne fama negligatur, ne civium benevolentia amittatur, ne virtus repudietur.
units.tr: The second is how far the less just wishes of friends are to be helped. That is, if it should ever happen that the less just wishes of friends must be helped, in difficult matters where their life and reputation are at stake, we should turn aside from the road; but with this caution: that baseness does not follow, that reputation is not neglected, that the goodwill of citizens is not lost, that virtue is not rejected.

units.la: Sed1 sæpè. Hoc loco incipit explicare primum terminum, ac primo reprehendit exsententia Scipionis eos, qui in amicitia contrahenda negligentes sunt a dissimili, cuius tria membra sunt: 1. homines sciunt, quot capras & oves habeant: amicos quot nes-cient. 2. in illis parandis curam & diligentiam adhibent: in amicis eligendis non ite.
units.tr: "Sed saepe." Here he begins to explain the first limit, and first he criticises, through the opinion of Scipio, those who are careless in forming friendships, by a dissimilar comparison, whose three parts are: (1) men know how many goats and sheep they have, but do not know how many friends; (2) they take care and diligence in acquiring those, but not in choosing friends; (3) they have signs by which they distinguish good from bad, but in judging friends they have none.

units.la: 1 Sed sæpè. (Marginal reference not legible; probably "1" as a note marker.) 3.habent signa, quibus bonos a malis discer-nant, in amicis vero judicandis nullas habent. Sunt igitur firmi. Primum praeceptum de amicitia constituenda est, ut eligamus constantes & firmos. Constantia autem exploranda primo tempus exponit: quod incidit in ipsam amicitiam: idque confirmatur ab effectu amicitiae: illa enim praecurrit judicium, tollitque potestatem experiendi. Deinde modum describit duobus similibus, quorum prius petitum est a stadii cursoribus, alterum ab aquis. Sensus est: Ut qui stadium currunt seipsos cohibent: sic in amicitia cursum affectuum refraenare & cohibere debemus: & ut aquam, antequam plenius hauriamus, primis labris degustamus: sic animorum mores prius probabimus, actum demum amabimus.
units.tr: 1 But often. (Marginal reference not legible; probably "1" as a note marker.) 3. They have signs by which they distinguish good from bad, but in judging friends they have none. They are therefore firm. The first precept about forming friendship is that we choose constant and firm people. Constancy, however, must be tested first by time, which falls into friendship itself, and this is confirmed by the effect of friendship: for friendship runs ahead of judgment and removes the opportunity of trying. Then he describes the manner by two similar comparisons, the first taken from runners in the stadium, the second from waters. The meaning is this: just as those who run the stadium restrain themselves, so in friendship we ought to check and restrain the course of our feelings; and just as we taste water with the first sips of the lips before we drink it more deeply, so we shall first test the characters of minds, and only then love the deed.

units.la: Tertio subjectum, in quo amicorum mores periclitandi sunt, triplex proponit, pecuniam, honores, pericula: qui enim in tribus i-stis nihil praeter constantiam admiserit, eum vere constantem judicare possumus. Propo-nuntur autem tria illa gradatione quadam logica, quae a minoribus ad majora procedi-tur. Difficile est amicitiam anteponere pe-cunia, difficilius honori, difficillimum peri-culu[?] culis. Primus gradus augetur distributione ex adiunctis: quidam parva pecunia moventur, quidam magna. Alter gradus ornatur inductione specierum honorum, magistratuum imperiorum, potestatum, opum, deinde amplificatur ab adiuncto humanae naturae: illa enim imbecilla est ad contemnendam potentiam. Tertius gradus augetur adiuncto, id est, paucitate eorum, qui ad societates calamitatum descendat: nec non argumento diversorum: quanquam amicus certus in re incerta cernitur, tamen honores & calamitates plerosque levitatis convincunt. Fir-mamentum Quarto exponit causam procreantem, & conservantem constantiae quae est fides: quod confirmatur a contrario: quia nihil est stabile quod infidum est. Simpli-cem. Alterum praeceptum de constituenda amicitia est, ut eligamus simplicem communem, consentientem & qui eisdem rebus moveatur. Ratio praecepti additur a contrario: quia multiplex & tortuosum ingenium fidum esse non potest: neque qui non eisdem rebus movetur & consentit fides aut stabilis esse potest. Addendum. Tertium praeceptum est: ne criminibus delectetur amicus aut credat oblatis: cujus finis, ad quem refertur, explicatur: is autem est, de qua ante dixit, constantia. Ita verum. Praeceptorum haec tenus traditur consectarium: amicitiam inter bonos esse non posse: cui rursus subiicit duo amicitiae propria adiuncta: primum exponitur ex oppositio vitio: ut nihil sit in amicitia fictum, nihil simulatum: ratio additur a comparatione minorum: quia magis ingenuum est aperte aliquem odisse, quam fronte occultare sententiam. Alterum est ut vitetur suspicio, quod proponitur comparatione minorum. Non solum ab aliquo oblatas criminationes depellere, sed ne, ipsum quidem esse suspiciosum, consequens explicatur descriptione suspiciosi qui semper aliquid existimat ab amico esse violatum. Accedat huc. Quartum praeceptum est, ut accedat suavitas morum, et sermonis: quod primo commendatur ab adjuncto per metaphoram: non mediocre, hoc est, amicitiae condimentum: deinde illustratur a contraria tristitia et severitate: quae removetur ab amicitia argumento adjunctorum per diversum expositio.
units.tr: Third, he sets out a threefold subject in which the characters of friends must be tested: money, honours, and dangers. For if someone has allowed nothing but constancy in these three, we can judge him truly constant. These three are set out in a certain logical gradation, proceeding from the lesser to the greater. It is difficult to put friendship before money, more difficult before honour, and most difficult before dangers. The first step is enlarged by distribution according to circumstances: some are moved by a small sum of money, some by a large. The second step is adorned by induction of the kinds of honours: magistracies, commands, powers, and wealth; then it is amplified from the attribute of human nature, for it is weak in despising power. The third step is enlarged by an attribute, that is, by the fewness of those who go down to share in calamities; and also by the argument of contrary cases: although a certain friend is seen in an uncertain matter, nevertheless honours and calamities convict most people of fickleness. Firmness. Fourthly, he sets out the cause that produces and preserves constancy, which is faith; this is confirmed by the contrary, because nothing is stable that is faithless. Simple. The second precept about forming friendship is that we choose a friend who is simple, agreeable, consenting, and moved by the same things. The reason for the precept is added from the contrary: a manifold and tortuous disposition cannot be faithful, nor can one who is not moved by the same things and does not consent be faithful or stable. To be added. The third precept is that the friend should not delight in accusations nor believe those brought to him; its end, to which it is referred, is explained; this end, however, is that of which he spoke before, constancy. Thus true. As a corollary of the precepts so far given: friendship cannot exist among the wicked. To this he again attaches two properties peculiar to friendship. The first is explained by the opposite vice: that nothing in friendship be feigned or pretended; the reason is added from a comparison with lesser things: because it is more honourable to hate someone openly than to hide one's opinion behind a countenance. The second is that suspicion be avoided, which is set forth by comparison with lesser things. Not only to repel accusations brought by someone, but not even to be suspicious oneself, is explained as a consequence by a description of the suspicious man, who always thinks that something has been violated by his friend. Let this be added here. Fourthly, the precept is that sweetness of manners and speech be added: this is first commended from an attribute by metaphor, as no small seasoning of friendship; then it is illustrated by the contrary sadness and severity, which is removed from friendship by an argument from attributes, through the exposition of the opposite.

units.la: Existit autem hoc loco quaedam quaestio stio subdifficilis. Num quando amici novi nō indigni amicitia veteribus sint anteponendi, ut equis vetulis teneros anteponere solemus? Indigna dubitatio homine. Non enim amicitiarum esse debent sicut aliarum rerum satietates. Veterrima quæque (ut ea vina,quæ vetustatem serunt) esse debent suavissima,verumq; illud est,quod vulgo dicitur:Multos modios sale simul edendos esse, vt amicitiæ munus expletum sit.
units.tr: There arises here a question that is somewhat difficult: whether new friends, not unworthy of friendship, should sometimes be preferred to old ones, just as we are accustomed to prefer young horses to old ones. The doubt is unworthy of a man. For the satieties of friendships ought not to be like those of other things. The oldest things (like those wines that keep their age well) ought to be the sweetest, and that saying which is commonly repeated is true: that many bushels of salt must be eaten together before the duty of friendship is fulfilled.

units.la: Novitates autem, si spem afferunt, ut tanquam in herbis non fallacibus fructus apparcat,non sunt illæ quidem repudiandæ:vetustas tamen suo loco cōservanda est. Maxima est enim vis vetustatis, & consuetudinis. Atqui in ipso equo(cujus modo mentionem feci) si nulla res impediat, nemo est qui non eo, quo consuevit, libentius utatur, q; intractato &novo. Nec modo in hoc, ꝗ[?] est animal,sed in iis etiam,quæ sunt inanimata, consuetudo valet, cum locis etiam ipsis montuosis deleƈtemur, & sylvestribus, in quibus diutius commorati sumus.
units.tr: New things, however, if they bring hope, as fruit appears on plants that are not deceptive, are certainly not to be rejected; yet old age must be preserved in its own place. For the power of age and custom is very great. And indeed, in the horse itself (of which I just spoke), if nothing hinders, no one fails to use more willingly that to which he is accustomed than the untried and new. Nor is this so only in an animal, but custom has its force also in inanimate things, since we take delight even in mountainous and wooded places in which we have dwelt for a long time.

units.la: Existit. Præceptis explorandorum amicorum subiicit q[?]stionē de veteribus & novis amicis. Vocat autem hanc quæstionē difficile, opinione nimirum stultorum hominum, qui amicitiam nec usu nec ratione cognitam habent. Indignam vero hominis dubitatione, respectu hominum prudentum & peritorum. Sed quæritur an amici novi veteribus sint anteponendi: idq; illustratur similitudine: ut equos teneros vetulis anteponimus. Indigna. Respondet ad quæstionem dissimili: non ut caeterarum rerum, sic amicitiæ debet nos capere satietas. Deinde argumento minorum: reliquæ res sunt suaves; sed omnium suavissima debent esse vetustissima: idq; illustrat simili à vino vetusto, & novo suavius est, & libetius bibitur. Tertio testimonio, i. proverbio veterum quod monet amicitiæ munus non expleri antequam multos modios salis una comederimus. i. antequam amicitia diu multumq; durârit & culta sit.
units.tr: Existit. With the precepts for testing friends, he adds the question about old and new friends. He calls this question difficult, of course in the opinion of foolish men, who have not come to know friendship either by experience or by reason. But he calls it unworthy of a man's doubt, with respect to prudent and skilled men. But the question is whether new friends should be preferred to old ones, and this is illustrated by a comparison: just as we prefer young horses to old ones. Unworthy. He answers the question with a dissimilar case: satiety should not seize us in friendship as it does in other things. Then by an argument from the lesser: other things are pleasant, but the most pleasant of all ought to be the oldest; and this he illustrates by a comparison with old wine, which is sweeter and drunk more willingly than new. Third, by the testimony of the ancients, that is, a proverb, which warns that the duty of friendship is not fulfilled until we have eaten many bushels of salt together, that is, until friendship has lasted long and been cultivated.

units.la: Noviautem. Concedit etiam novos amicos recipiendos esse, si spem afferat bonorum amicorum: ita tamen ut veteribus non continuò anteponantur: cuius rationem reddit ab adjuncto: quia magna vis est vetustatis & con & consuetudinis. Atqui in. Respondet ad similitudinem, qua quaestione antea illustrari diximus, argumento parium, (quae species argumenti vulgo inversio dicitur) quo par pari reponitur: nemo est, qui non equo, quo consuevit, utatur libentius quam intracta-to & novo. Hoc vero rursus confirmat & amplificat argumento minorum: Neq; hoc solum fit in animalibus, sed etiam in rebus inanimis: quod rursus illustrat inductione specierum: quia locis montosis, & sylvestri-bus, in quibus diutius commorati sumus: de-lectamur.
units.tr: But new. He concedes that new friends are also to be received, if they bring the hope of good friends, yet in such a way that they are not at once preferred to the old ones. He gives the reason for this from an adjunct: because the power of age and custom is great. Yet in. He answers to the comparison by which, as we said, the question was illustrated earlier, by an argument from equals (which kind of argument is commonly called inversion), by which like is set against like: no one fails to use the horse to which he is accustomed more willingly than the untried and new. This he again confirms and amplifies by an argument from the lesser: this happens not only in animals, but also in inanimate things; this again he illustrates by an induction of species: because we take delight in mountainous and wooded places in which we have dwelt for a long time.

units.la: Sed maximum est in amicitia, super-riorem parem esse inferiori. Sæpe enim excellentiæ quædam sunt qualis erat Scipionis in nostro, (ut ita dicam) grege. Nunquam se ille Philo, nunquam Rutilio, nunquam Mummio antepo-suit, nunquam inferioris ordinis amicis. Q. vero Maximū fratrem egregium virum omninò sibi nequaquā parem, quod is anteibat ætate, tanquam superiorem colebat. Quod faciendum imitandumq; est omnibus: ut si quam præstantiam virtutis ingenii, fortunæ consequuti sunt, impartiat eam suis, communicentq; cum proximis, ut si parentibus nati sunt humilibus, si propinquos habeant imbecilliores vel animo, vel fortuna eorum augeant opes, ciisq; honori sint, & dignitati: ut in fabulis, qui aliquandiu propter ignorantiam stirpis, & generis in famulatu fuerint, cum cogniti sunt, & aut deorum aut regum filii inventi, retinent tamen charitatem in pastores, quos patres multos annos esse duxerunt. Quod quidem est multo profecto magis in veris patribus, certisq; faciendum. Fructus enim ingenii, & virtutis omnisq; praestantiae tum maxime capitur cum in proximum quoq;[?] confertur. Ut igitur ii, qui sunt in amicitiae, conjunctionisq; necessitudine superiores, aequare cum inferioribus debent, sic inferiores dolere non debet, sed à suis amicis, aut ingenio, aut fortuna, aut dignitate superari. Quorum plerique aut queruntur semper aliquid, aut etiam exprobrat, eoq; magis, si aliquid habere se putat, quod officiose aut amice, & cum labore aliquo suo factum queant dicere. Odiosum sanè genus hominū officia exprobrantium: quæ meminisse debet is, in quem collata sunt, non commemorare qui contulit. Quamobrem ut ii, qui superiores sunt submittere se debent in amicitia, sic quodammodo inferiores extollere. Sunt enim quidam, qui molestas amicitias faciunt, cū ipsi se conteni putant. Quod non fere contingit nisi iis qui etiam contemnedos se arbitrantur: qui hac opinione non modò verbis, sed etiam opere levandi sunt. Tantum autem cuique tribuendū est primum, quantum ipse efficere possis, deinde etiam quātum ille, quem diligas, atq; adjuves, possit sustinere. Nō enim tu possis (quātumvis licet excellas) omnes tuos ad honores amplissimos perducere: ut Scipio P. Rutilium potuit. consulem efficere, fratre eius Lucium non potuit. Quod si etiam possis quidvis deferre ad alterum, videndum est tamen quid ille possit sustinere
units.tr: But the greatest thing in friendship is for the superior to be equal to the inferior. For there are often certain eminences, such as Scipio's was among our own flock, so to speak. He never put himself before Philo, never before Rutilius, never before Mummius, never before friends of lower rank. And indeed he cherished his brother Quintus Maximus, an outstanding man, who was by no means at all equal to him, because he was older in age, as if he were his superior. This ought to be done and imitated by all: that if they have attained any pre-eminence of virtue, talent or fortune, they share it with their own, and communicate it with their nearest kin; so that if they were born to humble parents, or have relatives weaker in spirit or fortune, they increase their wealth and make them an honour and a dignity. As in the stories, those who for a while were servants, because of the ignorance of their stock and birth, when they are recognised and found to be sons of gods or kings, nonetheless keep their affection for the shepherds whom they had regarded as fathers for many years. This indeed ought to be done much more by true and certain fathers. For the fruit of talent, virtue and all excellence is then most fully gained when it is conferred on one's neighbour too. Therefore, just as those who are superior in the bond of friendship and union ought to level themselves with their inferiors, so inferiors ought not to grieve at being surpassed by their friends in talent, fortune or dignity. Of these, most either complain constantly about something, or even upbraid, the more so if they think they have something that they can say was done dutifully or in friendship, and with some labour of their own. Truly a hateful kind of men are those who upbraid services; the one to whom they were given ought to remember them, not the giver to mention them. Wherefore, just as those who are superior ought to lower themselves in friendship, so in some measure they ought to raise up their inferiors. For there are some who make friendships troublesome when they think themselves despised. This happens scarcely except to those who also think themselves contemptible; these men ought to be relieved of this opinion not only by words but also by deeds. Moreover, one must first assign to each as much as he himself is able to effect, and then also as much as that one whom you love and help is able to bear. For you cannot (however much you may excel) bring all your people to the highest honours: as Scipio was able to make Publius Rutilius consul, but was not able to do so for his brother Lucius. And if you could indeed bestow anything whatever on another, it must nevertheless be considered what he is able to bear.

units.la: Sed maximum. Hactenus constituendi amicitiam fines prÆscripsit:nunc confer-vadi ea præcepta tradit:atq; in ea æqualitate requirit. Propositio est:multu refert amicum superiorem inferiori parem esse. Sæpè enim. Illustrat propositionem & confirmat exemplo Scipionis: quod amplificatur ex oppositis:Cato nunquam se amicus inferioribus anteposuit:sed eos colebat, suosq; omnes per se ampliores esse cupiebat. Quod faciendum.
units.tr: But the greatest thing. Thus far he has laid down the limits of establishing friendship; now he hands down the precepts for preserving it, and in this he requires equality. The proposition is: it matters much that a superior friend be equal to an inferior one. For often. He illustrates and confirms the proposition by the example of Scipio, which is amplified by the opposites: Cato never put himself before inferior friends, but cherished them and wished all of his own to be greater through themselves. This ought to be done.

units.la: Accommodat exemplum Catonis omnibus hominibus:ubi primum recitatur causæ,quibus alter alterum,excellit q sunt,virtus,ingenium, fortuna: deinde exponitur modus,quo superior inferiori par fit:quando scilicet suâ præstantia impartit suis, & communicat cum proximis. Quod rursus declarat distributione subiecti,quod sunt parentes humiles, aut propinqui imbecilliores vel animo vel fortuna, quorum opes augenda sunt,& honor promovendus:idq; rursus illustrat exemplo e scena desumpto. Vt enim in fabulis,qui aliquandiu famuli fuerunt propter ignorantiam stirpis & generis,postea regum aut Deorum filij inventi,tamen retinent amorem in pastores, quos patrum loco multos annos coluerunt. Concludit autem hoc exemplum argumento minorum hoc silicet in veris certisq; patri-bus multo magis faciendum esse. Hanc conclusionem ornat egregio persimate[?], quo effecta[?] sive fructus beneficiorum in proximos collaturum exponit: Fructus enim ingenii, virtutis, omnisq; praestantiae tum maxime capitur, cum in proximum quemq; confertur. Vt igitur ii. Per comparationem parium etiam inferioribus praeceptum tradit: Vt enim superiores se aequare cum inferioribus debent: sic inferiores dolere non debent se a suis superari. Huius praecepti ratione[?]m reddit a factis utriusq;: quia superiores saepe inferioribus beneficia exprobrant: inferiores vero semper queruntur aliquid, & se contemni putant. Primum igitur genus reprehendit argumento adjunctorum: odiosum est genus hominum beneficia exprobrationem: eusq; rationem reddit a relatis. Beneficia meminisse debet is qui accepit: non commemorare qui dedit. Alterum genus reprehendit argumento effectorum: nam qui se contemni putat molestias faciunt amicitias: 2.explicatione subiecti contemtionis: ÿ contemnuntur fere, q[?] contemnendos se arbitratur. Tandē causas, quibus isti suspicioni occurritur, exponit argumento minorum: nam ij non solùm verbis, sed operæ etiam levandi sunt. Tantùm autem. Haëtenus præcepit amicos inferiores à superioribus extollendos esse & juvandos: nùc in sequentibus modum ejus exponit in subjecto & adjuncto.
units.tr: He applies the example of Cato to all men: where first he recites the causes by which one surpasses the other, which are virtue, talent and fortune; then he sets out the manner in which a superior becomes equal to an inferior, namely when he imparts his pre-eminence to his own and shares it with his neighbours. This again he makes clear by a distribution of the subject: that they are humble parents, or kinsmen weaker in spirit or fortune, whose wealth is to be increased and whose honour is to be advanced; and this again he illustrates by an example taken from the stage. For as in the stories, those who for a while were servants because of the ignorance of their stock and birth, afterwards found to be sons of kings or gods, nevertheless retain their love for the shepherds whom they cherished for many years in place of fathers. He concludes this example by an argument from the lesser: that this ought much more to be done in true and certain fathers. He adorns this conclusion with an excellent sentence, in which he sets out the fruit of benefits being conferred on one's neighbours: for the fruit of talent, virtue and all excellence is then most fully gained when it is conferred on one's neighbour. Therefore just as those who... By a comparison of equals he also gives a precept for inferiors: just as superiors ought to level themselves with inferiors, so inferiors ought not to grieve at being surpassed by their own. He gives the reason for this precept from the deeds of both: because superiors often upbraid inferiors with their benefits, while inferiors always complain about something and think themselves despised. He therefore reproves the first kind by an argument from adjuncts: it is a hateful kind of men who upbraid benefits; and he gives the reason for this from the things related: the one who received benefits ought to remember them, not the giver mention them. He reproves the second kind by an argument from effects: for those who think themselves despised make friendships troublesome; by an explanation of the subject, of contempt: they are generally despised who think themselves contemptible. Finally he sets out the causes against which such suspicion is met, by an argument from the lesser: for these men must be relieved not only by words but also by deeds. Moreover, one must first... Thus far he has taught that inferior friends are to be raised up and helped by their superiors; now in what follows he sets out the manner of this in the subject and the adjunct.

units.la: Adjunctum hic appello eum, qui opes amici auget, subjectum, qui augetur & juvatur.
units.tr: I call the one who increases a friend's resources the adjunct, and the one who is increased and helped the subject.

units.la: Attendendum ergo erit quid possit quus deferre in alterum, & quid ut[?], qui adjuvatur sustinere possit. Cuius præcepti rationem reddit ab adjunctis utriusq;. Nemo siquidem omnes suos, quavis excellat, ad amplissimos honores perducere potest: neq; omnes tales sunt, ut quosvis honores tueri & sustinere possint. Hæc verò omnia illustrat, & probat exemplo Catonis, P. Rutilij, & fratris ejus Lucilij: Cato P. Rutilium consulem efficere potuit: fratrem ejus Lucilium non potuit.
units.tr: Attention must therefore be paid to what a man of means can bring to another, and what the one who is helped can bear. He gives the reason for this precept from the circumstances of both parties. For no one, however excellent, can raise all his friends to the highest honours, and not all of them are such that they can hold and sustain any honours whatever. He illustrates and proves all this by the example of Cato, Publius Rutilius and his brother Lucilius: Cato was able to make Publius Rutilius consul, but he was not able to make his brother Lucilius one.

units.la: Omninò amicitiæ corroboratis jam, confirmatisq; & ingeniis, & ætatibus judicandæ sunt. Nec si qui ineunte ætate venādi, aut pilæ studiosi fuerint, eos habere necessarios oportet, quos tum eorum studio præditos dilexerunt: isto enim modò nutrices, & pædagogi jure vetustatis plurimum benevolentiæ postulabunt, qui negligendi quidem non sunt, sed alio quodam modo colendi: aliter enim amicitiæ stabiles permanere non possunt. Dispares enim mores disparia studia sequuntur, quorum dissimilitudo amicitias dissociat: nec ob aliam causam ullâ boni improbis, improbi bonis amici esse non possunt, nisi quod tanta est inter eos, quanta maxima potest esse morum, studiorumque distantia.
units.tr: Friendships must be judged altogether once minds and ages have already been strengthened and settled. Nor, if some people in their early years were devoted to hunting or to ball games, is it necessary to hold as necessary friends those whom they loved at that time because they shared that enthusiasm. For in that way nurses and tutors, by the right of their seniority, would claim a great deal of goodwill; they are not to be neglected, but they are to be cherished in some other way, for otherwise friendships cannot remain stable. For unlike characters follow unlike pursuits, and their unlikeness dissolves friendships. And for no other reason can good men never be friends with bad men, nor bad men with good, except that the distance between them in character and pursuits is as great as it can possibly be.

units.la: Omninò. Repetit tempus judicandi a-micitias, idque proponit argumento dissenta-neorum: Amicitiæ judicandæ sunt corrobo-ratis jam & confirmatis ingeniis & ætatibus: neq; verò necessarios habere oportet eos, qui ineunte ætate eodem studio præditi fuerunt: argumenti consequens primò ornatur enumeratione studiorum ineuntis ætatis, quæ sunt venatio, & pila: sub quibus etiam reliqua intelliguntur: deinde confirmatur à pari. Siy[?], qui ineunte ætate iisdem studiis quibus nos, delectati fuerunt pro amicis habendi sunt eodem modo amici habendi erunt padagogi & nutrices : quæ quidem negligenda non sunt sed alio modo colenda. Tertio idem præceptum confirmatur a contrario: quia aliter amicitiæ stabiles permanere no possunt: & hoc rursus explicat ab effectis disparium studiorum: quæ sunt dispares mores: quæ dissimilitudo dissociat amicitias: adque idcirco inter bonos & malos non potest esse amicitia: quod scilicet studijs moribusq; quam maxime discrepant.
units.tr: He repeats the time for judging friendships, and proposes this with the argument from contraries: friendships are to be judged once minds and ages have already been strengthened and confirmed, and it is not necessary to hold as necessary friends those who in early youth were devoted to the same pursuit. The consequence of the argument is first adorned by an enumeration of the pursuits of early youth, which are hunting and ball games, and under these the rest are understood. Then it is confirmed from a like case: those who in early youth took delight in the same pursuits as we do are to be held as friends in the same way that tutors and nurses are to be held as friends, and yet they are not to be neglected but cherished in another way. Third, the same precept is confirmed from the opposite: because otherwise friendships cannot remain stable; and this he again explains from the effects of unlike pursuits: these are unlike characters, and this unlikeness dissolves friendships. And for this reason there cannot be friendship between good and bad, because they differ most of all in pursuits and character.

units.la: Recte etiam præcipi potest in amicitiis, ne quis intemperata quadam benevolentia (quod persæpe fit) impediat magnas amicorum utilitates. Nec enim (ut ad fabulas redeam) Troiâ Neoptolemus capere potuisset, si Lycomedem, apud quem erat educatus, multis cum lachrymis iter fuü impedientem audire voluisset. Et sæpè incidunt magnæ res, ut discedendum sit ab amicis, quas qui impedire vult, quod desiderium non facile ferat, is & infirmus est, mollisq; natura, & ob eam ipsam causam in amicitia parum justus. Atqui in omni re consideranda [?] est, & quod postules ab amico, & quod patiare à te impetrari.
units.tr: It may also rightly be taught concerning friendships that no one, through a certain immoderate goodwill (which very often happens), should hinder the great advantages of his friends. For (to return to the fables) Neoptolemus could not have captured Troy if he had been willing to listen to Lycomedes, with whom he had been brought up, hindering his journey with many tears. And great matters often arise so that one must part from friends; whoever wants to hinder these, being unable easily to bear the longing, is both weak and soft of nature, and for that very reason rather unfair in friendship. Yet in every matter one must consider both what you demand from a friend and what you may fairly obtain from yourself.

units.la: Rectè etiam. Alterum præceptum de conservanda amicitia est ut nemo intempe-rata quadam benevolentia impediat magnas utilitates amicorum idq; declarat exem-plo fabuloso Neoptolemi & Lycomedis. Unde colligit aliquado incidere res magnas, ut di-scedendum sit ab amicis. Hinc describit eum, qui, quod amici desiderium non facile ferat, res utiles & honestas impedire vult: est .n. infirmus, mollis natura, & in amicitia pa-rum iustus. Hinc concludit præceptu ab opposito: considerandu est in omni re quid postules ab amico, & quid patiaris a te impetrari.
units.tr: Rightly so. The second precept concerning the preservation of friendship is that no one, through an immoderate goodwill, should hinder the great advantages of his friends, and he makes this clear by the fabulous example of Neoptolemus and Lycomedes. From this he infers that sometimes great matters arise so that one must part from friends. Hence he describes the man who, because he cannot easily bear his friend's longing, wishes to hinder useful and honourable things: for he is weak, soft by nature, and rather unjust in friendship. Hence he concludes the precept by the opposite: in every matter one must consider what you demand from a friend and what you may fairly obtain from yourself.

units.la: Est etiam quasi quædam calamitas in amicitiis dimittendis nonnunquam necessaria. Jam enim a sapientum familiaritatibus ad vulgares amicitias no-stra delabitur oratio. Erumpunt sæpè vitia amicorum tum in ipsos amicos tū in alienos, quorum tamē ad amicos re-dundat infamia. Tales igitur amicitiæ sunt remissione usus levandæ & (ut Ca-tonem dicere audivi)dissuendę magis, quam discindendæ sunt: nisi quædam admodum intolerabilis injuria exarse-rit, ut neq; rectum, neq; honestum fit, neq;fieri possit, ut nō statim alienatio, diljunctioq; facieda fit. Sin autem morum,aut studiorum commutatio quæ-dā (ut fieri solet) facta erit,aut in reipu-partibus diffetio intercesserit,( loquor enim,ut paulo ante dixi, nō de fapien-tum,sed de communibus amicitiis)ca-vendum erit ne nō solum amicitiæ de-positæ, sed inimicitiæ etiam susceptæ videantur. Nihil enim turpius, quam cum eo bellum gerere, quo cum fami-liariter vixeris.Ab amicitia Qu[?] Popeii meo nomine fe removerat (ut scitis) Seipio: propter dissensionem autem, quæ erat in repub. alienatus est à colle-ga nostro Metello: utrumq; egit graviter authoritate,& offensione animi nō acerba. Quamobrem primum danda opera est,ne qua amicorum dissidia fi-ant: sin tale aliquid evenerit,ut exrin[?]-[?]ctae potius amicitiæ,quàm oppressæ videatur. Cavendum vero est,ne etiam in graves inimicitias convertat fe amicitiæ e quibus jurgia,maledicta,contu-meliæ gignuntur. Quæ tamen fi tolerabiles erunt,ferendæ [?]unt: & hic honos veteri amicitiæ tribuendus est, utrisin culpa sit, qui faciat, non qui patiatur injuriam.
units.tr: Sometimes, too, it is necessary to dismiss friendships, which is a kind of calamity. For our discourse now descends from the intimacies of the wise to common friendships. Vices of friends often break out, both against the friends themselves and against outsiders, though the disgrace of these redounds upon the friends.
