Such friendships, then, are to be lightened by withdrawal from intercourse and (as I have heard Cato say) are to be unstitched rather than torn apart, unless some quite intolerable wrong has flared up, so that it is neither right nor honourable, nor could it be, that estrangement and separation should not be made at once. But if some change of character or of pursuits has taken place (as usually happens), or a disagreement has come between the parties in public affairs (for I am speaking, as I said a little earlier, not of the wise but of common friendships), care must be taken that not only is the friendship seen to be laid aside, but that enmities are not taken up as well. For nothing is more shameful than to wage war with one with whom you have lived on intimate terms. Scipio, as you know, withdrew from his friendship with Quintus Pompeius on my account; but on account of the disagreement that existed in the commonwealth he became estranged from our colleague Metellus. Both acted seriously with authority, yet with a displeasure of mind that was not bitter. Therefore, first, care must be taken that no quarrels arise among friends; but if something of that kind should happen, that the friendship appears to be relaxed rather than crushed. And care must indeed be taken that the friendship does not turn into bitter enmity, from which quarrels, slanders and insults are born. Yet if these are bearable, they must be borne; and this honour must be given to an old friendship, that the one who causes the injury, not the one who suffers it, be regarded as at fault.

units.la: Est etiam quasi. Hæc de amicitia conservanda: sequitur doctrina dimittendæ. Principio autem agit de subiecto, id est, de ea specie amicitiæ, quæ dissolvenda nonnunquam est, ea vero est vulgaris & communis, quam familiaritati sapientum opponit. Secundo causas dimittendæ amicitiæ exponit, quæ sunt vitia amicorum, morum & studiorum commutatio, atq; in repub administranda dissensio. Tertio de modo dissolvendæ amicitiæ disputat: dissuendæ magis, i. paulatim dimittendæ potius sunt, quàm discindendæ, id est, præpropere abrumpendæ. Huic vero modo addit limitationem à causa necessaria: aliquando .n. tam intolerabilis exardet injuria, ut neq; rectum, neq; honestum sit, neq; fieri possit, ut non statim alienatio, distinctio faciendæ sit. Deinde cavendum erit ne non solùm amicitiæ depositæ, sed inimicitiæ etiam suspectæ videantur: cuius rationem reddit ab adjuncto per comparationem pariū: Nihil enim tur pius est, quàm cum eo bellum gerere cum quo antea familiariter vixeris. Ab amicitia.
units.tr: Sometimes, too, This is about preserving friendship; there follows the teaching about dissolving it. First he treats of the subject, that is, of that kind of friendship which sometimes must be dissolved, and this is the common and ordinary friendship, which he opposes to the intimacy of the wise. Second, he sets out the causes for dismissing a friendship, which are the vices of friends, a change of morals and pursuits, and disagreement in administering the commonwealth. Third, he discusses the manner of dissolving friendship: friendships are to be unstitched rather, that is, to be dismissed gradually, rather than torn apart, that is, broken off rashly. To this manner he adds a limitation from the necessary cause: for sometimes so intolerable a wrong flares up that it is neither right nor honourable, nor could it be, that estrangement and separation should not be made at once. Then care must be taken that not only is the friendship laid aside, but that enmities are not also suspected to have arisen; the reason for this he gives from the circumstance, by comparison of the parts: for nothing is more shameful than to wage war with one with whom you previously lived on intimate terms. From friendship.

units.la: Illustrat modum exemplo Catonis: qui ab amicitia Q.[?] Pompeij Lælij nomine se removerat: propter dissentionem autem, quæ erat in Repub. alienatus est a Q.[?] Metello: utrumq; egit graviter authoritate & sine offensione acerba. Unde modum amicitiæ dissolvendæ repetit.
units.tr: He illustrates the manner by the example of Cato, who, in Laelius's name, had withdrawn from his friendship with Quintus Pompeius; but on account of the disagreement that existed in the commonwealth he became estranged from Quintus Metellus; both acted seriously with authority and without bitter offence. Hence he returns to the manner of dissolving friendship.

units.la: Omninò omnium horū vitiorum, atq; incommodorum una cautio est, atq; una prouisio, ut ne nimis cito diligere incipiamus, neue indignos. Digni autem sunt amicitia, quibus in ipsis inest causa cur diligantur. Rarum genus (& quidem omnia præclara rara) nec quicquam difficilius, quam reperire, quod sit omni ex parte in suo genere perfectū. Sed plerique neq; in rebus humanis quicquam bonum norunt, nisi quod fructuosum sit: & amicos, tanquam pecudes, eos potissimū diligunt, ex quibus sperat se maximum fructum esse capturos. Itaq; pulcherrima illa, & maxime naturali caret amicitia, per se, & propter se expetenda, nec sibi ipsi exemplo sunt, hæc vis amicitiæ qualis, & quanta sit. Ipse enim se quisq; diligit non nō vt aliquā à seipso mercedem exigat charitatis suæ:sed quod per se sibi quisque charus est: quòd nisi idem in amicitiam transferatur, verus amicus nunquā reperietur. Est enim is amicus quidem,qui est tāquam alter idem. Quòd si hæc apparent in bestiis volucribus agrestibus, natatibus, suibus, ficuribus, feris,primum se ut ipsi diligat( id enim pariter cum omni animante nascitur) deinde ut requirant, atq; appetant aliquas alias animantes,ad quas se applicent eiusdem generis idq; faciunt cum desiderio,& cum quadam similtudine amoris humani:quātò id magis in homine fit natura,qui & se ipse diligit, & alterum acquirit, cuius animum cum suo comisceat: ut efficiat pene unū ex duobus:Sed pleriq; perverse,ne dicam impudenter amicum habere talem volunt,quales ipsi esse non possūt:quæq; ipsi non tribuunt amicis,hæc ab his desiderant.Par est autem, primum ipsam esse virum bonum, tum alterum simile sui quærere. In talibus ea,quā jamdudum tractabamus, stabiles amicitiæ confirmari potest cum homines benevolentia conjuncti primum cupiditatibus iis, quibus cæteri seruiunt, imperabunt: deinde æquitate, justitiaq; gaudebunt omniaq; alter, pro altero suscipiet: neq; quicquam unquam nisi honestum, & rectum alter ab altero postulabit, neq; solum colent se inter se, ac diliget, sed etiam verebuntur. Nam maximum ornamentum amicitiæ tollit, qui ex ea tollit verecundiam. Itaq; in iis perniciosus est error, qui existimant libidinū, peccatorumq; omniū patere in amicitia licentiam. Virtutum enim amicitia adjutrix a natura data est, non vitiorum comes quæ si quos inter societas aut est, aut fuit, aut futura est, eorum est, habendus ad summum naturæ bonum optimus, beatissimusq; comitatus. Hæc est, inquam, societas, in qua omnia insunt, quæ putant homines expetenda, honestas, gloria, tranquillitas animi, atque jucunditas: ut cum hæc adsint, beata vita sit, & sine his esse non possit. Quod cum optimum, maximumque o-[?] quæ sit, id volumus adipisci, virtuti opera dāda est:sine qua neq; amicitiam, neq; ullam rem expetendam consequi possumus.Ea vero neglecta, qui se amicos habere arbitrantur, tam se deniq; errasse sentiunt, cum eos gravis aliquis casus experiri cogit. Quocirca (discen-dum est enim sæpius) cum judicaveris, diligere oportet: non cum dilexeris judicare.
units.tr: Altogether, there is one caution and one provision against all these vices and inconveniences: that we should not begin to love too quickly, nor love the unworthy. Those are worthy of friendship in whom there is a reason why they should be loved. It is a rare kind (and indeed all excellent things are rare), and nothing is more difficult than to find one that is perfect in every respect in its own kind. But most people know nothing good in human affairs except what is profitable, and they love friends as they would cattle, chiefly those from whom they hope to reap the greatest profit. And so that most beautiful and most natural friendship, to be sought for its own sake and for itself, lacks exemplars, and people do not see what kind and how great the power of friendship is. For each person loves himself, not so as to exact some wage of his affection from himself, but because each is dear to himself in himself; and unless this same feeling is transferred into friendship, a true friend will never be found. For he is a friend who is, as it were, another self. If these things appear in wild creatures, birds, beasts of the field, swimmers, pigs, wild animals: first, that each loves itself (for this is born alike with every living creature), and then that they seek and desire certain other creatures to which they may attach themselves, of the same kind, and they do this with longing and with a certain likeness to human love; how much more is this so in man, who by nature both loves himself and acquires another, whose soul he mingles with his own, so as to make almost one out of two! But most people, to put it bluntly, perversely and even shamelessly, wish to have a friend of such a kind as they themselves cannot be; and what they do not give to their friends, these they demand from them. It is fitting, however, first to be a good man oneself, and then to seek a like one. In such men, that which we have been discussing for some time, stable friendship can be established; when men united by goodwill will first command those desires which others serve; then they will rejoice in fairness and justice, and each will undertake everything for the other; neither will one ever ask of the other anything but what is honourable and right; and they will not only cherish and love one another, but also revere one another. For he who removes reverence takes away the greatest ornament of friendship. Therefore those are in error who think that licence for lusts and for all sins is allowed in friendship. For friendship was given by nature as a helper of virtues, not as a companion of vices. Whatever partnership there is, or has been, or will be, among those who are the best and happiest companions for the highest good of nature, is to be counted as such. This, I say, is the partnership in which all those things are present which men think worth seeking: honour, glory, tranquillity of mind and delight; so that when these are present, life is blessed, and without them it cannot be. Since this is the best and greatest thing, which we wish to attain, effort must be given to virtue, without which we can attain neither friendship nor any thing worth seeking. But when virtue is neglected, those who think they have friends perceive at last how greatly they have erred, when some grave misfortune compels them to test them. Wherefore (for it must be taught repeatedly) when you have judged, you ought to love; do not judge after you have loved.

units.la: Omninò omnium. Malorum modò expositorum cautionem & remedium subiicit: in quo duo spectanda sunt, adjunctū temporis & subiectum. Tempus exprimitur his verbis: ne nimis cito diligere incipiamus subjectum: néve indignos. Dignos autem nominat quibus in ipsis inest causa cur diligātur: quos amplificat ab adjuncto: Rarum, inquit, genus hominum: id quod confirmat à genere: omnia præclara rara, nec quicquam difficilius quàm reperire, quod sit ex omni parte in suo genere perfectum. Sed pleriq;. Reprehendit vulgi stultitiam, ꝙ [?] neq; in rebus humanis quicquam bonū novit, nisi ꝙ fructuosum sit: & amicos tanquā pecudes eos potissimum eligunt, è quibus sperant se maximum fructum esse capturos. Hac igitur stultitiam amplificat à privanti: Itaq; inquit, caret pul-cherrima illa & maxime naturali amicitia perse & propter se expetenda, nec àseipsis ex-emplum sumunt, illa amicitiæ vis qualis & quanta sit. Unde colligit author argumento parium: quemq; ita amare debere amicum ut seipsum: seipsum autem amat quisq; non ut mercedem charitatis exigat sua, sed quod si-bi quisq; per se charus est: quod idem in ami-citiam transferendum est. Quod rursus pro-bat de scriptione amici: amicus est tanquam alter idem. Tandem suam sententiā illustrat comparatione minorum: Si bestiæ & feræ na-turæ impulsu seipsæ primò diligunt: deinde ac-quirunt aliquas aliâs animantes, ad quas se applicent eiusdem[?] generis, idq; faciunt cum desiderio: quanto magis id in homine fieri de-bet natura, non spe mercedis. Antecedens or natur distributione bestiarum duplici: qua-rum prior desumitur è natura ipsarum, qua alia cicures sunt, alia feræ: posterior è subie-loco, quo respectu aliæ dicuntur volucres a-liæ agrestes, aliæ natates. Sed plerisq;. Con-sequens amplificat à contrario hominum fa-cto, & plenius explicat: ut primò quisq; sit bo-nus vir: deinde quærat alium sui similem. In talibus. Commendatio amicitiæ naturalis ab effectu & adjunctis: Effectū est stabilitatis confirmatio: ejusq; 5. causæ exponūtur: 1. imperium in cupiditates, quod amplificatur à contrario: 2. æquitas & justitia: 3. inservien di studium: 4. honestorum tantùm & rectorum postulatio: 5. reverentia & verecundia. Hæc est inquam. Altera commendatio ab adjunctis, quæ sunt honestas, gloria, tranquillitas animi, jucunditas, vita beata. Quocirca. Concludit locum de tempore amādi, & nominatim monet judicium amorem præcedere debere, non autem amorem judicium.
units.tr: Above all, of all things. He gives a warning and a remedy against bad people just described, in which two things must be considered: the time and the subject. The time is expressed in these words: that we not begin to love too quickly, nor love the unworthy. He calls them worthy those in whom there is in themselves a reason why they should be loved; and he amplifies them from their attribute: "A rare kind of men," he says, which he confirms from the genus: all excellent things are rare, and nothing is more difficult than to find what is perfect in every respect within its kind. But most people... He rebukes the folly of the crowd, which knows nothing good in human affairs unless it is profitable, and they choose especially as friends, as if they were cattle, those from whom they hope to reap the greatest profit. He therefore amplifies this folly from its privative: "Therefore," he says, that most beautiful and most natural friendship, to be sought for its own sake and for its own sake, is lacking, and they do not take from themselves an example of what the power of friendship is, and how great it is. From this the author draws an argument from equals: that each one ought to love his friend as himself; and each one loves himself not so that he may demand a reward for his affection, but because each is dear to himself through himself; and this same thing must be transferred to friendship. This he proves again from the definition of a friend: a friend is as it were another self. Finally he illustrates his opinion by a comparison with lesser things: If beasts and wild animals by the impulse of nature first love themselves, then acquire certain other living creatures to which they attach themselves of the same kind, and they do this with longing, how much more ought this to happen in man by nature, not from hope of reward. The antecedent is distributed by a twofold division of beasts: of which the first is taken from their nature, by which some are tame and others wild; the second from their habitat, by which respect some are called birds, others land animals, others swimmers. But most people... The consequent amplifies from the opposite conduct of men, and explains more fully: that first each one be a good man, then seek another like himself. In such matters... The commendation of natural friendship from its effect and attributes: The effect is the confirmation of stability; and its five causes are set out: (1) control over the desires, which is amplified from the contrary; (2) equity and justice; (3) zeal for serving; (4) the demand only for honourable and right things; (5) reverence and modesty. This is, I say. The second commendation from its attributes, which are honour, glory, tranquillity of mind, pleasantness, and a blessed life. Therefore: he concludes the topic of the time of loving, and expressly warns that judgment ought to precede love, and not love judgment.

units.la: Sed cum multis in rebus negligētia plectimur, tū maximè in amicis & diligendis, & colendis. Prępostèris enim utimur consiliis, & acta agimus, quæ vetamur, veteri proverbio. Nā implicari ultrò & citrò, vel usu diuturno, vel etiā officiis, repentè in medio cursu amicicias exorta aliqua offensione, dirumpimus. Quò etiam magis vituperanda est rei tam maximè necessariæ tāta injuria. Vna est enim amicitia in rebus humanis de cuj' utilitate omnes uno ore cōsentiunt, quãquàm à multis ipsa virtus contemnitur,& venditatio quędã,atq; ostētatio esse dicitur. Multi diuitias despiciunt, quos parvo contentos tenuis victus,cultusq; delectat:honores vero, quorum cupiditate quidam inflamantur,quam multi ita contēnunt ut nihil inanius esse, nihil levius existiment. Item cætera quæ quibusdā admirabilia videntur,permulti sunt,qui pro nihilo putent. De amicitia omnes ad unum idem sentiunt & hi qui ad rempu. se cō-tulerūt,& ii qui rerum cognitione doctrinaq; delectantur, & ii qui suum negotium gerunt otiose,postremò ii,qui se totos voluptatibus tradiderunt,sine amicitia vitam esse nullam sentiunt, si modò velint aliqua ex parte liberaliter vivere.Serpit enim nescio quomodo ꝑ omnium vita amicitia , nec ullam ætatis degendæ ratione patitur esse sui expertem. Quin etiam si quis ea est asperitate,& immanitate naturæ ut cōgressus , & sotietatem hominum fugiat, atque oderit, qualem fuisse Athenis Titomem nescio quem accepimus: ramen is pati non posset ut non acquirat aliquem, apud quem evomat virus suae acerbitatis. Atq; hoc maxime judicaretur, si quid tale posset contingere, ut aliquis nos Deus ex hac omnium frequentia tolleret, & in solitudine uspiam collocaret, atq; ibi suppeditans omnium rerum quas natura desiderat, abundantiam, & copiam, hominis omnino aspiciendi potestatem eriperet, quis ta esset ferreus, q eam vitam ferre posset? cuiq; non auferret fructu voluptatu omnium solitudo? Verum ergo illud est, quod a Tarentino Archyta, ut opinor, dici solitum nostros senes commemorare audivi ab aliis senibus auditu: Si quis coelum ascendisset, naturamq; mundi, & pulchritudinem syderum perpexisset, insuavem illa admiratione ei fore: quae jucundissima fuisset, si aliquem cui narraret, habuisset. Sic natura solitarium nihil amat, semperq; ad aliqd tanquam adminiculum, annittitur, quod in ami cissimo quoq; dulcissimum est.
units.tr: But although we are struck by negligence in many things, most of all in choosing and cultivating friends. For we use plans put in the wrong order, and do things that are forbidden, to use the old proverb. For we break off friendships that have been formed by mutual entanglement, either by long practice or even by services, suddenly in the middle of the course, because of some offence. All the more is such a great wrong to a thing so very necessary to be blamed. For there is one friendship in human affairs about whose usefulness all agree with one voice, although by many virtue itself is despised, and it is said to be a kind of display and ostentation. Many despise riches, and are delighted to be content with a small and meagre livelihood and way of life; but honours, by the desire for which some are inflamed, many despise so much that they think nothing is emptier, nothing lighter. Likewise there are very many who regard as nothing the other things that seem admirable to some. Concerning friendship, all think alike: both those who have devoted themselves to public affairs, and those who delight in the knowledge and learning of things, and those who conduct their own business at leisure, and finally those who have surrendered themselves wholly to pleasures, feel that without friendship there is no life at all, if only they wish to live in some measure as free people. For friendship creeps, I know not how, through the life of all, and does not allow any way of spending one's age to be without its share of it. Indeed even if someone is of such harshness and savagery of nature that he shuns and hates the company and fellowship of men, as we have heard Timon of Athens was, whoever he was, yet he could not bear not to acquire someone before whom he might vent the poison of his bitterness. And this would be judged especially so if something of this kind could happen, that some god should take us from this crowd of all people and place us somewhere in solitude, and there, supplying an abundance and plenty of all the things nature desires, should snatch from us altogether the power of seeing a man: who would be so iron-hearted as to be able to bear such a life? And to whom would not solitude take away the fruit of all pleasures? True, then, is that saying which, as I think, was commonly attributed to Archytas of Tarentum, as I have heard our elders recall, having heard it from other old men: if someone had ascended to heaven and had surveyed the nature of the universe and the beauty of the stars, that admiration would be unpleasant to him, which would have been most pleasant if he had someone to whom he might tell it. Thus nature loves nothing solitary, and always strives toward something as a support, which is sweetest even in the dearest friend.

units.la: Sed cum multis. Amplificat superiorem doctrinam a contrarys hominu factu.i. negligentia, quae plectuntur in amicitiis deligendis & colendis: quod rursus amplificatur adjuncto subiecti, i. amicitiæ circa quam homines negligentes sunt: amicitia enim est omnium rerum maximè necessaria. Vna e-nim est. Amicitiæ necessitatem probat a factis omnium hominum, quæ augentur comparatione dissimili, hoc modo. Homines caeteras res, quæ expetenda vulgò putatur, aliquando contemnunt, & negligunt: de amicitia omnes ad unum idem sentiunt, videlicet esse rem maximè necessariam. Protasis amplificatur inductione trium specierum: virtutis, quam multi ostentationem & venditationem esse dicunt & contemnunt: divitiarum, quas multi tenui victu cultuq; conteti despiciunt: honorum, quos multi ita aspernantur, ut nihil inanius esse, nihil levius existiment. Antapodosis augetur distributione vitæ humanæ è subiectis, quibus illa occupatur: alia versatur in rebus administrandis: alia rerum cognitione, doctrinaq; delectatur: alia otio pascitur: alia se totum libidinibus voluptatibusq; dedit.
units.tr: But although many. He amplifies the previous teaching from the contrary conduct of men, namely the negligence by which they are struck in choosing and cultivating friendships; which in turn is amplified by an attribute of the subject, that is, of friendship, in which men are negligent: for friendship is the most necessary of all things. For there is one. He proves the necessity of friendship from the actions of all men, which are amplified by a dissimilar comparison, in this way. Men sometimes despise and neglect other things that are commonly thought worth seeking; but concerning friendship all think alike, clearly that it is a most necessary thing. The protasis is amplified by an induction of three kinds: of virtue, which many say is ostentation and display and they despise; of riches, which many despise, being content with a small livelihood and way of life; of honours, which many so scorn that they think nothing emptier, nothing lighter. The apodosis is enlarged by a distribution of human life according to the subjects with which it is occupied: one part is engaged in the management of affairs; another delights in the knowledge and learning of things; another is fed by leisure; another has given itself wholly to lusts and pleasures.

units.la: Quin etiam. Antapopofin[?] rursus amplificat duobus exemplis fictis: quorum prius est hominis asperi & immanis, congressus societatemq; hominum fugientus: alterum hominis ex hac omnium frequentia sublati, & insolitudinem uspiam collocati, atq; ibi omnium rerum copia affluentus, homines autem aspiciendi potestatem non habentis. Neutrum horum amicis omnino carere posse testatur Cicero. Verum ergò illud. Confirmatio duorum exemplorum ex argumento inartificiali i. testimonio Architaæ Taretini:cuius testimonium rursus commendatur & confirmatur testimonio veterum Romanorum:q; id crebris sermonibus usurparunt: & suis quoq; posteris tradiderunt-
units.tr: Indeed. He again amplifies the opposite by two fictional examples: of these the first is that of a harsh and savage man, shunning the company and fellowship of men; the other of a man taken from this crowd of all people and placed somewhere in solitude, where he is overflowing with an abundance of all things but has no power of seeing men. Cicero testifies that neither of these can altogether lack friends. True, then, that. The confirmation of the two examples from an inartificial argument, that is, the testimony of Archytas of Tarentum: whose testimony is in turn commended and confirmed by the testimony of the ancient Romans, who used it in frequent conversations and also handed it down to their posterity.

units.la: Sed cum tot signis eadē natura declaret quid velit, acquerat, quid desideret, obsurdescimus tamen nescio quomodo, nec ea quæ ab ea movemur, odimus. Est enim varius & multiplex usus amicitiæ, multæq; causæ suspicionum, offensionumq; dātur, quas tum evitare tum elevare, tum ferre sapientis est. Vna illa sublevanda offensio est, ut & utilitates in amicitia & fides retineatur: Nam & movendi amici sæpe sunt & obiurgandi: & hæc accipieda amicè, cum benevolè fiunt. Sed nescio quomodo verum est, quod in Andria fami-liaris meus Terentius dixit:
units.tr: But although nature declares by so many signs what she wishes, what she seeks, what she desires, we nevertheless grow deaf, I know not how, and we do not hate the things by which we are moved. For the use of friendship is varied and manifold, and many causes of suspicions and offences arise, which it is the mark of a wise man either to avoid, or to lessen, or to bear. Only that one offence is to be removed, so that both the advantages and the trustworthiness are kept in friendship. For friends are often to be moved and also to be rebuked; and these things should be received in a friendly way, when they are done kindly. But I know not how it is true, what my familiar Terence said in the Andria:

units.la: Obsequium amicos, veritas odiū parit.
units.tr: Compliance makes friends, truth makes hatred.

units.la: Molesta veritas est, siquidē ex ea na-scitur odium, qp[?] est venenum amicitiæ: sed obsequiū multo molestius, qp[?] peccatis indulgens, præcipitē amicū ferre finit. Maxima autem culpa in eo est, qui & veritatem aspernatur, & in fraudem obsequio impellitur. Omnis igitur hac in re habēda ratio, & diligentia est: primum, ut monitio acerbitate: deinde, ut obiurgatio cōtumelia careat. In ob-sequio autē (quoniam Terentiano verbo libēter utimur) comitas absit, assen-tatio vitiorū adjutrix procul amovea-tur: quæ non modò amico, sed ne libe-ro quidem digna est. Aliter enim cum tyranno, aliter cum amico vivitur. Cu-jus autem aures clausæ veritati sunt, ut ab amico verum audire nequeat, huius salus desperāda est. Scitum est enim illud Catonis: multo melius de quibusdam acerbos inimicos mereri, quā eos amicos, q dulces videantur: illos verū sæpè dicere, hos nūq[?]. Atq; aliud absurdum est:qp ii scilicet q monentur, eam molestiā,q̄ debet capere nō capiunt,eā capiunt qua debent carere. Peccasse.n. se nō angūtur,obiurgari molestē ferūt: qp cōtra oportebat, delicto dolore, obiurgatione gaudere.
units.tr: Truth is troublesome, since from it arises hatred, which is the poison of friendship: but compliance is much more troublesome, since it indulges in faults and lets a friend rush headlong to ruin. The greatest fault, however, lies in the one who both spurns the truth and is driven by compliance into deceit. In this matter, therefore, there must be a consideration and diligence: first, that admonition lack bitterness; then that rebuke lack insult. In compliance (since we gladly use Terence's word) let courtesy be absent, let flattery, the helper of vices, be far removed: which is worthy not only of a friend, but not even of a free man. For it is one thing to live with a tyrant, another with a friend. And whoever has ears closed to the truth, so that he cannot hear the truth from a friend, his salvation is to be despaired of. For that saying of Cato is apt: it is much better to deserve well of certain bitter enemies than of those friends who seem sweet: the former often tell the truth, the latter never. And another thing is absurd: that those who are admonished do not feel that trouble which they ought to feel, but feel that which they ought to be free from. For they are not grieved that they have sinned, but take it hard to be rebuked; whereas on the contrary they ought to rejoice in rebuke, with the fault grieved over.

units.la: Sed cum tot. Post explicatam veră doctrinam suo more digreditur Lælius in reprehensione hominum stultorum: q̄ natura monita surdis auribus prætereunt,& negligunt. Hanc vero hominum oscitantia & negligentia exaggerat adjunctus qbusdā amicitiæ,q̄ sunt varius et multiplex usus: multæ causæ suspicionum & offensionum, q̄ partim evitandæ, partim elevandæ, partim feredæ sunt. Nam & movendi. Causas suspicionū & offensionum multas esse pbat pprijs amicitiæ adjunctis: q̄ sunt monere, obiurgare: & hæc accipere amicè: si modo benevole fiant. Sed nescio. Propriis amicitiæ nunc quasi p[?]lepsin subiicit dictum Terentij: obsequium amicos veritas odium parit. Obiici enim poterat sententia hæc contra id qp sæpe monendi & objurgadi sint amici: illa autem objectio disputatur gradatione quadam logica ad hunc locum valde accomodata: cujus tres sunt gradus,qbus à minoribus ad maiora asceditur[?].
units.tr: But although so many... Having set out the true doctrine, Lælius, in his usual way, turns aside to rebuke foolish men, who pass by warnings given by nature with deaf ears and neglect them. Indeed, this carelessness and negligence of men Lælius heightens by adding the various and manifold uses of friendship: there are many causes of suspicions and offences, which must partly be avoided, partly lightened, and partly borne. For there are both the duty of moving... He shows that there are many causes of suspicion and offence in the very adjuncts of friendship, namely to admonish and to rebuke, and to receive these in a friendly spirit, provided they are done kindly. But I do not know... Now, by a kind of prolepsis, he introduces, as a proper adjunct of friendship, the saying of Terence: "Obsequiousness wins friends, truth breeds hatred." For this saying could be objected against the fact that friends must often be admonished and rebuked; but that objection is discussed by a certain logical gradation, very well suited to this place, of which there are three steps, by which one ascends from the lesser to the greater.

units.la: 1. Molesta inqt, est veritas: ratio additur ab effecto: qa ex ea nascitur odium: qp odium augetur adjuncto p metaphoram: odiū venenū, id est, interitus amicitiae est. 2. Sed molestius obsequiū: ratio additur ab effectis: qa peccatū indulget, & amicum praecipitē ferri sinit. 3. Maxima autem culpa in eo est, q veritatem aspernatur, & obsequio se infraudem inducit patitur. Omnis igitur. Insequentibus docet, quaratione tribus istis malis occurratur, idque facit descriptione adjunctorū, quae cuiq; adesse debent. Monitio igitur careat acerbitate: objurgatio contumelia in obsequio suavitas adsit, assentatio pcul amoveatur: hoc q; postremum confirmatur argumento causarū, qa assentatio est causa adjuvans vitiorū: nec non argumento majorum: qa non modo amico, sed nelibero quidē digna est. Eum vero q verū ab amico audire nō potest notat suo adjuncto: est enim talis, cujus salus desperanda est. Quod confirmatur testimonio Catonis: q dixit inimicos acerbos de quibusdam melius mereri: q blandos amicos: idq; confirmavit contrarys factis: quia illi saepe verū dicunt, hi nunquā. Atq; illud. Concludit disputationem illius dicti reprehensione hominum, qui semp contrarium agunt: dolent illi monitione & obiurgatione, sed peccatis suis nō anguntur: q; contra fieri deberet.
units.tr: (1) Truth, he says, is troublesome: a reason is added from the effect, because hatred arises from it; and the hatred is intensified by the added metaphor: hatred is poison, that is, it is the destruction of friendship. (2) But obsequiousness is more troublesome: a reason is added from its effects, because it indulges sin and allows the friend to be carried headlong. (3) The greatest fault, however, lies in this, that one spurns the truth and suffers oneself to be led into flattery. Therefore, everything... In what follows he teaches by what method these three evils are to be met, and he does so by describing the adjuncts that each must have. Admonition, then, should be free of harshness; rebuke should be free of insult; in obsequiousness let there be kindness, and let flattery be kept far away. This last point is confirmed by an argument from causes, because flattery is a cause that promotes vices; and also by an argument from the greater, because it is worthy not only of a friend but not even of a free man. He who cannot hear the truth from a friend he marks by his own adjunct: for he is such a man whose salvation is to be despaired of. This is confirmed by the testimony of Cato, who said that bitter enemies deserve better of certain men than flattering friends; and he confirmed this by contrary facts: for the former often tell the truth, the latter never. And this he concludes with the saying... by a rebuke of men who always act to the contrary: they grieve at admonition and rebuke, yet are not stung by their own sins, when the reverse ought to happen.

units.la: Utigitur & monere, & moneri ppriū est vere amicitiæ: & alterū libere facere, nō asperè: alterū patienter accipere, nō repugnanter: sic habēdum est, nulla in amicitiis pestē esse maiore, q; adulatione, blanditias assentatione, q̈uis enim multis nominibus est hoc vitiū notan-dum leviū hominum, atq; fallacium, ad voluptate loquentium omnia, nihil ad veritate. Cum aut̄ omnium rerum simulatio est vitiosa(tollit.n.judicium veri, idq; adulterat)rum[?] amicitiæ repugnat maximè: delet enim veritatē, sine qua nomen amicitiæ valere nō poterit. Nā cū amicitiæ vis sit in eo, ut unusquisque animus fiat ē pluribus: qui fieri poterit, sine in uno quidē quoq; unus animus erit, idemq; semp sed varius, commutabilis, multiplex? Quid enim potest esse tā flexibile, tam devium, q̈ animus ejus, q̈ ad alterius nō modò sensū, ac voluntatem, sed etiā vultum, atq; nu tū cōvertitur? Negat qs? nego: aitaio[?]. Postremò imperavi egomet mihi omnia assentari, ut ait, idē Terentius: sed ille sub Gnatonis persona, quamici[?] genus ad hibere omnino levitatis est. Multi autē Gnatonū similes, cū sint loco, fortuna, fama superiores, horū est assentatio: molesta, cū ad vanitatē accessit authoritas.
units.tr: Therefore both to admonish and to be admonished is the mark of true friendship; and to do so freely, not harshly, and to receive it patiently, not with resistance. Thus it must be held that there is no greater pest in friendships than flattery, fawning and compliance; for although this vice is to be branded with many names, it belongs to light and deceitful men who speak everything for pleasure and nothing for truth. But since every kind of pretence is faulty (for it removes the judgement of the truth and corrupts it), it is especially opposed to friendship: it destroys truth, without which the name of friendship cannot hold. For since the strength of friendship lies in this, that out of many souls each becomes one, how can it come about, if in each one there is one soul, always the same but varying, changeable and manifold? For what can be so flexible, so inconstant, as the soul of a man who turns himself not only to another's feelings and will but also to his face and nods? Does someone deny it? I deny it: you assert it. Finally, I have ordered myself to agree with everything, as Terence also says; but he speaks in the person of Gnatho, and to adopt such a kind of person is altogether a mark of levity. Many who are like Gnatho, though they are superior in rank, fortune and reputation, practise this compliance, which is troublesome when authority is added to vanity.

units.la: Utigitur. Excurrit in reprehensionem assentationis: blanditiarum adulationis: in qua veritas esse non potest. Primum igitur argumentum sumitur a contrario comparatione parium tractato: Ut enim monere & moneri proprium est amicitiae, & alterum libere facere, non acerbe: alterum patienter accipere, non repugnanter: sic in amicitia nulla maior pestis est, quam adulatio, blanditia, assentatio: tot enim nominibus hoc vitium a Cicerone notatur. Consequens augetur descriptio subiecti[?] adulatorum ab adiunctis & factis: sunt enim homines leves & fallaces, atque ad voluptatem omnia loquuntur nihil ad veritatem. Cum autem omnium. Alterum argumentum sumitur a comparatione minorum: Simulatio vitiosa est cum in omnibus rebus, tu amicitiae repugnat maxime. Antecedes confirmatur ab effectis simulationis: tollit enim iudicium veri, idq; adulterat. Consequens primo probat ab effectis adulationis: tollit enim veritatem, sine qua amicitia esse non potest. Deinde a contrario: amicitia est simplex, animus vero assentatoris multiplex & varius: qp confirmatur ab effectis per comparationem minorum, & testimonio, sive exemplo Gnathonis Terentiani.
units.tr: Therefore... He runs into a rebuke of compliance and flattery, of fawning and flattering, in which truth cannot exist. The first argument is taken from the contrary, by comparison of equals: just as to admonish and to be admonished is proper to friendship, and to do so freely, not harshly, and to receive it patiently, not with resistance, so in friendship there is no greater pest than flattery, fawning and compliance; for Cicero marks this vice with so many names. The consequence is amplified by a description of flatterers' subject matter from its properties and deeds: for they are light and deceitful men, and they say everything for pleasure and nothing for truth. But since every kind of pretence... The second argument is taken from a comparison of lesser things: pretence is faulty, and it is especially opposed to friendship. The antecedent is confirmed from the effects of pretence: for it removes the judgement of the truth and corrupts it. The consequence first proves from the effects of flattery: for it removes the truth, without which friendship cannot exist. Then from the contrary: friendship is simple, but the soul of the flatterer is manifold and changeable; this is confirmed from effects by comparison of lesser things, and by the testimony or example of Terence's Gnatho.

units.la: Secerni autem blandus amicus à vero, & internosci tā potest, adhibita diligentia, q omnia fucata, & simulata à lynceris, atq; veris. Cōcio, quę ex imperitissimis cōstat tamen judicare solet, qd interfit inter popularē, id est, assentatorem, & leve civē & inter cōstantem, feverū, & grave. Quibus blanditiis C. Papyrius consul nuper influebat, in aures cōciones, cum ferret legem de Tribunis plebis reficiendis? Dissuasimus nos. Sed nihil de me, de Scipione dicam libentius. Quanta illi (Dii immortales) fuit gravitas, quanta in oratione majestas? ut facile duce pop. Rō. nō comitem diceres: sed affuistis, & est in manibus oratio. Itaq; lex popularis suffragiis populi repudiata est. Atq;(ut ad me re-dicā)[?] meministis Q.Maximo fratre Scipionis & L.Micino cōsulibus, q;popu-laris lex de sacerdotiis C. Licinii Crassi videbatur: cooptatio enim collegiorū ad populi beneficiū trāsferebatur. Atq; is primo instituit versibus agere cū populo. Tamē illius vendibile orationem religio deorū immortaliū, nobis defen-dentibus, facile vincebat. Atq; id actū est prætore me, quinquennio ante, q; cōsul sum factus. Itaq; re magis, q; authoritate causa illa defensa est. Quod si in scena, id est, in concione in qua rebus fictis, & adūbratis loci plurimum est: tamen verū valet, si modò id patefactum, & il-lustratum est: qd in amicitia fieri oportet, q; tota veritate ppenditur, in qua nisi, (ut dicitur) apertum pectus videas, tuūq; ostēdas, nihil fidum, nihil explo-ratum habeas ne amare quidem, aut a-mari possis, cum id q; vere fiat, ignores. Quanq; ista assentatio, quis pniciosa[?] sit, nocere tamen nemini potest, nisi ei, q; ea recipit, atq; ea delectatur. Itaq; fit, ut iy[?] assentatoribus suis aures patefaciat maximè, qipse sibi assentetur& se maximè ipse delectet. Omninò est amans sui virtus,optimè.n.se ipsa novit,quãq; amabilis sit intelligit.Ego autè non de virtute nunc loquor, sed de virtutis opinione. Virtute enim ipsa nō tā multi prædití esse, q videri volunt. Hos delec-tat assentatio: his fictus ad eorū voluptatē sermo cum adhibetur, oratione illā vanā testimonium esse laudum suarum putant.Nulla est igitur hæc amicitia,cùm alter verū audire nō vult, alter ad mentiendum paratus est,nec parasitorū in comœdiis assentatio nobis facceta viderctur, nisi esset milites gloriosi.
units.tr: A flattering friend can be separated from a true one, and distinguished, with proper diligence, just as things painted and feigned are distinguished by the sharp-eyed from the genuine. A sermon, which consists of the most unskilled people, is nevertheless accustomed to judge what difference there is between a popular man, that is, a flatterer, and a light citizen, and between a steady, severe and serious one. With what flatteries did Gaius Papirius the consul lately pour into the ears of the assemblies, when he brought forward the law concerning the reform of the tribunes of the plebs? We opposed him. But I will speak of nothing more gladly than of Scipio. What gravity he had, O immortal gods, what majesty in his speech! So that you would call the Roman people easily led, not a companion; you were present, and the speech is in your hands. Thus the popular law was rejected by the votes of the people. And (to return to myself) you remember that in the consulship of Quintus Maximus, brother of Scipio, and Lucius Micinius, a popular law concerning priesthoods of Gaius Licinius Crassus seemed to be proposed: for the co-option of colleges was transferred to the benefit of the people. And he first began to act with the people in verses. Yet the religion of the immortal gods, defended by us, easily overcame that saleable speech of his. And this was done when I was praetor, five years before I was made consul. Thus that cause was defended more by the matter than by authority. But if in the theatre, that is, in an assembly in which much place is given to feigned and shadowy things, truth nevertheless prevails, provided it has been laid open and made clear; this must be done in friendship, which is weighed by the whole truth, in which, unless (as they say) you see an open breast and show yourself, you have nothing faithful, nothing tested; you cannot even love, or be loved, since you do not know what is truly done. Although how pernicious this flattery is, it can harm no one except the man who receives it and takes delight in it. Thus it comes about that he especially opens his ears to his flatterers, and most of all flatters himself and takes the greatest delight in himself. In short, virtue is a lover of itself, for it knows itself best and understands how lovable it is. But I am speaking now not of virtue, but of the opinion of virtue. For many do not wish to be thought of as virtuous, as they are in fact not so. Flattery delights these men: when feigned talk is brought in for their pleasure, they think that such vain speech is a testimony to their praises. There is therefore no friendship here, since one does not wish to hear the truth and the other is ready to lie; nor would the flattery of parasites in comedies seem witty to us, were it not that the soldiers are boastful.

units.la: Magnas verò agere gratias Thais mihi?
units.tr: "Do you truly give me great thanks, Thais?"

units.la: Saris[?] erat respõdere,magnas:ingentes,inquit.Semper augetur[?] assentatio id, qꝑ is[?], cujus ad voluntatem dicitur, vult esse magnum. Quamobrem quamvis blanda ista vanitas apud eos valeat, qui ipsi illam allectant, & invitant, tamen etiam graviores, constantioresq; admonendi sunt, utanimadverrā[?]: nec callida assentatione capiantur. Aperte enim adulantem nemo nō videt, nisi q admodum est excors. Callidus ille & occultus ne se insinuet, studiose cavendum est: nec enim facile agnoscitur, quippe qui etiam adversando saepe assentetur: & litigare se simulans, blandiatur, atque ad extremum det manus, vinciq; se patiatur, ut is, q illusus sit, plus vicisse videatur. Quid autē turpius, quā illudi? Quod ne accidat magis cavendum est, ut in Epicureo:
units.tr: It was the duty of the slave to answer "great": "huge," he says. Flattery always magnifies whatever he wants to be great, to whose will it is spoken. Therefore, although that smooth vanity prevails among those who themselves invite and entice it, yet the more serious and steadier men must also be admonished, so that they may take heed and not be caught by crafty flattery. For no one fails to see a flatterer who is openly so, unless he is quite senseless. The crafty and hidden one, who creeps in, must be guarded against with care; for he is not easily recognised, since he often flatters even by opposing, and pretending to quarrel he fawns, and at last gives way and lets himself be overcome, so that the one who has been deceived seems to have gained more. But what is more shameful than to be made a fool of? That this may not happen, one must be more careful, as in the Epicurean:

units.la: Hodie me ante omneis coamicos stul-tos senes Versaris, atq; luseris lautissime.
units.tr: Today you have made fools of me, your elderly co-friends, and played with us most lavishly.

units.la: Haec etiam in fabulis stultissima persona est im,puidorum[?] & credulorū se-num. Sed nescio quo pacto ab amicitiis pfectorum[?] hominum, id est, sapientum, (de hac dico sapientia, q videtur in hominem cadere posse) ad leves amicitias defluxit oratio.
units.tr: In stories, this is the most foolish role of the unwary and credulous old men. But somehow, by some means, my speech has slipped from the friendships of perfected men, that is, of the wise (I mean that wisdom which seems able to fall upon a human being), down to light friendships.

units.la: Secerni autem. Hactenus assentationè vitium detestabile esse quibusdam argumentis probavit: nunc rationem & modum secernendi blandum amicum, i. assentatore à vero ostendit. Proponit autem hanc rem argumento adiunctorum per comparationem parium: Tam facile est secernere assentatorem ab amico, & internoscere, q omnia fucata & simulata a sinceris atq; veris. In hac vero p-positione exprimitur etiam causa secernedi, quae est diligetia. Concio quae. Cosequens probat exemplo vulgi, & imperitissimorum hominum: qi iudicare solent quid interfit inter assentatorem & levem cive & inter constantem, severum & gravem. Concionis. Metonymia subiecti, concio pp populo q in cocione versatur. Quibus blanditiis. Vulgi exemplum confirmat duobus contrariis exemplis C. Papyrii cosulis blandi & levis, & Scipionis viri gravis & constantis: nam illius blanda sententia repudiata: huius vero gravis oratio approbata fuit. Atq; (ut ad me.) Proponit duo alia exempla Lalij & C. Licinij Crassi: quorum prior populi suffragiis sua sententiam grave obtinuit: posterior vero, quamvis valde popularis fuerit eius oratio & vendibilis, victus abiit. Quod si in scena. Concludit exemplum vulgi argumento minorum: Quod si in scena verum valet: quato magis id in amicitia fieri debet. Vtraq; pars argumenti augetur suis adiunctis: Scenae ad-ficta sunt res ficta & adubrata[?]: Amicitia verò veritas & apertum pectus. Quãquam. Per correctionem exponit subiecti cui nocere potest assentatio: id autem est homo qui ea recipit, atq; ea delectatur: q ipse sibi assentatur, & se maximè ipse delectet. Omnino.
units.tr: Now, to separate them. Up to this point he has shown by certain arguments that the vice of flattery is detestable. Now he shows the method and manner of distinguishing a flattering friend, that is, a flatterer, from the true one. He sets this out by an argument from adjuncts, through comparison of like things: it is as easy to separate a flatterer from a friend and to tell apart what is feigned and pretended from what is sincere and true. In this proposition the cause of separating is also expressed, which is diligence. Assembly, which... He proves the consequence by the example of the common crowd and the most inexperienced people, who are accustomed to judge what difference there is between a flatterer and a light citizen, and between a steadfast, severe and serious man. Of the assembly: a metonymy of the subject, the people who are engaged in the assembly. With which flatteries: he confirms the example of the crowd with two contrary examples, that of Gaius Papirius, the consul, flattering and light, and that of Scipio, a man serious and steadfast; for the flattering opinion of the former was rejected, but the serious speech of the latter was approved. And (as to me): he sets out two other examples, of Laelius and of Gaius Licinius Crassus; of whom the former, by the votes of the people, carried his serious opinion, but the latter, although his speech was very popular and saleable, departed defeated. But if on the stage: he concludes the example of the crowd with an argument from the lesser: if truth prevails on the stage, how much more ought it to happen in friendship. Each part of the argument is enlarged by its adjuncts: on the stage, things are feigned, and the fictions are adorned; but friendship is truth and an open heart. Although: by correction he sets out the subject whom flattery can harm: this is a man who receives it and delights in it, who flatters himself and most takes pleasure in himself. Altogether.

units.la: Prolepsis: obiici poterat: at virtus est amans sui, seipsam optimè novit, & quàm amabilis sit intelligit, ac propterea sui laudatione libentissimè audit. Respondet Cicero p distinctione amoris sui, alia enim est φιλαυτία[?] virtutis non reprehendenda: virtus enim nullam aliam mercedem suorum laborum exigit praeter hanc laudis, & gloriæ. Alia deinde est persuasionis & opinionis virtutis, quā hoc loco notat Cicero. Nec parasitorum.
units.tr: Prolepsis: it could be objected: but virtue is a lover of itself; it knows itself best and understands how lovable it is, and therefore hears its own praise most gladly. Cicero replies by a distinction of self-love: for there is one kind of self-love of virtue that is not to be blamed, since virtue demands no other reward for its labours besides this praise and glory. Then there is another kind, of persuasion and opinion of virtue, which Cicero here marks. Nor of parasites.

units.la: Alia prolepsis: obiici poterat at grata est in comœdys persona gnathonum. Huic obiectioni occurrit Cicero argumento subiecti: explicat enim verum & opportunum hominum genus, circa quos versantur assentatores, qui sunt non viri graves & constantes, sed milites gloriosi. Nam Gnatho, inquit, Hieronymus Wolfius, sic tractaret Socratē aut Catonem non modò nō facetus, sed & improbissimus, & stolidissimus haberetur. Gloriosis autem militibus maximè convenire assentatores probat ab esse-ctu stu[?]:quia semper augent id, qp is, ad cuius voluptatem dicitur, vult esse magnū: idq; rursus confirmat exemplo Gnathonis:qui Thaidis gratiarum actionem amplificat argumento minorū hoc modo:Non est qp dubites Thaidē agere magnas gratias cum egat ingentes. Quamobrem. Correctio eius qp supra dixit, assentationem ijs tantum nocere qui eā allectant,per distinctionem adulatoris:alius enim est apertus, quem nemo non videt, nisi qui admodum est excors:alius vero callidus & occultus,quibus etiam graviores & praestantiores,nisi sibi caveant, circumveniuntur. Idq; pbat descriptione callidi adulatoris ab effectu: Callidus enim adulator est, qui etiam adversando sæpe assentitur, & litigando blanditur, & ad extremum manus dat, vinciq; se patitur. Hoc postremū amplificat à fine. Ut is qui illusus sit plus vicisse videatur: quem finem rursus amplificat argumento parium ꝑ negatione imparis: nihil est turpius quam illudi, id quod confirmatur exemplo & testimonio Epicureorum,nec non persona improvidorum & credulorum senum, qua in fabulis stultissima est.
units.tr: Another prolepsis: it could be objected: but the character of the flatterers is pleasing in comedies. Cicero meets this objection with an argument from the subject: he explains the true and fitting class of men around whom the flatterers move, who are not serious and steadfast men but boastful soldiers. For Gnatho, he says, as Hieronymus Wolfius says, would not merely be considered witty, but also most wicked and most stupid, if he treated Socrates or Cato in that way. He proves that flatterers belong most of all to boastful soldiers from the effect: because they always magnify whatever he wishes to be great, to whose pleasure they speak; and this he again confirms by the example of Gnatho, who magnifies Thais' thanks with an argument from the lesser in this way: there is no doubt that Thais gives great thanks, since she is given great things. Wherefore. The correction of what he said above: flattery harms only those who entice it, by a distinction of the flatterer: for one is open, whom no one fails to see except one who is very foolish; another is clever and hidden, by whom even men who are more serious and outstanding are, unless they take care, circumvented. And he proves this by a description of the clever flatterer from his effect: for the clever flatterer is one who often agrees even while opposing, and flatters while disputing, and at last gives way and allows himself to be bound, so that he who was deceived seems to have prevailed more. He enlarges this last point from its end: so that the one who was deceived seems to have prevailed more; and he again enlarges this end by an argument from like things through the negation of unlike: nothing is more shameful than to be deceived; which is confirmed by the example and testimony of the Epicureans, and also by the character of the unwary and credulous old men, who is most foolish in stories.

units.la: Quamobrē ad illa prima redeamus, caq;ipsa cōcludamus aliquādo. Virtus, inquam, C. Fanni, & tu Q. Muti, & conciliat amicitias & confervat, in ea est enim coveniētia rerum, in ea stabilitas, in ea cōstantia. Quæ cum se extulit, & ostendit tamē suum & idem aspexit, agnovitq; in alio, ad id se admovet, vicifsimq́ue illud accipit, ꝗ in altero est: ex quo eorū ardescit sive amor, sive amicitia utrumq; enim dictum est ab amā-do. Amare autem nihil aliud est, nisi eū ipsum diligere, quem ames, nulla indigentia, nulla utilitate quæsita. Quæ tamen ipsa eflorecit ex amicitia, etiam si tu eā minus sequutus sis. Hac nos adolescētes benevoletia senes illos L. Paulum, M. Catonem, C. Gallum, P. Nasicam, T. Gracchum Scipionis nostri socerum dilexīmus. Hæc etiam magis elucet inter æquales, ut inter me, & Scipionem, L. Furium, P. Rutilium, Sp. Mummium. Vicissim autē senes in adolescētiā charitate acquiescimus, ut in vestra, & in Q. Tuberonis, equidē admodum adolescētis, & P. Rutilij, A. Virginij familiaritate delector. Quandoquidē.n. ita ratio coparata est vitæ, naturæq; no-stræ, ut alia ætas oriatur ex alia, maxime quidem optādum est, ut cū æqualibus possis vivere, quibuscum tanquā e carceribus emissus, cūm iisdem ad calcem (ut dicitur) pervenire possis.) Sed quoniā res humanæ fragiles, caducæq; sunt, semper aliqui sunt inquirēdi, quos diligamus, & à quibus diligamur. Charitate enim, benevolentiaq; sublata, omnis est è vita sublata jucunditas. Mihi quidem Scipio, quāquā subito est ereptus, vivit tamē, semperq; vivet. Virtute enim semper amavi illius viri, quæ extincta non est: nec mihi soli ante oculos versatur, quī illā semper in manibus habui: sed etiam posteris erit clara, & insignis.
units.tr: Wherefore let us return to those first things and at some time conclude them themselves. Virtue, I say, Gaius Fannius, and you, Quintus Mucius, both wins friendships and preserves them; for in it is the agreement of things, in it stability, in it constancy. When it has displayed itself, and has shown its own and has seen the same in another, and has recognised it there, it draws itself toward that, and in turn receives from the other what is in him; from this there kindles either love or friendship, for both are named from loving. To love, moreover, is nothing other than to cherish him whom you love, with no need and no advantage sought. Yet this very thing springs forth from friendship, even if you have followed it less. By this goodwill we, as young men, loved those old men, Lucius Paulus, Marcus Cato, Gaius Gallus, Publius Nasica, Tiberius Gracchus, the father-in-law of our Scipio. This also shines out more among equals, as between me and Scipio, Lucius Furius, Publius Rutilius, Spurius Mummius. In turn, we old men find rest in the affection of the young: as I, indeed, a man very young, delight in the familiarity of you and of Quintus Tubero, and of Publius Rutilius, and of Aulus Virginius. For since reason is so arranged for life and for our nature, that one age arises out of another, it is most of all to be wished that you may live with your equals, with whom, as if sent out from the starting gates, you may come together to the goal (as it is said) with the same people. But since human affairs are fragile and perishable, there are always some whom we must seek to love and by whom we must be loved. For with affection and goodwill taken away, all the pleasantness is taken away from life. To me indeed, Scipio, although he was suddenly snatched away, yet lives, and will always live. For I have always loved the virtue of that man, which has not been extinguished; nor does it dwell before my eyes alone, who always had it in my hands; but it will also be bright and distinguished for posterity.

units.la: Nemo unquam animo, aut spe majora suscipiet, qui sibi nō illius memoriam, atq; imaginē proponendā putet. Equidem ex omnibus rebus, quas mihi aut fortuna, aut natura tribuit, nihil habeo ꝑ[?] cum amicitia Scipionis possit cōparari. In hac mihi de Republ. fuit consen-sus, in hac rerum privatarū consiliū, in eadē requies plena oblectationis fuit: nunquàm illum ne minima quidem re offendi quod quidem senserim: nihil audivi ex eo ipse, quod nollem. Vna domus erat, idem victus, ifq; communis: neq; solum militia, sed etiam peregrinationes, rusticationesq; communes. Nam qd ego de studiis dica cognoscendi semper aliquid, atq; discendi? in quibus remoti ab oculis populi omne otiū tempusq; cōtrivimus. Quarum rerum recordatio, & memoria, si una cum illo occidisset, desiderium cōiunctissimi viri, atq; amantissimi ferre nullo modo possem.Sed nec illa extincta sunt, alunturq; potius, & augentur cogitatione, & memoria, & si illis plane orbatus essem, magnum tamē afferret mihi ætas ipsa solatium,diutius enim,in hoc desiderio esse non possum.Omnia autem brevia, tolerabilia esse debent,etiam si magna sint.Hæc habui de amicitia,quę dicerem. Vos autem hortor, ut ita locetis virtutem (sine qua amicitia esse non potest) ut ea excepta,nil amicitia præstabilius esse putetis.
units.tr: No one will ever undertake greater things in mind or hope who does not think that the memory and image of that man should be set before himself. Indeed, of all the things that either fortune or nature has given me, I have nothing that can be compared with the friendship of Scipio. In this there was for me agreement about the commonwealth, in this counsel about private affairs, and in the same there was a repose full of delight; I never offended him in even the smallest matter, so far as I perceived; I never heard from him anything that I would not have wished. We had one house, the same food, and a common table, and not only in military service but also in journeys and country sojourns we were together. For what shall I say of our studies, of always learning and coming to know something? In these, withdrawn from the eyes of the people, we spent all our leisure and time. If the recollection and memory of these things had perished together with him, I could in no way bear the longing for a most closely joined and most loving man. But neither have those things been extinguished; rather they are nourished and increased by thought and memory; and even if I were wholly bereft of them, age itself would bring me great consolation, for I cannot remain long in this longing. Moreover, all things that are brief should be bearable, even if they are great. These are the things I had to say about friendship. But I urge you to value virtue (without which friendship cannot exist) in such a way that, virtue excepted, you may think nothing more excellent than friendship.

units.la: Quamobrem. Conclusio disputationis de amide amicitia, in qua duo agit: primò in genere de amicitia disputat: deinde specialiter de amicitia, quae fuit inter ipsum & Scipionem disserit. Virtus. Hoc est primum membrum, in quo duo observantur: primò causa amicitiae deinde vera amicitiae exempla. Causa amicitiae procreans & conservans est virtus: quod probatur eius adjunctis, & factis: adjuncta sunt convenientia rerum, stabilitas, constantia: facta explicantur argumento relatorum: sunt autem seipsam efferre, lumen suum ostendere, & idem aspicere, agnoscere[?] in alio, ad idse admovere, vicissimq; accipere illud quod est in altero: unde exardescit amor sive amicitia: quae Ciceroni idem sunt: quod probatur notatione, & definitione: utrumq; enim dicitur ab amando: amare autem nihil aliud est quam eum ipsum diligere quem ames, nulla indigentia, nulla utilitate quaesita. Hac nos adolescentes. Exempla amicitiae duplicia sunt ratione subiecti aliquando.n.est inter adolescetes & senes adolescentes.n.interdum senes diligunt, ut Lælius L.Paulum et reliquos: quaequuntur in textu: aliquando senes in charitate adolescentum acquiescunt, ut Lælius in charitate suorum generorum, & aliorum: Aliquando est inter aequales, ut inter Lælium & Scipiones, Lucium Furium, &c.Hanc autem praestantio-rem esse docet egregio simili à cursoribus desumpto: sed alteram quoq; colendam esse probat adjuncto rerum humanarum: quoniam res humanæ fragiles & caducæ sunt, semper aliqui acquirendi, quos diligamus, & à quibus diligamur. Mihi quidem, Alterum conclusionis membrum, quo primo commendat Scipionem ab adjuncta virtute: deinde amicitiam extollit & laudat à distributione subiecti, in quo versata est. Atq; hæc est ana-lysis logica dialogi de amicitia. Deus omnis scientiæ fons & author logicæ studium in animis hominum quotidie magis atq; magis accedat: quod ex animo precor.
units.tr: Therefore. The conclusion of the disputation on friendship, in which the author does two things: first he disputes about friendship in general; then he treats specifically the friendship that existed between himself and Scipio. Virtue. This is the first member, in which two things are observed: first the cause of friendship, then the true examples of friendship. The cause that produces and preserves friendship is virtue, which is proved by its attendants and deeds. The attendants are the agreement of things, stability, and constancy; the deeds are explained by the argument of what is related. They are: to show oneself forth, to display one's own light, to see the same thing in another and recognise it, to draw it to oneself, and in turn to receive what is in the other; from this love or friendship is kindled, which for Cicero are the same thing. This is proved by the etymology and the definition: for each word is derived from loving. To love is nothing other than to cherish the very person whom you love, with no need sought and no advantage pursued. Friends such as we, young men. Examples of friendship are twofold in respect of their subject: sometimes it is between young men and old men, the young sometimes loving the old, as Laelius loved Lucius Paulus and the rest, who are named in the text; sometimes the old find their delight in the affection of the young, as Laelius did in the affection of his sons-in-law and others. Sometimes it is between equals, as between Laelius and the Scipios, Lucius Furius, etc. He shows that the latter kind is the more excellent by an apt simile taken from runners; but he proves that the other kind too is to be cultivated, by the attendant circumstance of human affairs: since human affairs are fragile and perishable, we must always acquire some people whom we may love and by whom we may be loved. For my part, [the second member of the conclusion, by which he first commends Scipio from his attendant virtue, then extols and praises friendship from the distribution of the subject in which it was exercised. And this is the logical analysis of the dialogue on friendship. May the God, the fount of all knowledge and author of logic, increase the zeal for it in the minds of men more and more each day: this I pray from my heart.]
